What this computer is now

This laptop now runs The Complete Secure Linux Package. The Full Fedora profile uses the KDE Plasma desktop; Lite uses Xfce, Min uses LXQt, and the Debian routes have their own desktop choices. See the compatibility and profile chapters before choosing a route for another computer.

Three ideas shaped everything on this machine:

  • Privacy first. The package does not add a Microsoft account, Copilot or advertising-driven Start-menu entries. Online accounts, apps and network services still have their own privacy terms and behaviour.
  • Secure by default. The whole drive is encrypted. A firewall blocks incoming connections. Updates install themselves. Many smaller protections run quietly in the background.
  • Open-source apps. Most included programs are free and open source. Optional services, such as a VPN account, can require a separate paid subscription.

It will feel different from Windows 11 at first. That is normal. The basics are similar: a panel at the bottom, an app menu in the corner, and windows you can drag and resize.

How to use this guide

  • Read this chapter first. It ends with the ten things to do in your first hour.
  • Read "Your disk-encryption password" next. It is the one thing you must not get wrong.
  • Dip into the rest when you need it. "Linux basics for Windows users" is the best place to start learning. "Troubleshooting" is there for when something goes wrong.
  • Looking for something? Type a word into the search box at the top of this page ("printer", "VPN", "backup") and every chapter and app guide that mentions it appears. On the computer itself, press the Meta key and type the same word: the guide is searchable from the app launcher too. If an error message baffles you, copy it (Ctrl+C) and open Explain This Error from the app menu.
  • Honest labels. Where something has not been tried on real hardware yet, or has a limit, the guide says so in a shaded box marked "Honest note". Where there is a choice, the pros and cons are given.
  • Text that looks like this is a command. You type it into the terminal (an app called Konsole; open it with Ctrl+Alt+T). Press Enter to run it.
  • Commands that start with sudo change the system. They ask for your login password. Nothing appears on screen while you type it. That is normal. Type it and press Enter.
  • Where a command shows something in angle brackets, like <your-username>, replace the whole thing (brackets included) with your own value.

There is also a file called SETUP-REPORT.txt on your Desktop. It was written when the automatic setup finished. Open it now. Look at the section called Problems. If it is empty, everything installed correctly. If it lists anything, see "App installs failed during setup" in the Troubleshooting chapter.

The 10 things to do in your first hour

Work through these in order. Each one only has to be done once.

  1. Reboot. Click the app menu, then the power button, then Restart. This finishes the setup. For example, it adds you to the group that is allowed to control the VPN. When the computer starts, type your disk-encryption password, then your login password.
  2. Turn on the VPN. Open the terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) and run these three commands, one at a time:
    Terminal
    nordvpn login
nordvpn set killswitch on
nordvpn set autoconnect on
    nordvpn login opens a sign-in page in your browser. Sign in to your NordVPN account there. The kill switch is NordVPN's upstream feature for limiting traffic if the VPN connection drops; this guide has not independently verified leak protection. Autoconnect asks the VPN to connect when you start the computer. Check it worked with nordvpn status. If the VPN stops your phone or home server from talking to the laptop, see "The VPN blocks my home network" in Troubleshooting.
  3. Add Bitwarden to your browser. Your web browser is LibreWolf, a privacy-focused version of Firefox. It already includes the uBlock Origin ad blocker. Open LibreWolf, go to addons.mozilla.org, search for Bitwarden and click Add to LibreWolf. Sign in to your Bitwarden account. Bitwarden will now fill in your passwords. The Bitwarden desktop app is also installed if you prefer a separate window.
  4. Sign in to your everyday apps. Open each one from the app menu and sign in:
    • Tuta: encrypted email and calendar.
    • Signal: private messaging. It links to Signal on your phone by scanning a QR code.
    • Ente Auth: your two-factor (2FA) codes. Sign in with your Ente account so your codes sync from your phone.
    • Steam: games. Your Windows games that support Linux, plus many that run through Steam's Proton, will appear in your library.
  5. Pair your phone. Install these apps on your phone, then connect each one to the laptop while both are on the same Wi-Fi:
    • KDE Connect: shows phone notifications on the laptop, shares the clipboard, sends files, and lets your phone act as a remote. On the laptop, open KDE Connect from the app menu or the system tray, choose your phone, click Request pairing, and accept on the phone.
    • LocalSend: like AirDrop. Open it on both devices and they find each other.
    • Syncthing (on Android, the app is called Syncthing-Fork): keeps folders in sync between devices without any cloud. On the laptop, open http://localhost:8384 in LibreWolf to see Syncthing's control page. Add the phone's device ID, then choose which folders to share.
  6. Compare models in Private AI. Open Private AI and review the maintained catalogue, or run secure-linux-ai route --workload balanced. The router checks feasible fit before using same-device decode measurements as interactive tie-breakers; it does not guess speed from parameter count, RAM or GPU presence. Download only after review. Alpaca can then connect to the same Ollama instance for chat.
  7. Meet Network protection. It watches which apps use the internet. The first time a brand-new app wants to go online, a small window asks once, and Always allow is already picked, so one click on Allow is enough. Apps that came with this computer are already approved, so you will rarely see the window. It also blocks websites known for malware, phishing and tracking; if it ever blocks something you need, a message offers Allow once, Always allow and Keep blocked. Open Network Monitor from the app menu to look around. The chapter "Network Monitor: which apps may go online" explains the rules and troubleshooting. Read each prompt rather than relying on an old timeout claim.
  8. Set up Pika Backup. Plug in an external drive. Open Pika Backup, create a new backup on that drive, and turn on a schedule. The "Backups" chapter explains this in detail. Do it today. A laptop without a backup is one accident away from losing everything.
  9. Optional: Cloudflare WARP / Zero Trust. Only if you use Cloudflare Zero Trust (for example, for work or to reach your home server). Run warp-cli registration new <your-team-name> and follow the sign-in page. Use either NordVPN or WARP at one time, not both. Running two VPN clients together can cause routing conflicts.
  10. Move your Google Photos to Immich. If you have a home server running Immich, you can bring your whole Google Photos library across. Download your photos from Google Takeout as .zip files. In the Immich web page, go to your account settings and create an API key. Then, in the folder holding the zips, run:
    Terminal
    immich-go upload from-google-photos --server=<IMMICH_URL> --api-key=<KEY> takeout-*.zip
    Replace <IMMICH_URL> with your server's address, such as http://192.168.1.50:2283. It keeps albums and dates. Large libraries can take hours; leave it running. There is a guided version of this, with a test run first, in Bring My Stuff from Windows: see Google Photos to Immich.

Your first week, in short

The ten steps above are the essentials. These make the computer yours. Each has a short section in this guide, and every one can be skipped and done later.

  • The five-screen welcome opens at first login: recommended setup, identity/Wi-Fi/passwords, applications/protection, optional extras, then final review. Nothing changes until Confirm, and there is no countdown. Run it again from Welcome & Setup Choices; open the longer migration and server topics only when needed. See the welcome wizard.
  • Bring My Stuff from Windows moves your passwords, bookmarks, photos, OneDrive, notes and more. See Bringing your stuff over from Windows.
  • Make a disk recovery key and print your Emergency Kit (recovery key, Emergency Kit).
  • Run the Hardware Check (2 minutes) so a faulty speaker, microphone or camera shows up now: Hardware Check.
  • Glance at Secure Linux Status & Fixes (green, orange and red dots): the Status window.
  • Read the daily tips that appear for 14 days: tips of the day.

Two more good habits

  • Run a security check-up now and then: sudo lynis audit system. It prints suggestions. Many are aimed at servers, so you don't need to act on all of them.
  • Open Secure Linux Status & Fixes from the app menu when you wonder "is it OK?". Green means fine; orange or red has a Fix it button.
  • Check for firmware updates (BIOS, SSD, and so on) in Discover under Updates, or run fwupdmgr update.

Welcome. You already know more than you think.

If you have used Windows all your life, this chapter is for you. You have never seen Linux before. That is completely fine.

Here is the good news. A computer is still a computer. There is a bar along the bottom of the screen. There is a menu in the corner. Windows open, close, minimise and resize. Ctrl+C still copies and Ctrl+V still pastes. Most of your habits will just work.

What changes are mostly the names. Windows calls something "File Explorer". Here it is called "Dolphin". It does the same job. This chapter is a translation guide. Each section says "On Windows you did this. Here you do that."

A few words you will see a lot:

  • Linux is the engine underneath, like the engine in a car. You rarely see it.
  • Fedora is the complete system built on that engine. Think of it as "the make of car".
  • KDE Plasma (version 6) is the desktop: the panel, menus, windows and settings you look at and click. Think of it as the dashboard and seats.
  • Xfce is a lighter desktop used on older PCs (the "lite" setup). It is simpler and uses less memory. Where it differs, this chapter says so in a short note.

Take it slowly. Nothing you click in the normal desktop will break the computer. If you get stuck, the last sections of this chapter tell you exactly where to look.

Your first 5 minutes: the desktop at a glance

Look at the screen. You will recognise the layout straight away.

On Windows you had...Here you have...What it does
The taskbar at the bottomThe panel at the bottomShows open apps, pinned apps, the clock and small status icons. Same idea, different name.
The Start buttonThe app launcher (the icon at the far left of the panel)Click it to see your apps, search, and the power options (sleep, restart, shut down).
The system tray (bottom right, by the clock)The system tray (bottom right, by the clock)Wi-Fi, sound volume, battery, Bluetooth, clipboard, and background apps like KDE Connect. Click the small up-arrow to see hidden icons.
Notifications (Action Center)Notifications (the bell icon in the system tray)Messages pop up in the bottom-right corner. Missed ones wait under the bell. You can turn on Do Not Disturb there too.
The Windows keyThe Meta key (the same physical key)Linux calls it "Meta" or "Super" because it isn't Microsoft's key here. Press it on its own to open the app launcher, just like Start.
The desktop with iconsThe desktop with iconsFiles you save to the Desktop folder appear here. Right-click the desktop for options like changing the wallpaper.

Try this now: press the Windows/Meta key. The app launcher opens. Type dolphin and press Enter. The file manager opens. Congratulations: you have just used Linux.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: the layout is similar, but simpler. The menu is usually called the Whisker Menu. The panel may be at the top or bottom. Everything still works the same way: click the menu, find the app, open it.

Where things are: the big translation table

This is the most useful table in the chapter. When you think "where is the Windows thing for this?", look here. The easiest way to open any of these is to press the Meta key and start typing the name.

The system itself

On Windows you used...Here you use...How to find it
Start menuApp launcherClick the icon at the left of the panel, or press Meta.
Windows SearchKRunner, or just type in the launcherPress Alt+Space and a search bar drops down from the top of the screen. Type an app name, a file name, or even a sum like 12*7. Or press Meta and start typing.
Settings and Control PanelSystem SettingsOne app replaces both. Search "System Settings" in the launcher. It has its own search box at the top left. Use it: it is faster than browsing.
Task ManagerMission Center (also KDE's System Monitor)Mission Center looks a lot like Task Manager. It shows CPU, memory, disk and network use, and lets you end a stuck app. Ctrl+Esc opens KDE's System Monitor, which does the same job.
File ExplorerDolphinPress Meta+E, the same shortcut as Win+E.
This PC and drive letters (C:, D:)No drive letters. Your Home folder and the sidebar in DolphinSee "Files and folders" below. USB sticks and extra drives appear in Dolphin's left sidebar.
Recycle BinTrashShown in Dolphin's sidebar. Deleting a file moves it to Trash. You can restore it from there.
Downloads, Documents, Pictures, Music, VideosThe same folders, inside your Home folderShown in Dolphin's sidebar under "Places".
Microsoft StoreDiscoverThe app store. Search, click Install. Free. No account needed.
Windows UpdateAutomatic updates, plus Discover > UpdatesUpdates install themselves every day. To check by hand, open Discover and click Updates.
Control Panel > Programs and FeaturesDiscover (Installed section) or WarehouseSee installed apps and remove ones you don't want.
Device ManagerMostly not needed. To look: System Settings > About this System, or the Info Center appDrivers for most hardware are built in. You don't hunt for them. See the note below.
Disk ManagementKDE Partition ManagerShows drives and partitions. Be careful in here, just like on Windows. Look, but don't change things unless you know why.
Command Prompt / PowerShellKonsole (the terminal)Press Ctrl+Alt+T, or search "Konsole". You don't need it for everyday use. See below.
Windows Security / DefenderA firewall, ClamAV antivirus, OpenSnitch, and the Secure Linux Status appSee "Security" below.
BitLockerLUKS disk encryptionYour whole drive is encrypted. You type the disk-encryption password every time you switch on.
System RestoreSnapshots, managed with Btrfs AssistantLets you undo a bad system update. Your own files are not touched.
File History / Windows BackupPika BackupBacks up your Home folder to an external drive. Set it up in your first week.

A note on drivers. On Windows you often downloaded drivers from a manufacturer's website. Here you almost never do. Drivers for Wi-Fi, sound, graphics, printers and most gadgets come with the system and update with it. If a device doesn't work, don't go looking for a "driver download". Ask for help instead (see "If you're stuck").

On the lite (Xfce) setup: the file manager is Thunar, the terminal is Xfce Terminal, and settings live in the Settings Manager. Mission Center is installed on both setups.

Everyday apps

All of these are free. Most are open source, which means anyone can check how they work. None of them show you adverts.

On Windows you used...Here you use...Notes
Edge or ChromeLibreWolfA privacy-focused version of Firefox. It blocks ads and trackers out of the box. This is your main browser.
A site that "only works in Chrome"Ungoogled ChromiumChrome without the Google tracking. Keep it for the odd site that misbehaves in LibreWolf.
Outlook (mail and calendar)TutaEncrypted email and calendar. Open the Tuta app and sign in.
Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint)LibreOffice (Writer, Calc, Impress)Opens and saves .docx, .xlsx and .pptx files. Simple documents look the same. Very complex layouts can shift a little, so check before you send.
NotepadKWriteA simple text editor. Kate is its bigger sibling for longer files and code; if it isn't there, install it from Discover.
Snipping ToolSpectaclePress the Print Screen key. Choose the whole screen, a window or a rectangle. You can draw arrows and highlights before saving.
PhotosGwenviewDouble-click any picture to open it. Use the arrow keys to flick through a folder.
Media Player / Films and TVVLCPlays almost any video or music file you throw at it.
PaintKrita for drawing, GIMP for editing photosKrita is great for sketching and painting. GIMP is closer to Photoshop.
PhotoshopGIMP (and Krita)Different menus, similar power. Give yourself time to learn it.
ClipchampKdenliveA full video editor. If you prefer Clipchamp, it runs in Ungoogled Chromium as a website.
OneDriveSyncthing, or your home serverSyncthing keeps folders in step between your devices directly, with no cloud company in the middle.
Phone LinkKDE ConnectPair your phone. See its notifications, send files, use it as a remote, share the clipboard. Install KDE Connect on the phone too.
Nearby SharingLocalSendLike AirDrop. Open it on both devices and send files over your Wi-Fi.
Xbox app / Game BarSteam for games, OBS Studio for recording and streamingSteam runs many Windows games on Linux automatically. See "Things that are different" for the exceptions.
OneNoteJoplinNotes and notebooks, with sync if you want it.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: to keep old PCs fast, fewer apps are installed. You will have LibreWolf, Tor Browser, LibreOffice Writer and Calc, VLC, KDE Connect, LocalSend, Syncthing, Bitwarden and Mission Center. The big creative apps and games are only on the main laptop.

Virtual desktops are like having several screens' worth of space. Put your email on one and your work on another. Windows has them too, but few people use them. Add more in System Settings (search "Virtual Desktops"). If a shortcut ever doesn't work, search "Shortcuts" in System Settings. You can see, and change, every shortcut there.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: Alt+Tab, Alt+F4, Ctrl+C/V and Print Screen work the same. Other shortcuts differ. Look in Settings Manager > Keyboard > Application Shortcuts.

Installing and removing apps the safe way

This is the biggest habit to change. Please read this section twice.

The Windows habit

On Windows you probably did this: search the web for an app, find a download page, download an .exe file, run it, click "Next" a few times. It worked, but it was risky. Fake download sites, bundled toolbars and malware all spread this way.

The new habit

Here you get apps from Discover, the built-in app store. Think of it like the app store on a phone.

  1. Open Discover from the app launcher.
  2. Type what you want in the search box. You can search for the name ("Spotify") or the job ("video editor").
  3. Click the app, read the description, and click Install.
  4. If a password box appears, type your login password. (More on this below.)
  5. The app appears in your app launcher. Done.

To remove an app, open Discover, click Installed, find the app and click Remove. Warehouse is another app that lists and removes apps, if you prefer it. Nothing is left behind cluttering the system, unlike some Windows uninstallers.

Why not just download from websites?

  • Never download .exe files. They are Windows programs. They won't run here by double-clicking. A random .exe is also the most common way malware spreads.
  • Apps from Discover are checked and kept up to date for you. A program installed from a random website won't update itself. Over time it becomes a security hole.
  • Most apps from Discover run in a "sandbox". That is a sealed box that limits what the app can touch. A badly behaved app can't easily reach the rest of your system.
  • Be wary of any website that says "paste this command into your terminal". That is the Linux version of a dodgy .exe. If you're not sure, ask first.

Some trusted companies do offer Linux downloads on their own websites (files ending in .rpm or .AppImage). Check Discover first. Nine times out of ten, the app is already there.

The odd Windows program: Bottles

Sometimes there is one small Windows program you really need. Maybe an old game or a tool for a gadget. Bottles can often run it. It creates a pretend mini-Windows (a "bottle") for the program to live in. Open Bottles, create a bottle, and run the program's installer inside it. It doesn't work for everything, especially big commercial apps. But it's worth a try before giving up.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: there may be no app store window. Ask whoever set up the computer to add an app for you, or see the "Linux basics" chapter for the flatpak install command.

Files and folders

Your Home folder

On Windows your files lived in C:\Users\YourName. Here they live in your Home folder, which is /home/yourname. Dolphin opens there by default. Inside are the folders you know: Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Music, Pictures, Videos.

Everything you own lives in Home. Keep your files there and you never need to go anywhere else. The rest of the system is in other folders. You can look, but you can't change things there without your password. That is a safety feature.

No drive letters

On Windows...Here...
C:\ is the main drive/ (called "root") is the top of everything. There is just one tree of folders.
C:\Users\Sam\Documents/home/sam/Documents
A USB stick appears as E:A USB stick appears in Dolphin's sidebar, under its own name (for example "SANDISK").
Paths use a backslash: \Paths use a forward slash: /, like web addresses
%USERPROFILE%~ (the tilde) is short for your Home folder. ~/Downloads means your Downloads folder.

Things that behave a little differently

  • Names are case-sensitive. Photo.jpg and photo.jpg are two different files here. On Windows they were the same. Just be consistent and you will never notice.
  • Hidden files start with a dot. A file called .config is hidden. Press Ctrl+H in Dolphin to show or hide them. Most hidden files are app settings. Leave them alone unless a guide tells you otherwise.
  • File extensions are still used. .pdf, .jpg, .docx all mean what they did before. Dolphin shows them by default, which helps you spot a fake. A file called invoice.pdf.exe is not a PDF.
  • Delete goes to Trash. Press Delete and the file moves to Trash, like the Recycle Bin. Shift+Delete deletes for good, with no way back. Avoid Shift+Delete until you're comfortable.
  • Double-click or single-click? Dolphin uses double-click to open, like Windows. If yours opens files on a single click, search "click" in System Settings to change it.
  • Type a path. Press Ctrl+L in Dolphin to type a folder location, just like clicking the address bar in File Explorer.

USB sticks and external drives

  1. Plug the drive in. A small notification appears, and the drive shows in Dolphin's sidebar.
  2. Click it to open it. Copy and paste files as normal.
  3. When you're done, click the small eject icon next to the drive's name in the sidebar. Wait until it disappears or says it's safe.
  4. Now unplug it.

Ejecting matters even more here than on Windows. Linux sometimes finishes writing in the background. Pull the drive out early and the last files you copied can be damaged.

Your Windows files still open

  • Windows-formatted drives work. USB sticks and external drives formatted on Windows (NTFS, exFAT or FAT32) open and can be written to.
  • Office files open in LibreOffice. PDFs open in the built-in viewer (Okular). Photos, music and videos open as you would expect.
  • Shortcuts (.lnk) and programs (.exe) won't work. Those are Windows-only.

Shared folders on your home network

On Windows you might have typed \\SERVER\Photos to reach a shared folder on another PC or a NAS box. Here, open Dolphin, press Ctrl+L, and type:

Terminal
smb://SERVER/Photos

Replace SERVER with the computer's name or its address (for example smb://192.168.1.20/Photos). Notice the forward slashes. Dolphin may ask for the share's username and password. To keep it handy, right-click an empty spot inside the shared folder and choose Add to Places. It then stays in the sidebar.

Passwords: which one is which?

This confuses almost everyone at first. There are only two passwords to remember, plus one kind of question.

When you see...Which passwordWhat it does
A plain screen right after switching on, asking for a passphrase to unlock the diskYour disk-encryption passwordUnlocks the encrypted drive, like BitLocker. Without it, nobody can read anything on the laptop, even if it's stolen. If you lose it, your data is gone for ever. Keep a paper copy somewhere safe at home.
The login screen with your name on itYour login passwordLogs you in to your account, like your Windows sign-in.
The lock screenYour login passwordSame as above.
A box saying "Authentication Required" when you install something or change a system settingYour login passwordThis is like the Windows "Do you want to allow this app to make changes?" box. Here it asks for your password, not just a "Yes" click.
A terminal saying [sudo] password for yourname:Your login passwordSame idea, in the terminal. As you type, nothing appears on screen: no dots, no stars. That is normal. Type it and press Enter.

What is "sudo"?

sudo means "do this as the administrator". Your everyday account can't change the core system on its own. That's deliberate: it stops a bad website or a buggy app from wrecking anything. When something genuinely needs to change the system, you are asked for your password. Typing it is you saying "yes, I really mean it".

When is it safe to type your password?

  • Safe: you just did something that obviously needs it. You clicked Install in Discover. You opened Btrfs Assistant. You ran a command from this guide that starts with sudo.
  • Stop and think: a password box pops up out of nowhere, while you weren't doing anything. Click Cancel. It's rarely dangerous, but there is no reason to approve something you didn't ask for. Ask about it later.
  • Never: a website asks for your computer's password. Websites never need it. Close the tab.
  • Never: a stranger, a forum post or a "support" caller tells you to type sudo followed by a long command you don't understand.

Updates: no more surprise restarts

You know the Windows routine. You're in the middle of something and Windows decides to restart. Or you shut down and see "Updating, don't turn off your computer" for 20 minutes. That doesn't happen here.

  • Updates install themselves quietly every day. System updates and app updates both happen in the background while you work.
  • The computer never restarts by itself. Not at night, not while you're working, not ever.
  • Some updates need a restart to take full effect. When that happens, a notification appears: "Restart to finish updates". Restart when it suits you: at lunch, at the end of the day, tomorrow. Try not to leave it more than a few days, because some security fixes only start working after a restart.
  • Restarting is quick. There is no long "Working on updates" screen on a normal restart. You type your disk-encryption password, log in, and carry on.
  • One place updates everything. On Windows, every app had its own updater: Chrome, Adobe, Java, Zoom... Here one system updates the whole computer and every app from Discover.

Want to check for updates by hand? Open Discover and click Updates. Or open Secure Linux Status and choose "Install all updates now".

About every six months a new version of Fedora comes out (45, then 46, and so on). That's a bigger upgrade, like going from Windows 10 to 11, but free and much quicker. Discover offers it under Updates. You will get a notification when it's time. You have a few months, so there's no rush.

If an update ever goes wrong (rare), the main laptop takes automatic snapshots. They let you roll the system back to how it was before. The "Backups" chapter explains how.

Security: what replaced Windows Defender

Windows Security bundled everything into one app. Here the same jobs are done by several small tools working together. You don't have to manage them. They run on their own.

Windows had...Here you have...What you'll notice
Windows FirewallA firewall (firewalld)Nothing. It blocks unwanted incoming connections silently.
Microsoft Defender antivirusClamAV (with the ClamTk window)It scans your Downloads folder once a week. If it finds something, you get a notification. Nothing is deleted without you deciding.
"Allow this app through the firewall?"Network protection (the Network Monitor window, made by OpenSnitch)The first time a brand-new app tries to go online, a small window asks once ("Always allow" is already picked). Apps that came with the computer are already approved, so you will rarely see it. It also blocks known malware, phishing and tracking sites. See "Network Monitor: which apps may go online".
The Windows Security dashboardSecure Linux Status & FixesOne screen with green [ OK ] and red [ !! ] checks for encryption, firewall, updates, VPN and more. Each problem tells you which number to press to fix it.
BitLockerLUKS encryptionThe password at power-on.

Linux is not magic. You can still be tricked by a fake website or a phishing email. Use your password manager (Bitwarden), don't reuse passwords, and be suspicious of urgent emails. But day-to-day, the risk is much lower than on Windows, and you'll see far fewer scary pop-ups.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: the firewall, encryption and automatic updates are there. ClamAV, the app firewall's question window and system snapshots are only on the main laptop, to keep old PCs fast. (Lite PCs with 3 GB of memory or more still get the quiet block lists.)

Do I ever need the terminal?

The terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. Konsole is the app. It's like Command Prompt or PowerShell.

Honestly: for everyday use, no. You can browse, email, write, watch, install apps and update the system without ever opening it. Some parts of this guide show a command because it's the quickest way to explain something exactly. You can copy and paste them: in Konsole, paste is Ctrl+Shift+V (Ctrl+V alone doesn't paste in most Linux terminals).

A few safe commands to try one day, just to see:

Terminal
fastfetch
df -h
ls ~/Documents

The first shows a summary of your computer. The second shows how full your drives are. The third lists your Documents folder. None of them change anything.

Things that are genuinely better here

We won't oversell it. But after a few weeks, most people notice these:

  • No ads, anywhere. No "suggested apps" in the menu. No adverts on the lock screen. No nagging to use Edge, Bing or OneDrive.
  • No tracking. Nothing sends a record of what you do to Microsoft or an advertiser. Privacy is the default, not a setting you have to hunt for.
  • No Microsoft account required. Your computer is yours. You don't sign in to anyone's cloud to use it.
  • Updates don't hijack the PC. They happen in the background. You choose when to restart.
  • One place to update everything. No more ten different updaters nagging you.
  • The apps are free. LibreOffice, GIMP, Krita, Kdenlive, VLC and the rest cost nothing. No subscriptions, ever.
  • You can change almost anything. Panel position, colours, fonts, how windows behave, what every key does. Windows 11 locked a lot of this away. Plasma doesn't.
  • It stays fast. It doesn't slow down over the years the way Windows tends to. On an old PC, the lite setup can make a "too slow for Windows" machine useful again.
  • Viruses are rare. Most malware is written for Windows. Combined with the app store habit, you are far safer.

Things that are different or harder (honestly)

It would be unfair not to tell you about the rough edges. Here they are, with what to do about each.

The problemHow to cope
Adobe apps (Photoshop, Premiere, Lightroom) don't run on Linux.Use GIMP or Krita for Photoshop, Kdenlive for Premiere, Darktable for Lightroom. Some Adobe tools (like Adobe Express) work in the web browser. They take some learning, so start with small projects.
Microsoft Office isn't available as an app.LibreOffice handles most files. For perfect compatibility, use the free Office web apps in your browser (office.com).
Some games won't run, mainly online games with strict anti-cheat (some big multiplayer shooters).Before you buy a game, look it up on ProtonDB (protondb.com). It lists how well each game runs on Linux. Most single-player games run fine through Steam.
A small Windows-only program you rely on.Search Discover for an alternative first. Then check if there's a web version. Then try Bottles.
A gadget's companion app (some printers' utilities, some smart devices) is Windows-only.The device itself usually works fine, for example printing. Only the extra app is missing. Often there's a phone app that does the same job.
Help online is written for Windows by default.Add "Fedora" or "KDE" to your search. Use this guide's search first.
Things have different names.Keep this chapter handy for the first couple of weeks. It gets easier fast.

Make it feel like home

KDE Plasma is one of the most customisable desktops there is. You can make it look almost exactly like Windows, or nothing like it. Play freely: you can always change things back. These are the most useful changes.

The panel (taskbar)

  • Pin an app: open the app, right-click its icon on the panel, and choose to pin it. Or find it in the app launcher, right-click it and look for "Pin to Task Manager".
  • Move or resize the panel: right-click an empty part of the panel and choose Show Panel Configuration (or Enter Edit Mode). You can put it at the top, left, right or bottom, make it taller or thinner, or make it float.
  • Add useful bits: in edit mode, choose Add Widgets. Weather, a calendar, system load and more can sit on the panel or the desktop.

Looks

  • Wallpaper: right-click the desktop and choose Configure Desktop and Wallpaper. Pick one, or add your own photo.
  • Light or dark mode, and whole new looks: open System Settings and search for Global Theme. A Global Theme changes colours, icons, window style and more in one click. "Breeze" (light) and "Breeze Dark" are the built-in ones. Click Get New... to browse more, made by the community.
  • Colours, icons, fonts: each has its own page in System Settings. Search for the word.

Comfort

  • Text too small or too big? Search System Settings for Display. Change Scale (for example 125% or 150%). This is the same as Windows' display scaling.
  • Night Light warms the screen colours in the evening, like Windows' Night light. Search System Settings for "Night Light" and turn it on.
  • Touchpad: search System Settings for "Touchpad". Turn on tap-to-click, change scrolling direction ("natural scrolling"), and adjust speed.
  • Touchpad gestures: on most laptops, swipe four fingers up for the Overview of all windows, and four fingers left or right to switch virtual desktop. Two fingers scroll and pinch to zoom, as you'd expect.
  • Power and sleep: search System Settings for "Power" to choose when the screen turns off and when the laptop sleeps.
  • Default apps: search "Default Applications" to choose which browser or email app opens links and files.

Not sure where a setting is? Type a word into the search box at the top of System Settings. That's the single best tip in this section.

On the lite (Xfce) setup: right-click the panel and choose Panel > Panel Preferences to move or change it. Appearance (themes and fonts) and Display settings are in the Settings Manager.

Bringing your Windows life across

The helper Bring My Stuff from Windows (app menu) does the heavy lifting, one question at a time. The full walk-through is in the chapter "Bringing your stuff over from Windows". In short:

On Windows you had...Here it becomes...Where to read more

System Restore, Startup Repair, Safe ModeSystem snapshots, and Repair This Computer (also from the USB stick when nothing starts)My computer is broken: how do I fix it?
Reset this PCRepair This Computer, "Reset to factory state" (your files are kept)My computer is broken
BitLocker recovery keyA disk recovery key (secure-linux-recovery-key) on paper and in BitwardenYour disk-encryption password
Windows Hello PINAn optional PIN at power-on. Honestly: a convenience, not extra security, on this laptop.Every Secure Linux tool: Disk unlock extras
Family settings, GuestFamily Safety: family website filter, children's accounts, a guest account that wipes itselfLooking after yourself
Get Help, Quick AssistExplain This Error (private AI), RustDeskLooking after yourself
Battery saver, Battery report80% charge limit, "Charge to 100% for a Trip", battery health in the Status windowIs every part of my computer OK?

Reminders for things that expire (NordVPN, domain names, card dates) come from the care calendar, and a one-page Emergency Kit says where your recovery codes are kept. Both are in "Looking after yourself".

If you're stuck

Everyone gets stuck sometimes. Here is where to go, in order.

  1. Secure Linux Status & Fixes. Open it from the app launcher. It checks the important things and shows green [ OK ] or red [ !! ] for each. Every red item tells you which number to press. Option 3, "Repair setup", fixes most problems. Option 1 installs all updates now.
  2. This guide. Open START HERE - Secure Linux Guide from the app launcher (there's also a copy called START-HERE.html on your Desktop). Use the guide's search box: type the problem in plain words, like "printer" or "no sound".
  3. The Troubleshooting chapter. It covers the common problems with step-by-step fixes.
  4. Restart. Yes, really. Just like on Windows, it fixes a surprising number of things.
  5. Ask a person. The Fedora community is friendly and helpful at ask.fedoraproject.org. For questions about the desktop itself, try discuss.kde.org. Say what you were doing, what you expected, and what happened instead. Never post your passwords.

A few comforting facts. You can't break the system by clicking around in the normal desktop. Your files are separate from the system, so even a bad update doesn't touch them. And with snapshots and backups set up, almost anything can be undone.

Your 7-day "get comfortable" plan

One small thing a day, about 15 minutes each. By the end of the week this will feel like your computer.

DayDo thisWhy
Day 1Explore the app launcher. Press Meta, click through each category, and open three apps you've never seen. Pin your favourite browser and file manager to the panel.To learn what's on your computer and where.
Day 2Open Dolphin (Meta+E). Make a folder in Documents. Copy a file into it, rename it with F2, delete it, then restore it from Trash. Press Ctrl+H twice to see hidden files appear and disappear.Files are the heart of using any computer.
Day 3Open System Settings. Pick a wallpaper, try light and dark Global Themes, set your display scale, and turn on Night Light.Making it look like yours makes it feel like home.
Day 4Open Discover. Look at the Updates page. Install one free app you'd like (a game, a recipe app, anything). Then remove it again.To build the safe app-store habit.
Day 5Practise the shortcuts: Meta+E, Meta+L, Meta+D, Meta+Left/Right to snap two windows side by side, Meta+W for Overview, and Print Screen for a screenshot.Shortcuts make you fast. Most are ones you already know.
Day 6Connect your phone. Install KDE Connect on the phone and pair it. Send a photo from the phone to the laptop. Try LocalSend too.Your phone and computer working together, without any cloud.
Day 7Open Secure Linux Status and read each line. Plug in an external drive and set up Pika Backup. Open a Windows document in LibreOffice.Peace of mind: you know it's healthy, backed up, and your old files work.

That's it. After a week, try to remember the last time you thought "how do I do this on Windows?". Most people find they've stopped asking. Welcome home.

Welcome, Mac friend

If you have used a Mac all your life, this computer will feel strange for about a day. After that, it will start to feel like yours. By the end of the first week, most Mac people find they are doing everything they used to do, plus a few things they never could.

This page is your translation guide. It takes the things you already know on a Mac and shows you where they live here. You do not need to learn "Linux" as a big new subject. You just need to learn where the light switches are in a new house.

A few names first, so nothing sounds mysterious:

  • Linux is the engine underneath, like the part of macOS you never see.
  • Fedora is the name of this version of Linux. Think of it like "macOS" as a brand. Yours is Fedora.
  • KDE Plasma (usually just "Plasma") is the desktop: the panel, the windows, the menus, the look and feel. It is what you actually see and touch.
  • Xfce is a lighter desktop used on older PCs. If your computer is older and was set up with the lite setup, you have Xfce instead of Plasma. Most of this page still applies. Where Xfce is different, you will see a short note.

Nothing on this page can break your computer. Explore freely. Click things. Right-click things. That is how you will learn fastest.

Your first five minutes: the five big shifts

Almost everything that feels odd at first comes from five small differences. Learn these and the rest falls into place.

1. Ctrl does the job of Cmd

On a Mac, your thumb lives on the Command key. Here, your little finger moves to the Ctrl key (bottom-left of the keyboard). For everyday shortcuts, just swap Cmd for Ctrl:

On a Mac you pressHere you pressWhat it does
Cmd+C, Cmd+V, Cmd+XCtrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+XCopy, paste, cut
Cmd+ZCtrl+ZUndo
Cmd+SCtrl+SSave
Cmd+QCtrl+Q (works in most apps)Quit the app
Cmd+WCtrl+WClose the tab or document
Click the red buttonAlt+F4, or click the XClose the window

Your fingers will reach for the old spot for a few days. That is normal. It fades quickly.

Tip: the Alt key on a PC keyboard sits where Option sits on a Mac, and it does similar jobs.

2. The Meta key is your new Cmd+Space

Most PC keyboards have a key with a Windows logo on it, between Ctrl and Alt. Here it is called the Meta key (you may also see it called the Super key). It has nothing to do with Windows on this computer. Press it once and the app launcher opens. Start typing the name of an app and press Enter. That is the Spotlight habit you already have, and it works here too.

If you are using an Apple keyboard with this computer, the Cmd key usually acts as the Meta key.

3. Window buttons are on the right

On a Mac, the red, yellow and green buttons sit top-left. Here, the window buttons sit top-right: minimise (a small line or down arrow), maximise (a square or up arrow) and close (an X). Double-clicking a window's title bar makes it fill the screen, then double-click again to restore it.

4. Menus live inside each window

On a Mac, the menu bar (File, Edit, View…) always sits at the very top of the screen and changes with the app in front. Here, by default, each app has its own menu inside its own window, just under the title bar. Some modern apps tuck their menu into a single button with three lines (often called a "hamburger" menu) or three dots. Same menus, different place.

If you miss the Mac style, Plasma can do that too. There is a Global Menu widget you can add to a panel at the top of the screen. See "Making it feel like a Mac" further down.

5. The bottom panel is your Dock and menu bar in one

The strip along the bottom of the screen is called the panel. It does the job of both the Dock and the right-hand side of the Mac menu bar:

  • Left end: the app launcher button (your Launchpad and Apple menu, combined).
  • Middle: pinned apps and open windows, like the Dock.
  • Right end: the system tray (Wi-Fi, sound, battery, Bluetooth, notifications), then the clock. This is your Control Centre and menu bar icons.

Bonus: right-click is normal here

On a Mac, right-click (or Control-click) can feel like a hidden extra. Here, right-click is used everywhere, and it is often the quickest way to find an option. Right-click the desktop, the panel, a file, an app icon, a window title. On a trackpad, a two-finger click usually does a right-click (you can check this in the Touchpad settings).

Where things are: the big translation table

Here is the list you will come back to most. The left column is what you knew. The right column is where it lives now. To open any app named here, press the Meta key and type its name.

The desktop itself

On a Mac you used…Here you use…Notes

Apple menu (Shut Down, Restart, Log Out)The app launcherThe power options are at the bottom of the launcher.

Xfce note: on the lite setup the launcher is the Whisker Menu, the file manager is Thunar, and settings live in the Settings Manager. The ideas are the same; the names are different. Xfce has no KRunner, but typing in the Whisker Menu works the same way.

On a Mac you used…Here you use…Notes

Split view (two folders)(none)F3
Information panel with previewCmd+I / Quick LookF11

A word of care: Shift+Delete in Dolphin deletes a file permanently, skipping the Bin. Plain Delete is the safe one.

No Quick Look by default. Pressing Space on a file does not preview it in Dolphin. Use the information panel (F11), or just double-click to open the file. Gwenview and Okular open very fast.

Typing accents. On a Mac you may hold a letter to pick an accent, or use Option shortcuts. Recent Plasma versions can show accented letters when you hold down a key. If that does not happen for you, use the emoji and character picker (Meta+.) or add a second keyboard layout in System Settings (search for "Keyboard").

Xfce note: most app shortcuts (Ctrl+C and friends) are the same. Desktop shortcuts differ; look in Settings Manager > Keyboard > Application Shortcuts.

Trackpad gestures

If you have a laptop, you will want the trackpad to feel right. Plasma 6 has good gesture support, though it is not identical to a Mac.

Commonly available in Plasma 6:

  • Two-finger scroll up, down and sideways, as on a Mac.
  • Pinch to zoom in many apps, such as the browser, image viewers and PDF readers.
  • Four-finger swipe up to open the Overview (like Mission Control).
  • Four-finger swipe left or right to move between virtual desktops (like swiping between Spaces).
  • Two-finger click for right-click.

Gestures can depend on your trackpad hardware. To check and adjust things, open System Settings > Touchpad. Things worth looking at:

  • Tap to click. On a Mac this is optional. Turn it on or off here to taste.
  • Scrolling direction. Macs use "natural" scrolling, where content moves with your fingers. If scrolling feels backwards, look for the option called Natural scrolling or Invert scroll direction and switch it on.
  • Pointer speed, if the cursor feels slow or jumpy.

There is also a hot corner: in Plasma, pushing the pointer into the top-left corner of the screen usually opens the Overview. You can change corners in System Settings (search for "Screen Edges").

Xfce note: the lite setup supports two-finger scrolling and tapping, set in Settings Manager > Mouse and Touchpad. Multi-finger gestures are limited.

Installing and removing apps

This is where Linux is honestly nicer than a Mac. There is no hunting around websites, no .dmg files, no dragging to an Applications folder, no "are you sure you want to open this app downloaded from the internet?"

The easy way: Discover

  1. Open Discover from the app launcher.
  2. Search for what you want, such as "Spotify", "Zoom" or "Steam".
  3. Click the app, read the description, then click Install.
  4. Type your password if asked. The app then appears in your launcher.

To remove an app, find it in Discover (there is an Installed section) and click Remove. That is the equivalent of dragging an app to the Bin, but it cleans up properly.

What are Flatpaks?

Many apps in Discover come as Flatpaks. A Flatpak is an app that runs in its own sandbox, a fenced-off space, a bit like Mac App Store apps. It can only reach the files and devices it has been allowed to. The app Flatseal lets you see and change those permissions, like the Privacy and Security list in Mac settings.

What about the drag-to-Applications kind of app?

The nearest thing to a Mac .app that you just download and run is an AppImage. It is a single file that contains a whole app. Some companies offer their app this way. Open the AppImage with Gear Lever and it will add it to your app launcher properly, like dragging a .app into Applications. Gear Lever can also remove it again.

Only download AppImages from the official website of the app's maker. Always prefer Discover first.

What is .dmg, .pkg, .exe here?

Mac files (.dmg, .pkg, .app) and Windows files (.exe, .msi) do not run here. Do not worry; nearly every popular app has a Linux version or a good free alternative. Look in Discover first. Search the web for "app name Linux" second.

For the curious: the Homebrew equivalent

If you ever used Homebrew in the Mac Terminal, you will feel at home. Fedora has a built-in tool called dnf. For example, sudo dnf install htop installs the htop program. Flatpak apps can be installed from the terminal too, with flatpak install flathub followed by the app's ID. You never need the terminal for this, though. Discover does it all with clicks.

Files and folders

Your home folder

Just like on a Mac, you have a home folder with your name on it. Inside you will find familiar folders: Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Music, Videos and Desktop. Dolphin shows them in the sidebar on the left.

Paths: where files "live"

A path is the address of a file. On a Mac your home folder is /Users/yourname. Here it is /home/yourname. A file on your desktop might be at /home/yourname/Desktop/notes.txt. You will often see the home folder written as a wavy line: ~. So ~/Downloads means "the Downloads folder in my home folder". Same as on a Mac.

One small difference: file names here care about capital letters. Photo.jpg and photo.jpg can be two different files in the same folder.

Hidden files

As on a Mac, files whose names start with a dot (like .config) are hidden. They hold app settings. Press Ctrl+H in Dolphin to show or hide them. You rarely need to touch them.

USB drives and memory cards

Plug them in and they appear in Dolphin's sidebar under Devices, a little like a drive icon appearing in Finder. A small notice may also pop up in the system tray. Before pulling a drive out, click the eject (⏏) icon next to it in Dolphin, the same as ejecting on a Mac.

Drives formatted on a Mac

This is the one thing that catches Mac people out:

Drive formatOn a MacHere
exFATRead and writeRead and write. The best choice for sharing between Mac and Linux.
FAT32 (MS-DOS FAT)Read and writeRead and write. Fine for small files; files over 4 GB will not fit.
APFS (the modern Mac format)Read and writeNot readable out of the box.
Mac OS Extended (HFS+)Read and writeSometimes readable, often read-only. Do not rely on it.

How to move your files from your Mac: on the Mac, open Disk Utility and format a USB drive as exFAT (this erases the drive, so use an empty one). Copy your files onto it. Plug it into this computer and copy them off. Or use LocalSend on both machines to send files over Wi-Fi with no drive at all.

Network shares

On a Mac you might press Cmd+K in Finder and type smb://server. In Dolphin, press Ctrl+L, type the same kind of address (for example smb://192.168.1.20 or smb://myserver), and press Enter. You can also click Network in Dolphin's sidebar to browse. Right-click a folder you use often and add it to Places, so it stays in the sidebar.

The Bin

Deleted files go to the Trash (also called the Bin), just like on a Mac. You can open it from Dolphin's sidebar and restore things. Emptying it removes them for good.

Passwords: which one is which?

On a Mac you usually type one password. Here you may meet up to three prompts, and it helps to know what each one is for. On most setups the last two use the same password.

When you see itWhat it isMac equivalent
Right after you press the power button, before anything else loadsThe disk-encryption password. It unlocks your encrypted drive.FileVault unlock at start-up
At the login screen, or when waking from sleepYour login password, for your user account.The Mac login screen
When installing apps, changing system settings or updatingAn administrator prompt. A window asks for your password to confirm you mean it."Enter your password to allow this" on a Mac

In the terminal, the administrator prompt is called sudo (short for "superuser do"). Typing sudo in front of a command means "do this as the administrator". It asks for your password. Nothing appears as you type, not even dots. That is normal. Type it and press Enter.

The golden rule is the same as on a Mac: only type your password when you started the action. If a prompt appears out of nowhere, cancel it and think.

Please do not lose your disk-encryption password. If it is forgotten, the files on the drive cannot be recovered by anyone. Write it down and keep it somewhere safe at home.

The terminal (do not be scared)

You can use this computer happily without ever opening a terminal, just as most Mac people never open Terminal. But it is there when you want it, and some guides online will give you commands to copy.

  • The terminal app is called Konsole. Open it with Ctrl+Alt+T.
  • The Mac uses a "shell" (the program that reads your commands) called zsh. Fedora uses Bash. For everyday commands like ls, cd, cp and mv, they behave the same.
  • Copy and paste in Konsole use Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V. This is because Ctrl+C in a terminal means "stop the running command". It is a tradition from long before Macs existed.
  • Only paste commands from sources you trust, such as this guide or the official Fedora site.

Xfce note: the lite setup's terminal is the Xfce Terminal. It works the same way.

Staying safe: your Gatekeeper, but stronger

Your Mac quietly protected you with Gatekeeper (which checks apps) and XProtect (which scans for known malware). This computer has its own set of guards. Most of them run without you doing anything.

  • Flatpak sandbox: most apps run fenced off from the rest of your system.
  • Flatseal: lets you see what each Flatpak app is allowed to touch, and change it.
  • ClamAV (with the ClamTk window): scans files for known viruses, a bit like XProtect.
  • Network protection (Network Monitor): asks you the first time a brand-new app tries to connect to the internet, and also blocks known malware, phishing and tracking sites. If you ever used Little Snitch or LuLu on a Mac, this is the same idea. It asks only once per app, "Always allow" is already picked, and apps that came with the computer are already approved, so you will rarely see it. See "Network Monitor: which apps may go online".
  • Secure Linux Status: one app that shows whether your protections are switched on and healthy. If you are ever unsure if things are OK, open this first.
  • The firewall blocks unwanted incoming connections, and updates install themselves.

Your iPhone and this computer

Let us be honest: an iPhone is happiest with a Mac. But you can still live very well with both.

  • Sending files: install LocalSend on your iPhone (it is free in the App Store). It works like AirDrop between your phone and this computer.
  • Photos: the Immich iPhone app can back up your photos to your home server automatically. Then you can see them on this computer in a web browser.
  • Plugging in by cable: often, when you connect the iPhone and tap Trust on the phone, its photos appear in Dolphin. This does not work on every setup; LocalSend and Immich are more reliable.
  • KDE Connect: there is an iPhone version. It can share files, links and clipboard text. It cannot do everything it does on Android, because Apple limits what iPhone apps can do.
  • Messages and calls: iMessage and FaceTime do not work on Linux. Use Signal on both your iPhone and this computer for private messages and video calls.

What will feel better (honestly)

  • No Apple ID needed. No account to sign into before you can use your own computer. No nagging to turn on iCloud.
  • Any hardware. You are not tied to Apple's prices. Linux runs well on almost any PC, including old ones. The lite setup can bring a ten-year-old laptop back to life.
  • Customise everything. Panels, colours, fonts, window buttons, shortcuts, hot corners, even the start-up sound. If you can imagine it, Plasma can probably do it.
  • Free apps. Almost everything in Discover is free, with no subscriptions. LibreOffice, Kdenlive, Darktable, GIMP and many more cost nothing.
  • Privacy. Nothing here reports your activity to a company. No ads anywhere in the system.
  • Updates that respect you. No forced annual upgrade that drops support for your older machine.
  • Clipboard history and other little luxuries built in, like Meta+V and KRunner's calculator.
  • You are in charge. Your computer does what you ask. It does not decide for you.

What is different or harder (also honestly)

It would not be fair to pretend everything is the same. Here is what you give up, and how people cope.

What you will missHow to cope
iMessage and FaceTimeUse Signal with the people you talk to most. For an urgent iMessage, use your iPhone.
iCloud (Notes, Reminders, Photos, Drive)Visit icloud.com in your browser to reach your files, notes and photos. Over time, move photos to Immich and files to Syncthing or your home server.
Pages, Numbers, Keynote filesOpen them at icloud.com and export as Word, Excel or PowerPoint. Then LibreOffice opens them happily.
Final Cut Pro, Logic ProThese are Apple-only. Kdenlive is a capable video editor. For music, Audacity covers recording and editing; Discover has more advanced music apps if you want to explore.
Some commercial apps (for example Adobe and Microsoft Office)Many have web versions that work in the browser. Otherwise there are free alternatives: GIMP and Krita for images, Inkscape for illustration, LibreOffice for documents.
Apple's polish and "it just works" feelingPlasma is polished, but you may meet an odd setting or a rough edge now and then. The flip side: you can fix it, and help is easy to find.
Apple Pay, Apple Music app, Apple TV appApple Music and Apple TV+ have web versions. Some features may be missing.

A useful habit: when something seems missing, ask "is there a web version?" first, and "is there a free app in Discover?" second. One of those answers is almost always yes.

Making it feel like a Mac (if you want)

You do not have to do any of this. Many Mac people find the default layout comfortable after a few days. But if you want the familiar look, Plasma can get very close.

A top bar and a bottom dock

  1. Right-click an empty part of the desktop and choose Enter Edit Mode (the exact wording may differ slightly).
  2. Use the option to add a panel and choose an empty panel. Move it to the top of the screen.
  3. Add widgets to the top panel: the Global Menu (this gives you the Mac-style app menu at the top), a clock, and the System Tray.
  4. Now edit the bottom panel. In its settings you can make it narrower so it fits its content, centre it, make it float, and set it to hide when a window covers it. That gives you a Dock-like bar.
  5. Remove the clock and system tray from the bottom panel if you moved them to the top.

If you get in a muddle, do not worry. Panels and widgets can always be removed and added again. Nothing you do here can harm your files.

Themes

Open System Settings and look at the appearance section (search for "Global Theme" or "Colours"). You can pick a light or dark look, change accent colours, cursors, icons and fonts. There is also a button to download more themes made by the community, including some inspired by macOS.

Window buttons on the left

If you really want the buttons on the left, search System Settings for "Window Decorations". There you can rearrange the title bar buttons by dragging them.

Scrolling and size

  • Natural scrolling: turn it on in System Settings > Touchpad (and Mouse, for a mouse), as described earlier.
  • Size of everything (scaling): if text looks too small, as on a sharp laptop screen, search System Settings for "Display" and change the Scale setting, for example to 125% or 150%. This is like choosing "Larger Text" in Mac display settings.

Xfce note: Xfce can also have a top bar and a bottom dock-like panel. Right-click a panel and choose Panel > Panel Preferences to change its position and size. Xfce does not have Plasma's Global Menu widget by default.

Small habits that make life easy

  • Closing a window usually quits the app. On a Mac, closing the last window often leaves the app running. Here most apps quit when you close their window. A few, such as Signal, keep running in the system tray; right-click their tray icon to quit them fully.
  • Pin your favourite apps. Open an app, right-click its icon in the panel, and pin it. Now it is always there, like a Dock icon.
  • Use the Overview. Meta+W, then start typing. It finds windows and apps fast.
  • Right-click the desktop. That is where you change the wallpaper and enter edit mode.
  • Restart after big updates when asked. The computer will tell you.
  • Search System Settings. There is a search box at the top-left. Type what you want, like "printer", "sound" or "wallpaper", rather than hunting through menus.

More Mac-to-Linux translations

On your Mac you had...Here it becomes...Where to read more
Time MachinePika Backup to an external drive or your home server, plus hourly system snapshots for undoing bad updatesBackups
Disk Utility "First Aid"Repair This Computer, "Check and repair a disk"My computer is broken: how do I fix it?
macOS Recovery (hold the power button)The USB stick with SystemRescue and the repair menu. (On an Apple Silicon Mac running Linux, macOS Recovery is still how you repair macOS itself.)My computer is broken; Apple Silicon Macs
Activity Monitor, "About This Mac"Mission Center, and Hardware Health Check to test every partIs every part of my computer OK?
FileVaultDisk encryption with a power-on password (set at install). Add a recovery key.Your disk-encryption password
Parental Controls, Guest UserFamily Safety: a family filter, children's accounts and a guest account that wipes itself. Honestly: there are no screen-time limits.Looking after yourself
Siri Suggestions, "Look up"The searchable guide (press the Meta key and type) and Explain This Error, a private AI on this computerLooking after yourself
Find MyNo equivalent. Keep your laptop's serial number on the Emergency Kit page and see "The laptop is lost or stolen".When life happens
Migration AssistantNo equivalent. The Bring My Stuff from Windows helper is built for Windows moves. What carries over from a Mac: Bitwarden can import a passwords file exported from Safari or iCloud Keychain (look for its Safari or macOS option in the import screen; not tried here), bookmarks can be exported from Safari as an HTML file and imported into LibreWolf, and photos go to Immich. The helper does not automate the Apple steps; this part is by hand.Bringing your stuff over: Bookmarks, Passwords

If your Mac hardware is the question

  • Intel Mac: hold Option at power-on to pick the USB stick. A 2018 to 2020 Mac with the T2 chip needs a short extra step first. See "Starting the USB stick on any computer".
  • Apple Silicon Mac (M1, M2): the stick cannot start it. Fedora Asahi Remix is installed from macOS instead. See "Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and M2)".

If you are stuck

Being stuck is part of learning anything new. Here is where to go, in order:

  1. Open the Secure Linux Status app. It shows at a glance whether your protections, updates and backups are working.
  2. Search the START HERE guide. It has pages on almost every app on this computer, plus troubleshooting. Use its search box with a plain word, such as "printer", "backup" or "Wi-Fi".
  3. Search the app launcher or System Settings. Many "where is it?" questions are solved by typing the word.
  4. Restart. It works here as well as anywhere.
  5. Ask a friendly human. The official Fedora help forum, ask.fedoraproject.org, welcomes beginners. Say you are new, that you have Fedora with KDE Plasma (or Xfce), and describe what you clicked and what happened.

When searching the web, add "Fedora" or "KDE Plasma" to your search. For example: "KDE Plasma change wallpaper". That gets you answers that match your computer.

Your 7-day "get comfortable" plan

Do one small thing each day. Ten to twenty minutes is plenty. By day seven, this will feel like home.

Day 1: Look around

  • Press the Meta key and open a few apps by typing their names.
  • Practise Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V instead of Cmd. Write a short note in KWrite and save it with Ctrl+S.
  • Click every icon in the system tray (bottom-right) to see what it does. Connect to Wi-Fi if you have not already.
  • Open the Secure Linux Status app, just to see that everything is green and healthy.

Day 2: Make it yours

  • Right-click the desktop and change the wallpaper.
  • Pick light or dark mode in System Settings.
  • Set up the touchpad: tap to click and natural scrolling, if you want them.
  • Pin your five favourite apps to the panel.

Day 3: Files

  • Open Dolphin and explore your home folder.
  • Make a folder, rename it with F2, move a file into it, delete it, and restore it from the Bin.
  • Try split view with F3.
  • Bring some files over from your Mac using an exFAT USB drive or LocalSend.

Day 4: The web and your passwords

  • Open LibreWolf and import or rebuild your bookmarks.
  • Set up Bitwarden and its browser extension, so your passwords are with you.
  • Open Tuta for email and calendar.

Day 5: Your phone

  • Install LocalSend on your iPhone and send a photo to this computer.
  • Install Signal on your phone and computer, and link them.
  • If you have a home server, set up the Immich app on your phone.

Day 6: Apps and windows

  • Open Discover and install one app you want. Then remove one you do not need.
  • Try the Overview (Meta+W) and a second virtual desktop.
  • Snap two windows side by side with Meta+Left and Meta+Right.
  • Take a screenshot with Print Screen.

Day 7: Peace of mind

  • Set up Pika Backup to copy your files to an external drive or your home server.
  • Open Discover and look at the Updates section, so you know where it is.
  • Decide whether you want the Mac-style top bar and dock. Try it. Keep it or undo it.
  • Look back at how much you have learned. You switched from the only computer you have ever known. That is a big deal.

One last thing

The Mac taught you good habits: keeping things tidy, using shortcuts, trusting a clean design. All of that carries over. Plasma simply hands you more of the controls. Take it slowly, be curious, and do not be afraid to click around. Welcome home.

This chapter walks you through moving your life across: passwords, bookmarks, photos, OneDrive, notes, Word and Excel files, study tools, game saves, printers and more. Every item is its own short page in Bring My Stuff from Windows. These are on-demand pages: they do not form a long second queue after the five-screen first login. Choose one when you need it and leave the rest for later.

How to open it

  1. Open Secure Linux Welcome & Setup for a task-based journey, or Bring My Stuff from Windows for the full topic list.
  2. Pick one. It asks, explains and works one step at a time. You can go back or stop before confirming a change.
  3. Direct entries include Move My Passwords from Chrome or Edge, Install Apps & Fill In Missing Software, Customise My Apps & Desktop, Back Up My Files, Restore My Files from a Backup and Finish Setting Up My Computer.
  4. From the terminal, secure-linux-migrate shows the list and secure-linux-migrate page NAME opens one topic. Names include passwords bookmarks photos onedrive office study games printer display streaming meetings accessibility extras devices hibernate care before emergency family tips help.
  5. To review the five-screen welcome again, open Welcome & Setup Choices or run secure-linux-welcome --again.

Where the helper needs your Windows backup (bookmarks, Anaconda environments or a notes vault), it looks for the Windows backup folder on the backup drive or in your home folder. The existing ZenbookBackup-... folder name does not mean the computer must be a Zenbook. secure-linux-migrate find-backup prints where it found a backup.
