Passwords: Google Password Manager to Bitwarden

What it is. The easiest safe route to move every password saved in Chrome or your Google account into Bitwarden (already installed). It takes about 5 minutes and four steps. It opens Bitwarden, opens Google's password settings in your browser, notices the exported file arriving in Downloads by itself, tells you exactly which options to pick in Bitwarden's import screen, then securely deletes the file.

Why you want it. Bitwarden keeps one strong, different password per site, works on this computer and your phone, and does not belong to an advertising company.

  1. Step 1. Bitwarden opens. No account yet? Click Create account and choose a long master password you will never forget (a short sentence is good). Bitwarden cannot reset it.
  2. Step 2. In the browser, sign in to Google and click Export passwords. A file called Google Passwords.csv lands in Downloads. The helper spots it. If it cannot, it asks where the file is.
  3. Step 3. In Bitwarden choose File, Import data, format Chrome (csv), and pick the file. Then answer "yes" to the question Do your passwords show in Bitwarden now? Only then is the file deleted.
  4. Step 4. Switch off Google's own password saving and delete its copy (the page shows the buttons). On Android set Bitwarden as the autofill service. Install the Bitwarden add-on in LibreWolf.

Good to know. The exported file holds every password in plain text, so it is deleted straight away and must never be emailed or put on a USB stick. On an SSD a deleted file can in theory leave traces; that is acceptable here because the disk is fully encrypted.

If it fails. Nothing is lost. Run Move your passwords to Bitwarden again. If the import did not work, the file stays in Downloads and the page tells you so. Command line: secure-linux-migrate page passwords; delete a leftover file with secure-linux-migrate shred "FILE.csv".

Prefer no cloud at all? The same page also offers KeePassXC: your passwords live in one encrypted file on this PC, and nowhere else - no account, no company. It imports the same Google "Chrome (csv)" file (KeePassXC: Database, Import, format "Chrome (csv)"). The honest trade-off: with no cloud, nothing syncs by itself. Syncthing (installed) can share the KeePassXC file with your other computers on the home network if you ever want that.

Bookmarks

What it is. It finds the Chrome, Edge (and Firefox) bookmarks in your Windows backup and writes Bookmarks from Windows.html in Documents, one folder per browser and profile. Only web links are kept: "javascript:" bookmarklets are dropped for safety.

  1. Run Bring your bookmarks.
  2. In LibreWolf press Ctrl+Shift+O, then Import and Backup, Import Bookmarks from HTML..., and pick the file.
  3. They appear under Other Bookmarks. Drag your favourites to the toolbar.

If it fails. No backup found? Plug in the backup drive, or type the folder's location when asked. No Windows backup at all? In Chrome on another computer use Bookmark manager, the three dots, Export bookmarks, then import that file the same way. Command line: secure-linux-migrate bookmarks [FOLDER].

Google Photos to Immich (your own photo server)

What it is. It uploads your Google Takeout of Google Photos to Immich, the photo server at home, using the immich-go program. Albums, dates and places come across. Nothing is deleted from Google. The Immich address comes from your USB build settings, unless you saved another with the choice immich_url. Full setup only.

  1. Get your data at takeout.google.com: "Deselect all", tick only Google Photos, choose .zip and 50 GB files.
  2. Run Move your Google Photos to Immich. Point to the folder holding the takeout-....zip files.
  3. Create an Immich API key: your picture, Account Settings, API Keys, New API Key. Paste it in.
  4. A test run comes first: it reads your Takeout and shows what it would upload without uploading anything. If the summary shows your photos, say yes and the real upload starts in its own window.
  5. It can take hours. Keep the laptop plugged in and on your home Wi-Fi.
  6. Afterwards, delete the API key in Immich. (The key is given to the upload program as an option, so other programs on this computer could see it while it runs.)

If it stops: run it again. Photos already uploaded are skipped. Command line: secure-linux-migrate immich [--dry-run] PATH.... If the server cannot be reached, check you are on your home Wi-Fi or Meshnet (see "Your home server").

OneDrive to your laptop

What it is. It copies everything from OneDrive to a folder called OneDrive-Archive in your home folder, using a tool called rclone (rclone copy, never sync). Nothing is ever deleted from OneDrive. At the end it checks every file arrived.

  1. Run Copy your OneDrive and notes. A window opens.
  2. Sign in to Microsoft in the browser and click Accept.
  3. Let it copy. It can take hours for a big OneDrive; you can keep working.
  4. When the check says "All files are here", you may cancel the subscription if you want.

Not copied this way: OneNote notebooks and the Personal Vault. Export OneNote pages from the OneNote app, and move Personal Vault files out first. If it fails: run it again; it continues where it stopped. Command line: secure-linux-migrate onedrive [setup|copy|check].

Obsidian notes and your phone

What it is. It offers Obsidian (what you used before; free but not open source), or Joplin (already installed; fully open source; can import an Obsidian vault), or both. It finds your vault (a folder containing .obsidian) in the OneDrive copy or the Windows backup, copies it to ~/Vaults/NAME and shares that folder with your phone through Syncthing (home network only by default).

  1. On the phone: Android: install "Syncthing-Fork" (F-Droid or Play Store). iPhone: "Mobius Sync".
  2. On the laptop: open Syncthing, Add Remote Device, scan the phone's QR code, share the folder "NAME (notes)".
  3. Open that folder as the vault in Obsidian on the phone. In Obsidian on the laptop choose Open folder as vault.

Pros and cons. Obsidian looks after your existing vault exactly as it is; Joplin is fully open source but a different style. Choosing both is fine. If it fails: run secure-linux-migrate vault SOURCE NAME, or check the folder you pointed at really contains .obsidian.

Word, Excel and PowerPoint files

What it is. LibreOffice opens .docx, .xlsx and .pptx. Setup also installs Carlito (an exact-width stand-in for Calibri), Caladea (for Cambria) and the Liberation fonts (for Arial, Times New Roman and Courier New), so pages break in the same places as in Microsoft Office.

Aptos, Microsoft's newer default font, has no exact free twin. Documents that use it are shown in Carlito, which looks very close, but lines can wrap slightly differently.

The page Word, Excel and PowerPoint files can add two things:

OptionProsCons
OnlyOffice (full setup)Looks and lays out documents very much like Microsoft Office; good for assignments you hand in as .docx.A bigger program; not every feature is open source.
Microsoft 365 on the web (a menu entry opening office.com in its own window)Exactly Microsoft's own behaviour.Needs your Microsoft account and the internet; your documents live on Microsoft's servers.

Python, MATLAB and Android Studio

The page Study and coding tools (full setup) asks about three things, one at a time. Each can be skipped.

Python

uv is already installed: the modern, fast way to make Python projects (uv init myproject, uv add numpy, uv run python script.py). If you used Anaconda, choose "Yes, install conda". Environments you exported on Windows (conda env export --from-history > name.yml, or any .yml in the backup) are recreated; Windows-only packages and exact Windows build codes are removed automatically. Use one with conda activate NAME. If one fails, the window says how to export it again on Windows. Command line: secure-linux-migrate conda-envs [FOLDER].

MATLAB

  • GNU Octave (free, from Fedora): runs most MATLAB scripts (.m files) unchanged. Start with octave. Con: not every MATLAB toolbox exists.
  • Official MATLAB: uses your university licence. The page shows the mpm download steps (about 15 minutes, needs your MathWorks account). Fedora is not officially supported by MathWorks but MATLAB usually runs. If it will not start, run it inside an Ubuntu container with Distrobox (the BoxBuddy app). Release the old Windows activation first at mathworks.com, My Account, Licenses.
  • You can have both.

Android Studio

Installs Android Studio (about 3 GB on first start), adb and fastboot, a rule so your user can talk to any Android phone over USB, and puts you in the kvm group for fast emulators. On the phone: Settings, Developer options, USB debugging, plug in, tap Allow. Log out and in once. Full setup only.

Your games and saves

Steam games with Steam Cloud bring their saves back by themselves. Rocket League keeps cars, items and rank in your Epic account: sign in and they are there. For other games the Windows backup has a "Games" folder. Ludusavi (full setup) finds where each game keeps its saves on this laptop:

  1. Install and start the game once.
  2. Open Ludusavi, Backup mode, Preview, and click the game to see its save folder.
  3. Copy the files from the backup's Games folder into that folder.

Ludusavi's own Restore mode only reads backups that Ludusavi made. Use Backup mode now and then to protect your saves from here on. See also the Steam, Heroic, Bottles and GameMode app guides.

Printers and scanners ("Find my printer")

  1. Switch the printer on. Put it on the same Wi-Fi as the laptop (or plug in the USB cable).
  2. KDE: System Settings, Printers, Add. Xfce: Printers, Add.
  3. Pick the entry that says "driverless" or "IPP Everywhere" (most printers from the last 10 years).
  4. Not listed? Add it by address: ipp://192.168.x.x/ipp/print (the printer's IP address is on its screen or its network report).
  5. Scanning: Skanpage (KDE) or Document Scanner (Xfce) finds network scanners by itself.

HP printers also have HP's driver installed. If the printer is not found: at home the firewall lets the laptop see printers, but on other networks they stay hidden on purpose. Check you are on the home network (secure-linux-zone status says home or away; see "Home or away").

Screen size, touchpad and Australian English

  • Screen size: on the 2.5K laptop screen (full setup, KDE) the first login sets 150% scaling and a matching mouse pointer, like Windows' recommended setting. Change it in the wizard page Screen size or System Settings, Display & Monitor, Scale (125, 150, 175, 200).
  • Touchpad: set up like Windows: tap to click, two-finger click or tap for right click, ignores your palm while typing, natural scrolling. KDE: System Settings, Mouse & Touchpad.
  • Australian English: dates like 3/11/2026, dollars, A4 paper, English (Australia) spell-check, British-style spelling in menus (there is no separate Australian translation of the desktop).

Netflix and streaming

Netflix, Disney+, Stan and Binge need DRM (copy protection, in this case Google's Widevine) in the browser, which LibreWolf switches off for privacy. The page Netflix and streaming saves your choice (drm).

  1. Answer yes to turn it on.
  2. Restart LibreWolf. The first video asks to install the add-on once.

Pros: streaming works. Cons: you accept a closed-source component from Google in the browser. Browsers on Linux get up to 720p on Netflix and about 1080p on most others (the companies limit it). For the best picture use the TV's own app.

Video calls and chat

  • Discord: installed as Vesktop: your normal Discord account, but screen sharing with sound works on this desktop. (Old PCs get Discord's website as an app window.)
  • Microsoft Teams and Zoom run as web apps: menu entries "Microsoft Teams (web)" and "Zoom (web)" that open the website in its own window. Nothing extra to install; sign in with your account. For Zoom, join from the browser when asked.
  • The first time you share the screen the desktop asks which screen or window. That is normal; you stay in control.

Easier to see, hear and read

The page Easier to see, hear and read (also System Settings, Accessibility) offers bigger text, a bigger pointer, a high-contrast colour scheme (white on black with yellow highlights), colour-blindness filters (KDE), the Orca screen reader (switch it off with Meta+Alt+S), the OpenDyslexic font, and Live Captions (offline subtitles for any sound, English only; full setup). Pointer and font changes show fully after you log out and in.

Handy extras

  • Tools pack (full setup, about 1.5 GB): Speech Note (talk to type, read aloud, translate, all offline), NormCap and Frog (copy text out of a screenshot), PDF Arranger (merge, split, rotate pages), OCRmyPDF (ocrmypdf in.pdf out.pdf makes a scanned PDF searchable), Metadata Cleaner (removes hidden location, camera and author details before you share a file).
  • Everyday: Organic Maps (offline maps), Foliate (e-books), Calibre (e-book library) and RustDesk (help family remotely: they read you a code). Old PCs get only Foliate and RustDesk.

About RustDesk and privacy. By default connections are set up through RustDesk's public server (the screen itself is end-to-end encrypted). You can run your own RustDesk server on your home server so nothing goes through anyone else. Con of the default: a third party sees that a connection happened.

Friends' drives, iPhones, monitors and headphones

  • Drives: exFAT and NTFS USB drives open normally; zip, 7z and rar files open.
  • iPhone: plug in, tap Trust on the phone, open it in the file manager. Photos and files appear; USB tethering also works.
  • External monitor brightness: the brightness slider uses the monitor's own controls (DDC/CI). Check it is seen with ddcutil detect; set it with ddcutil setvcp 10 60. The monitor's own menu must have DDC/CI switched on.
  • Bluetooth headphones can use LDAC and AAC when they support them (System Settings, Audio, the device, Profile).
  • secure-linux-migrate devices shows what is ready.

Apps you used before

The wizard page Apps you used before maps the apps people know from Windows or a Mac to the open apps already installed here, then closes the last few gaps with one question each. Every question can be postponed, and nothing is installed without your yes. On the Debian setup the page only shows the mapping (Thunderbird is installed there already) and points to the three optional extras below; set one with secure-linux-choice and the next setup run (or "Repair setup") installs it.

You usedHereNotes
Outlook / Apple MailThunderbird (the classic, from Mozilla) or Betterbird (Thunderbird with extra fixes, from its community)Saved as choice email_client. Both do email, calendars and contacts, and sign in to Gmail, Outlook.com, iCloud and everything in between; your email password is typed into the app once and never leaves this computer. Webmail in the browser also works fine if you pick no app.

Loose ends from Windows ("before you started")

The page Loose ends from Windows checks four things: Clipchamp projects exported, CapCut projects exported, Adobe subscription cancelled or moved, and MATLAB licence released. For each one you missed it explains how to sort it out from this laptop and can open the right website. The replacements installed: Kdenlive (video), GIMP and Krita (Photoshop), Inkscape (Illustrator), Darktable (Lightroom).

More pages in the same helper

These have their own sections in other chapters:

Linux basics for Windows users

On this page 12 sections
  1. Files and folders
  2. No drive letters
  3. Installing apps
  4. Updating
  5. The terminal
  6. Users and passwords
  7. Permissions basics
  8. Processes and the Task Manager
  9. Where settings live
  10. Keyboard shortcuts
  11. Virtual desktops
  12. Windows equivalents

This chapter covers the everyday things that work differently from Windows 11.

Files and folders

Your personal folder is /home/<your-username>. It is the equivalent of C:\Users\<you> on Windows. Inside are the familiar folders: Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Music, Pictures, Videos. In commands, ~ is short for your home folder, so ~/Downloads means your Downloads folder.

The file manager is called Dolphin. It works like File Explorer. Open it with Meta+E (the Windows key plus E) or from the app menu. Useful tips:

  • Ctrl+H shows hidden files. On Linux, any file or folder whose name starts with a dot (like .config) is hidden. Many app settings live in these.
  • F4 opens a small terminal at the bottom of Dolphin, already in the current folder.
  • Ctrl+L lets you type a path, just like the address bar in File Explorer.
  • Deleted files go to the Trash (the Recycle Bin). Shift+Delete deletes immediately, without the Trash.

Linux treats Photo.jpg and photo.jpg as two different files. Paths use forward slashes (/), not backslashes.

No drive letters

There is no C: or D:. Everything lives in one tree that starts at / (called "root"). When you plug in a USB drive, it appears in Dolphin's left panel. Behind the scenes it is placed under /run/media/<your-username>/<drive-name>. Before unplugging a drive, click the eject icon next to it in Dolphin, so any unsaved data is written first.

Installing apps

Forget downloading .exe files from websites. On Linux, apps come from trusted repositories, which work like app stores.

  • Discover is the graphical app store. Search, click Install, done. It also shows updates.
  • Flatpak apps come from Flathub. They are sandboxed and update daily on their own. Most apps on this laptop are Flatpaks. Prefer these for desktop apps.
  • RPM packages come from Fedora itself, installed with the dnf command. These are system tools and some apps. Example: sudo dnf install htop.

In Discover, an app may be offered from more than one source. A drop-down near the Install button lets you choose. Flathub is usually the best choice for desktop apps.

Golden rule: never run commands like curl https://some-site/install.sh | bash from random websites or videos. It downloads a script and runs it immediately, without you seeing what it does. If it uses sudo, it can change anything. If an app isn't in Discover, ask someone you trust before installing it another way.

Updating

Updates mostly install themselves (see "What runs automatically"). To update everything by hand, open Discover and click Updates, then Update All. Or run sudo dnf upgrade --refresh and then flatpak update. Restart after big updates, especially when the kernel (the core of Linux) was updated.

The terminal

The terminal app is Konsole. Open it with Ctrl+Alt+T. You don't need it for daily use, but many fixes are quicker with it, and this guide uses it often. Key tips:

  • sudo in front of a command runs it as administrator, like "Run as administrator" in Windows. It asks for your login password. The password is invisible as you type. That is normal.
  • Tab completes names. Type the first few letters of a command or file name and press Tab. Press it twice to see all options.
  • Up arrow brings back earlier commands.
  • Ctrl+Shift+C copies and Ctrl+Shift+V pastes. Plain Ctrl+C does not copy in the terminal. It stops the running command.
  • q exits long listings and help pages.
  • man <command> shows the full manual for a command, for example man ls. <command> --help shows a shorter summary.
  • Handy commands: ls (list files), cd (change folder), pwd (show current folder), cp (copy), mv (move or rename), mkdir (make a folder), fastfetch (system summary), btop (live system monitor).

Be careful with rm (remove). It deletes immediately, without the Trash.

Users and passwords

You have one user account, which is allowed to use sudo. The separate "root" account is locked. To change your login password, go to System Settings, Users, or run passwd in the terminal. This does not change your disk-encryption password; that has its own chapter.

Permissions basics

Every file has an owner and permissions: who can read, write, and execute (run) it. Your files belong to you. System files belong to root. That is why changing them needs sudo. You can see permissions with ls -l, or in Dolphin by right-clicking a file, then Properties, then Permissions. A downloaded program or script won't run until it is marked executable. That is a safety feature. Don't use sudo or chmod 777 to "fix" permission errors you don't understand. Ask first.

Processes and the Task Manager

Mission Center looks and works much like the Windows Task Manager. It shows CPU, memory, disk, network and GPU use, and lets you end stuck apps. KDE's own System Monitor does the same; Ctrl+Esc opens it. If a window freezes, you can also press Ctrl+Alt+Esc. The pointer becomes a skull: click the frozen window to force it closed.

Where settings live

Almost everything is in System Settings (in the app menu). It replaces both Windows Settings and Control Panel: Wi-Fi, displays, sound, Bluetooth, printers, users, keyboard shortcuts, appearance and more. Use the search box at the top-left; it's quicker than browsing.

Keyboard shortcuts

The Meta key is the key with the Windows logo.

ShortcutWhat it does
MetaOpen the app menu (like Start)
Alt+SpaceKRunner: type to launch apps, find files, do sums, convert units
Meta+EOpen Dolphin (files)
Meta+LLock the screen
Ctrl+Alt+TOpen the terminal (Konsole)
Print ScreenSpectacle, the screenshot tool
Meta+VClipboard history
Alt+TabSwitch windows
Meta+WOverview of all windows and desktops

Meta+Left / Right / UpSnap a window to a side, or maximise
Ctrl+Meta+Left / RightMove to the previous or next virtual desktop

You can change any shortcut in System Settings, Keyboard, Shortcuts.

Virtual desktops

Virtual desktops are separate screens of windows, like Windows' Task View desktops. For example, one for work and one for games. Add or remove them in System Settings (search for "Virtual Desktops"). Switch with Ctrl+Meta+Left/Right or from the overview (Meta+W).

Fedora and KDE Plasma

On this page 8 sections
  1. Fedora's release cycle
  2. dnf: the system package manager
  3. Flatpak commands
  4. RPM Fusion and codecs
  5. SELinux basics
  6. Btrfs and snapshots
  7. Customising KDE Plasma
  8. A note on Xfce (old PCs)

Fedora's release cycle

Fedora releases a new version about every 6 months. Each version gets updates for about 13 months. That means you need to upgrade to the next version at least once a year. Upgrading every 6 months, a few weeks after each new release, is the comfortable rhythm.

This is different from Windows' big yearly feature updates, but similar in spirit. An upgrade keeps all your files, apps and settings.

Upgrading the easy way

When a new version is out, Discover shows a banner offering the upgrade. Make sure your backup is current and the laptop is plugged in, then click it and follow the steps. The computer restarts, installs the upgrade on a plain progress screen (this can take 30 minutes or more), and restarts again.

Upgrading with the guided helper

The simplest and safest way is secure-linux-upgrade (also the Upgrade Fedora button in Secure Linux Status). It is offered from about the fourth week after a release, checks the charger and free space, takes a snapshot, makes sure extra software sources are ready for the new version, downloads the upgrade, and asks before restarting. The tools chapter has the steps.

Upgrading from the terminal

Replace <N> with the new version number (for example 45):

Terminal
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
sudo dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=<N>
sudo dnf system-upgrade reboot

The first command brings the current version fully up to date. The second downloads the new version. The third restarts and installs it. Don't power off during the install.

dnf: the system package manager

dnf installs and removes system packages (RPMs) from Fedora's repositories. Commands that change things need sudo.

CommandWhat it does
dnf search <word>Find packages matching a word
dnf info <package>Show details about a package
sudo dnf install <package>Install a package
sudo dnf remove <package>Remove a package
sudo dnf upgrade --refreshUpdate everything installed by dnf
dnf history listList past install, remove and update actions, each with an ID number
dnf history info <ID>Show what one action changed
sudo dnf history undo <ID>Undo one action, for example an install you regret
sudo dnf autoremoveRemove packages nothing needs any more

Flatpak commands

Discover handles Flatpaks for you, but these are handy:

CommandWhat it does
flatpak listList installed Flatpak apps and runtimes
flatpak list --appList apps only
flatpak search <word>Search Flathub
flatpak install flathub <app-id>Install an app
flatpak updateUpdate all Flatpaks now
flatpak uninstall <app-id>Remove an app
flatpak uninstall --unusedRemove leftover runtimes no app needs. Frees disk space.

Warehouse is a graphical app for managing Flatpaks, if you prefer clicking.

RPM Fusion and codecs

Fedora only ships software with no patent or licensing problems. That leaves out some video codecs. RPM Fusion is a well-known extra repository that provides them. It is already enabled. The full FFmpeg and hardware video decoding drivers are installed, so videos play smoothly in VLC and other apps. You don't need to do anything else.

SELinux basics

SELinux is explained in "Your security, explained". Day to day you won't notice it. Things to know:

  • Check it with sestatus. It should say enabled and enforcing.
  • Don't disable it. Lots of old forum posts say "just turn off SELinux". That removes a major protection to hide a symptom.
  • If you suspect SELinux is blocking something, look at recent denials: sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent. Copy the output into a help request rather than trying to change rules yourself.
  • General system errors since the last start: journalctl -b -p err.

Btrfs and snapshots

The drive uses the Btrfs file system. Btrfs can take snapshots: instant, space-saving copies of the system at a moment in time. On this laptop, Snapper takes a snapshot of the system every hour and clears out old ones. Snapshots cover the system, not your home folder. So rolling back undoes a bad update but doesn't touch your documents.

To roll back after a bad update:

  1. Open Btrfs Assistant from the app menu. It asks for your password.
  2. Go to the Snapper tab and choose the root configuration.
  3. Pick a snapshot from before the problem started. The dates and times are listed.
  4. Click Restore, confirm, and restart.

Before doing something risky, take a snapshot by hand:

Terminal
sudo snapper -c root create --description "before trying X"

List snapshots with sudo snapper -c root list. Remember: snapshots live on the same drive. If the drive dies or the laptop is stolen, they go with it. They are not backups.

Customising KDE Plasma

Plasma is very flexible. You can make it look like Windows, macOS, or something of your own. Nothing here can break your system, so experiment freely.

  • Panels. Right-click the bottom panel and choose Enter Edit Mode (or Show Panel Configuration). You can move it to another edge, change its height, make it float, or add a second panel.
  • Widgets. In edit mode, choose Add Widgets. Drag clocks, weather, system monitors, sticky notes and more onto the desktop or panel.
  • Themes. System Settings, Colors & Themes has Global Theme (the whole look in one click), colours, window decorations, icons and cursors. Switch between light and dark here. Get New... buttons download community themes. Stick with well-rated ones.
  • Night Light. Reduces blue light in the evening. Search System Settings for "Night Light" and set it to follow sunset and sunrise, or a fixed time.
  • Display scaling. If text and icons look too small or too big on the laptop screen, open System Settings, Display & Monitor and change the Scale (for example 125% or 150%). You can also set resolution, refresh rate and the arrangement of external monitors here.
  • Wallpaper. Right-click the desktop and choose Desktop and Wallpaper.
  • Behaviour. Prefer double-click to open files, as on Windows? Search System Settings for "click" and change it.

A note on Xfce (old PCs)

Older PCs set up with the lite profile use the Xfce desktop. It uses less memory and runs well on old hardware. It looks simpler but works the same way: an app menu, a panel, windows. The differences:

  • The file manager is Thunar, not Dolphin.
  • Settings are in the Settings Manager in the app menu, not System Settings.
  • The terminal is Xfce Terminal. Ctrl+Alt+T opens it there too, and the same commands work.
  • Discover isn't installed. Use dnf and flatpak from the terminal, or GNOME Software if it is present.
  • On lite, all updates install automatically, not just security ones. SSH (remote login) is switched on and protected by fail2ban, so you can manage the PC from another machine.
  • No snapshots, ClamAV or OpenSnitch. Rename the PC with sudo hostnamectl hostname <new-name>.

Looking after yourself: emergency kit, family, reminders and help

On this page 7 sections
  1. Emergency Kit: where your recovery codes live
  2. Reminders before things run out (the care calendar)
  3. The daily backup check
  4. Children and visitors (Family Safety)
  5. Tips of the day and the shortcut poster

  7. The five-screen welcome, and every question later

This chapter covers the small helpers that look after you rather than the computer: the emergency kit, reminders before things expire, a safe setup for children and visitors, the daily tips, and how to get help when you are stuck.

Emergency Kit: where your recovery codes live

What it is. A page you print (Ctrl+P) and keep somewhere safe with your passport. It says where things are kept, never the secrets themselves: the Bitwarden master password hint, the Bitwarden recovery code, the disk recovery key, the Ente Auth recovery phrase, the backup passphrase, the phone PIN and PUK, and email recovery details. It fills in this laptop's name, model and serial number (useful for the police and insurance). It also has:

  • a two-step login checklist (email first, then Bitwarden, Google, Microsoft, Apple, banks and myGov, Steam, Discord, NordVPN, GitHub, social media, shops);
  • how to set up Bitwarden Emergency Access (web vault, Settings, Emergency access; it needs Bitwarden Premium for you and a free account for your contact; you choose the waiting time);
  • a pointer to haveibeenpwned.com to check for data breaches once a year, and IDCARE (1800 595 160) if your identity details leak;
  • what to do if the laptop is lost or stolen.

Why you want it. If something happens to you or the laptop, the people you trust can find the way in. And you will not forget to turn on two-step login for the accounts that matter.

  1. Open Emergency Kit from the app menu (or run secure-linux-emergency-kit). The page opens in your browser.
  2. Print it (Ctrl+P). Fill the blanks in by hand with a pen.
  3. Keep it in a safe place away from the laptop, such as with your passport.

A copy is saved as Emergency Kit.html in Documents. Make a fresh one any time. secure-linux-emergency-kit --out FILE writes it somewhere else without opening it. If it fails: if the page does not open, open the file from Documents yourself. Remember: never type your real secrets into the page; it is designed so you cannot.

Reminders before things run out (the care calendar)

What it is. The page Reminders before things run out asks for renewal dates: NordVPN, Cloudflare, Bitwarden Premium, a domain name, a card expiry. Leave blanks to skip. Dates in Australian form (18/03/2027), ISO form (2027-03-18) or card form (08/29, meaning the end of August 2029) all work. You get a notice 60, 30 and 7 days before, and on the day. Dates stay on this laptop. A few dates are worked out automatically (when your Fedora version stops getting updates, and a reminder to rebuild the USB stick a year after it was made).

  • See everything: secure-linux-care list.
  • Add one: secure-linux-care add nordvpn-renewal 2027-03-18 (the name may have letters, digits, - and _).
  • Remove one: secure-linux-care remove nordvpn-renewal.

If it fails. "Not a date": use one of the three forms above. Your own dates live in ~/.config/secure-linux/care-dates; you can fix a line there by hand.

The daily backup check

What it is. A quiet check, once a day, that your backups really happen. It warns if there has been no backup for 7 days, if backups were never set up, if your home-server backup is too old, and gives a monthly "try restoring a file" reminder. It also saves the list of apps you have installed into your backups, so a restore can reinstall them. It shows its notices through the usual notifier and the Status window, once a day at most. Run it by hand: secure-linux-backup-check (or --status to look without notifications). Set up the backups themselves in the "Backups" chapter.

Children and visitors (Family Safety)

Open Family Safety from the app menu (or secure-linux-family). It asks what you need and sets it up. There are three separate tools.

The family filter

What it is. It blocks adult and dangerous websites for everyone on this computer, even with the VPN on, using Cloudflare for Families (encrypted). secure-linux-family filter on, off or status.

Pros: one switch, covers every browser and app. Cons: no filter is perfect; it blocks by website name only; while it is on the VPN cannot replace the DNS (the VPN still hides your traffic); Cloudflare WARP is refused while it is on. A knowledgeable child with an administrator password could turn it off, so keep that password private.

Children's accounts

Choose add-child (or "Add a Family Member" in the app menu for an adult). These are standard accounts: they cannot install system software or change system settings. Parental Controls (secure-linux-family apps) lets you tick which apps each child may use, and set an age rating for installing apps.

Limits, honestly. There are no screen-time limits on KDE or Xfce. Only Flatpak apps are enforced (most apps here). And nothing stops someone who knows your password.

Guest account for visitors

The username is guest and the password is guest (the setup tells you; tell your visitors). Its home folder lives in memory only: everything is deleted at logout, power-off or restart. Visitors cannot see your files or install system software. Because the password is well known, it can only be used at the keyboard, not over the network. Remove it with secure-linux-family guest-remove; create it with secure-linux-family guest-setup. secure-linux-family status shows what is set up.

Adding an adult family member

App menu, Add a Family Member: it makes a standard account with VPN access and a short welcome. They make their own Bitwarden account.

Tips of the day and the shortcut poster

For your first 14 days one short tip a day appears as a small notification: Windows habits and their equivalents here (for example Win+E becomes Meta+E). After the 14th they stop by themselves. Each tip links to the guide page with more.

  • Switch off or on: secure-linux-tips --off and --on.
  • See them all: secure-linux-tips --list. Where you are: --status.
  • The printable A4 keyboard-shortcut poster (KDE and Xfce columns): Tips and Shortcuts in the app menu, or secure-linux-tips --poster.

Finding help later: guide search and "Explain This Error"

Search the guide

Type what you want into the app launcher (press the Meta key, then type): the guide is searchable, so "printer" or "VPN" finds the right page. The searchable copy is in Documents, Secure Linux Guide (one small page per chapter and per app). This page you are reading has its own search box at the top too. From the terminal: secure-linux-explain --search printer wifi.

Explain This Error

What it is. Copy an error message you do not understand (select it, then Ctrl+C) and open Explain This Error from the app menu. Your private AI (Ollama, running on this computer only; nothing is sent anywhere) explains it in plain English, then lists the matching guide pages. If the AI is not installed or not running, you still get the guide pages.

  1. Copy the message (Ctrl+C).
  2. Open Explain This Error.
  3. Read the explanation and the list of guide pages.

From the terminal: secure-linux-explain "error text", or some-command 2>&1 | secure-linux-explain - to explain what a command printed. --no-ai skips the AI and searches the guide.

Honest limits. The AI can be wrong, and it never runs anything for you. Read before you act, and never paste a command with sudo that you do not understand. A small model on a laptop is slower and less accurate than the big cloud ones; that is the price of privacy.

If it fails. "Not set up": the AI models download only after you say yes in the wizard (see the private AI section in "Every Secure Linux tool"). The guide pages still appear.

The five-screen welcome, and every question later

The default first login now has exactly five screens. Nothing has changed yet when the last screen appears. Confirm starts the steps you enabled, Back changes your answers, and closing the window cancels. There is no countdown.

Wizard file/IDWhat you see
00-coreTitleless shared infrastructure, not another question screen.
01-system1 of 5 — Your recommended setup
02-identity2 of 5 — You, Wi-Fi and passwords
03-apps-security3 of 5 — Applications and protection
04-extras4 of 5 — Optional extras
05-review5 of 5 — Review everything

On the protection screen, choose Recommended — everyday protection, Stricter — also VPN private mode and audit log, or Custom — keep current settings, then untick or tick below. The final review lists the enabled work before anything runs.

Open Secure Linux Welcome & Setup for the beginner journeys, or Welcome & Setup Choices to run the welcome again. The commands are secure-linux-setup-hub and secure-linux-welcome --again. secure-linux-welcome --status shows saved progress and secure-linux-welcome --add-family-member adds an adult account.

The longer migration, server and legacy questions are not a second queue you must finish on day one. Open one when needed with secure-linux-welcome --page PAGE or secure-linux-migrate. Built-in page IDs are browser homewifi vpn battery recovery backup ai syncthing netguard hwtest tpmpin mok.

  • Browser: LibreWolf, and whether to stay signed in to websites. Forgetting cookies gives more privacy but means signing in again.
  • Home Wi-Fi: tells the computer which network is home (see “Home or away”).
  • Syncthing password: protects Syncthing's local settings page.

The legacy protection page

The on-demand legacy page 05-security is called Choose your protection level. It opens the same current Control Centre choice; it is not a sixth first-run screen. You can also open Secure Linux Control Centre directly, or use its menu actions Review recommended protection and Open security status and fixes.

Using your computer

When life happens: lost laptop, new phone, selling, old drives

On this page 8 sections
  1. The laptop is lost or stolen
  2. A new phone
  3. Selling or giving away the laptop
  4. Your old Windows SSD
  5. A family member wants an account
  6. A new printer
  7. Going on a trip
  8. Things worth keeping safe

These are step-by-step checklists for the things that go wrong, or change, in real life. Keep this chapter in mind rather than memorised: it is here for the day you need it.

The laptop is lost or stolen

Your files are safe: the whole drive is encrypted, so a thief who switches it off and takes it cannot read anything (your disk password is the key; see "Your disk-encryption password"). What to do, in order, from another device:

  1. Change your Bitwarden master password, then your email password.
  2. Sign the laptop out of Signal (Linked devices), Tuta (Sessions), NordVPN (Devices) and Ente Auth.
  3. Make a police report with the laptop's serial number (it is on your Emergency Kit page).
  4. If you use a Bitwarden Emergency Access contact, nothing needs to change.
  5. Restore onto a new computer: install with the USB stick, open Pika Backup, choose Restore ("Backups" chapter).
  6. If you suspect identity theft, IDCARE is on 1800 595 160.

Honest limit: encryption only protects a laptop that is switched off. If it was stolen while on and unlocked, treat everything as exposed and change passwords straight away. Shut down (do not just sleep) when leaving it somewhere risky.

A new phone

  1. Install Bitwarden, Ente Auth, Signal, KDE Connect, LocalSend, Syncthing-Fork, Immich and NordVPN.
  2. Move your Ente Auth codes. Keep the old phone's codes until the new ones work.
  3. Re-pair KDE Connect with the laptop.
  4. In Syncthing on the laptop, add the new phone and remove the old.
  5. Wipe the old phone only when everything works.

Selling or giving away the laptop

  1. Check that a restore of your backup works first.
  2. Boot the USB stick, choose SystemRescue and use Wipe before selling (in "Repair This Computer"; you must type ERASE and the drive's name). This erases for good.
  3. In the BIOS (F2): clear the TPM and remove any BIOS password.
  4. Remove the laptop from the NordVPN, Signal, Tuta and Bitwarden device lists.

Your old Windows SSD

  • Put it in a USB enclosure (an M.2 2280 NVMe enclosure for most laptops). Keep it untouched for 3 to 6 months before reusing it.
  • If it was protected by BitLocker, click the drive in Dolphin and enter the 48-digit recovery key (find it at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey).
  • Your Windows licence is stored in the computer's firmware, not on the drive.
  • ASUS BIOS updates: use EZ Flash (F2, Advanced) from a FAT32 stick with the charger plugged in. Or see "Firmware updates" for the guided tool.
  • To see a Western Digital SN770 SSD's firmware version: sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep '^fr '.

A family member wants an account

App menu, Add a Family Member: a standard account, VPN access, and a short welcome. They make their own Bitwarden account. For children see "Looking after yourself".

A new printer

Same Wi-Fi as the laptop. Most printers from the last 10 years are driverless: System Settings, Printers, Add (Xfce: Print Settings). Scanning: Skanpage (full) or Document Scanner (lite). Printers are visible only on your home network (see "Home or away"). More in "Bringing your stuff over from Windows".

Going on a trip

  • Charge to 100% once with Charge to 100% for a Trip.
  • Turn on the VPN (secure-linux-vpn private) before you use hotel Wi-Fi. For the hotel's sign-in page use Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login.
  • Shut down (not sleep) in places where the laptop might be taken.
  • Away from home the laptop goes quiet on the network by itself (no phone link, file sharing or printer announcements).

Things worth keeping safe

  • The disk password, and the recovery key on paper (not with the laptop).
  • The Bitwarden master password and its recovery code.
  • The backup drive's password.
  • The USB stick (it has your Wi-Fi password and a hash of your login password on it if you chose that; see "The USB stick").

Secure Linux Welcome & Setup

Secure Linux Welcome & Setup (secure-linux-setup-hub) is the simplest place to find a task. It opens fixed existing graphical tools after confirmation; it has no web view, local server or hidden settings changes.

  1. Welcome & Setup Choices
  2. Finish Setting Up My Computer
  3. Install Apps & Fill In Missing Software
  4. Move My Passwords from Chrome or Edge
  5. Back Up My Files
  6. Restore My Files from a Backup
  7. Security & Privacy
  8. My Computer Activity
  9. Flipper Zero — Open qFlipper
  10. USB Drives — View, Format & Check
  11. Home Assistant
  12. Install System & App Updates
  13. Customise My Apps & Desktop

Secure Linux Control Centre

Open Secure Linux Control Centre or run secure-linux-control-center. The menu also provides Review recommended protection and Open security status and fixes. secure-linux-security-audit is the security status/fixes helper.

The window covers firewall, OpenSnitch, secure DNS, VPN private mode, automatic updates, weekly ClamAV, USBGuard, Fail2ban, screen lock, auditd, Secure Boot, disk encryption, Flatpak permissions and rootless Docker.

ChoiceWhat it owns
Recommended — everyday protectionFirewall, OpenSnitch, secure DNS, automatic updates, weekly ClamAV, Fail2ban and screen lock.
Stricter — also VPN private mode and audit logThe Recommended set plus VPN private mode and auditd.
Custom — keep current settings, then untick or tick belowPreserves current settings until you explicitly change an item.
  • USBGuard is never preselected.
  • Secure Boot and disk encryption are informational.
  • Flatpak permissions opens Flatseal; Docker opens Home & Server Helper.
  • Auditd can be enabled but not disabled in this window.
  • DNS “off” is only a 15-minute pause.

Every change has review, explicit Confirm and post-change verification. If something fails, earlier successful reversible changes are rolled back where possible. Partial or failed rollback is reported honestly.

My Computer Activity

My Computer Activity (secure-linux-activity) is a native GTK4/Libadwaita, local and read-only dashboard. It does not make network requests, capture packets, inspect browsing history or read document contents to build its report.

Sections cover current network connections; firewall and OpenSnitch alerts; Secure Linux background jobs; updates and scheduled runs; disk space and SMART; CPU, memory and storage; recent logins and admin actions; USB/device events; Docker and Home Assistant; backup, install and recovery; and security findings with next steps.

It reads local connection metadata from ss, service/timer state and journals, update records, df/lsblk/SMART data, /proc memory/load, last and sudo journals, USB/kernel events, container names/images/status, setup/Pika state, kit alerts/checks and ClamAV finding lines.

  • F5 refreshes; search filters card content.
  • Ctrl+E opens export review. HTML is written only after preview and your destination choice.
  • Username, IP/device-address and token/secret redactions default on. Arbitrary log lines can still contain private details, so review the preview.
  • Dashboard buttons open only fixed existing graphical tools after confirmation and never change settings themselves.

Private AI: compare, route, download and chat

Open Private AI (secure-linux-ai gui). Ollama and Colibri run supported models locally once downloaded. Local does not mean correct: review facts and code, and do not enable shell or agent tools from the frontend guidance.

Find a model that fits

Terminal
secure-linux-ai scan
secure-linux-ai models
secure-linux-ai route --workload interactive --engine ollama
secure-linux-ai route --workload balanced
secure-linux-ai route --workload quality
secure-linux-ai route --workload low-storage

The exact route interface is secure-linux-ai route --workload interactive|balanced|quality|low-storage [--engine ollama|colibri]. The router excludes fewer-refusals models, ranks feasible fit gates first, and uses only same-device measured decode results as interactive tie-breakers. It does not predict tokens per second from RAM, model size or GPU presence. RAM gates are wrapper fit heuristics, not throughput claims.

Maintained catalogueNotes
Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B, 7B and 14BOllama-only coding models; Colibri's pinned registry does not support qwen2.
Qwen2.5 Coder 7B fewer-refusalsExplicit legacy/alternative workflow; excluded from normal routing.
Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3BLarge coding option subject to the wrapper's fit gates.
Qwen3.6 35B-A3BGeneral-purpose and may help with code; not claimed to be a coding specialist.
Qwen3 4B fewer-refusalsExplicit alternative workflow; excluded from normal routing and never used as a Qwen2 alias.

Download, install and chat

Terminal
secure-linux-ai download MODEL --engine ollama --confirm
secure-linux-ai install MODEL --engine ollama --confirm
secure-linux-ai chat MODEL --prompt "Explain this error in plain English" --session my-session

Download and install accept [--engine ollama|colibri] [--confirm] [--offline]. Chat is secure-linux-ai chat MODEL --prompt TEXT [--session ID]; prompt - reads standard input. remove removes a selected model and chat-clear clears chat state after review. frontends lists the available fixed frontends.

Colibri commands are colibri-install, colibri-import, colibri-start, colibri-stop, colibri-status and colibri-rollback. Legacy setup, pull, import-unfiltered, vulkan on|off|bench|rollback and status remain.

Measure, do not guess

benchmark-ollama and benchmark-colibri require --backend cpu|vulkan and --confirm. Runs can be 1–9, tokens 1–1024, and cache states are unspecified, warm-process or cold-process. Cold-process does not mean a cold operating-system page cache.

The benchmark prompt is a short fixed prime-function prompt and records quality_assessed: false. It is not long coding-agent prefill or answer-quality evidence. Vulkan benchmarking uses warm-ups and three interleaved CPU/Vulkan rounds, retaining Vulkan only if median decode is more than 10% faster. A pre-benchmark rollback state is retained.

The legacy Qwen2.5 ChatML Modelfile template still needs verification against ollama show ... --modelfile. Tools and FIM are omitted; do not present that template as current proof of tool use, FIM or answer quality.

Install System & App Updates

Install System & App Updates opens secure-linux-update-gui. The reviewed terminal helper is secure-linux-update-now. Updates and scheduled history also appear in My Computer Activity. Restart when the update tool asks; do not turn off the computer during an offline update.

Finishing and readiness

Finish Setting Up My Computer opens secure-linux-finish --gui. It can restore remaining documents, photos and bookmarks, open app setup steps, export non-secret choices for another Secure Linux computer and save a care sheet. It never signs in for you and asks before replacing files. secure-linux-finish summary shows remaining work and secure-linux-finish care shows the care summary.

secure-linux-ready separately checks the core system, internet, desktop sound/video, guide, firmware where applicable, snapshots and chosen apps. A green result means those checks passed, not that every physical device or account was tested.

Flipper Zero Backup & Files

Flipper Zero Backup & Files launches secure-linux-flipper. Start with secure-linux-flipper status, explicitly select the mounted SD card and make a verified backup. The tool never assumes that any removable mount is the Flipper.

It supports verified SD backups/restores, encrypted computer backups, file and favourites organisation, reviewed RogueMaster release downloads, SD resource staging, qFlipper hand-off, Boot2Flipper payload preparation and release checks. A staged update or launched qFlipper process is not firmware-flash success. SD rollback is not internal firmware/radio rollback. See the Flipper companion README for the full command contract and limitations.

USB creation, portable copies and repair

Linux USB Installer Creator - Turn any blank USB into a Linux installer opens secure-linux-usb-creator-gui; the CLI is secure-linux-usb-creator. It supports list, create, clone, portable, measure, verify, status and an interactive menu.

Exact clone requires target capacity for the complete raw source image. On a larger target only the master-sized beginning is overwritten and verified; the remaining tail may retain old data. Portable copy is separate: a genuine Ventoy installation, saved file-tree copy and verification of every file.

Minimum size is calculated from content, allocation, Ventoy/filesystem overhead and a safety margin. 64 GB or 128 GB recommendations are headroom, not universal minimums. Nominal 32 GB is accepted only when enumerated bytes meet the calculated requirement. Confirmation waits for ERASE SERIAL-OR-WWN and has no timeout. Interrupted output remains incomplete and not verified.

Secure Linux USB Fixer opens secure-linux-usb-fixer-gui; the CLI is secure-linux-usb-fixer. It is image-first: diagnose, capture a raw image, recover files and repair a disposable image copy. Repair does not alter the original. Formatting is destructive and requires two different exact confirmations. Fixed disks, partitions and the system disk are refused; formatting is not secure erase.

Offline application bundles

secure-linux-offline-bundle verify checks the staged bundle selected on this computer. install installs only a verified, populated component. Incomplete metadata, missing dependencies, architecture mismatches and hash failures stop installation. report recounts real files and sizes. Building a bundle is a separate administrator workflow on a matching distribution and architecture.

Normal installers try signed online sources first. Cached copies are a fallback and may need updating. The current sealed cache has 548,477 payload/repository files, 31,478,979,440 logical bytes and 27,341,383,680 hardlink-aware physical allocated bytes. All 24 final metadata hashes and every requested system dependency closure pass.

  • Fedora Full: 40/40 Flatpak apps on x86_64; 21/40 on aarch64.
  • Fedora Lite: 6/6 on x86_64; 5/6 on aarch64. Debian Lite amd64 includes Bitwarden.
  • Individual ArtCraft RPM/DEB application payloads are included, not just a downloader.
  • Fedora Full ARM has 18 not-yet-cached apps and no cached Tor Browser Launcher; Fedora Lite ARM also lacks that launcher.
  • NordVPN, Cloudflare and some other external bootstrap components still need separate signed online acquisition. Accounts, models and server data are not bundled apps.

The offline regression run completed 40 tests successfully with one native-Zstandard test skipped; separate no-network Ollama checks passed. Hash-auditing the expanded 40-app x86_64 repository is not the same as natively installing all 40 apps without a network. Native RPM/DEB system-package installation and physical USB delivery remain separate acceptance steps. Exact current coverage lives in offline-bundle/README.md.

Release coherence and guide data

secure-linux-release show displays the release ID. Maintainers deliberately run secure-linux-release stamp after reviewed source changes, regenerate every affected output, then run secure-linux-release check. Add --master-store /path/to/master-store to include saved USB masters. Stamping alone never proves a physical USB or netboot render is current.

The maintained release summary is docs/RELEASE-NOTES.md. Guide chapters live in guide/src/chapters/; older page data is in guide/data/pages.json and related JSON; application entries are in guide/data/apps-a.json through apps-e.json. guide/data/pages-chapters.json is generated by the chapter packer and must not be hand-edited. Feature-to-anchor coverage is maintained in guide/tools/coverage-map.json.

Home or away: trusted networks

At home, phone linking, LocalSend, Syncthing, printers and network names can work. Away, the firewall blocks those local-sharing paths and Syncthing is paused. Check with secure-linux-zone status. Use set-home, unset-home and list to manage the saved networks.

Encrypted DNS and hotel Wi-Fi

DNS turns a website name into an address. The configured malware-blocking encrypted DNS and VPN DNS hand-over are shown by secure-linux-dns status. The family filter is managed with secure-linux-dns family on|off|status or Family Safety.

Open Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login or run secure-linux-hotspot for a public sign-in page. It pauses the configured VPN/DNS protections, opens the login helper and restores the prior state afterwards. The default window is 15 minutes; secure-linux-hotspot 30 selects 30. secure-linux-dns open [MINUTES] pauses only DNS and secure-linux-dns secure resumes it.

Disk unlock extras

Your normal disk password keeps working beside every optional extra. secure-linux-recovery-key creates a spare key and status checks for one. header-backup /path/on/a/USB saves the encryption header; an old header can retain old password slots, so protect it and refresh it after password changes.

FIDO2 security key

secure-linux-fido2 status, enroll and remove manage a supported security key. Register two keys and keep the ordinary password/recovery key. A Flipper U2F app is not the same disk-unlock workflow.

TPM PIN

secure-linux-tpm-pin status, enable and disable manage the optional PIN path when Secure Boot supports it. Treat it as convenience, not a replacement for the strong disk password.

Remove the installer's Secure Boot key

secure-linux-mok-remove starts the reviewed Ventoy-key removal and status lists the relevant keys. Afterwards the stick needs Secure Boot off or key enrolment again. Follow the blue MOK screen carefully.

Fedora upgrades and outside apps

secure-linux-upgrade is the guided Fedora version upgrade. It checks power and space, prepares a snapshot and repository state, downloads after review and asks before restarting. --now bypasses the ordinary waiting period and --to VERSION selects a version; current repository readiness still matters.

Applications outside Fedora

secure-linux-outside-apps shows managed outside-application versions and --update applies reviewed updates. The source verifies the pinned download fingerprint where that workflow is defined. Current upstream availability is not inferred from old guide dates.

Saved choices

secure-linux-choice list shows settings, get KEY reads one and sudo secure-linux-choice set KEY VALUE changes one. Changes take effect immediately only where a helper applies them; otherwise use Repair setup. Common keys include opensnitch, netguard_notify, netguard_prompt_duration, vpn_mode, nord_killswitch, nord_autoconnect, nord_lan_discovery, nord_threat_protection, warp, family_dns, battery_limit, hibernate, secureboot_intent, tpm_pin, mok_removed, recovery_key_done, default_browser, librewolf_keep_cookies, ai_models, ollama_vulkan, ai_abliterated, backup_target, immich_url, server_health_url, home_ssid, drm, power_tuning, power_battery_saver, privacy_countme_off, syncthing_lan_only, lite_auto_reboot, parts_autoinstall, and the fleet, app-selection and Home Assistant keys described in their chapters.

Checks, notifications and terminal

  • secure-linux-check turns problems into plain-English alerts and clears resolved ones. Its scheduled scans never delete antivirus findings automatically.
  • secure-linux-notify shows active alerts and one-off events without repeatedly nagging about the same unchanged item.
  • secure-linux-terminal COMMAND opens a command in the available desktop terminal and keeps output readable for menu workflows.

Staying safe

Your security, explained

On this page 19 sections
  1. Layer 1: Full-disk encryption (LUKS2)
  2. Layer 2: Your login password and sudo
  3. Layer 3: SELinux (enforcing)
  4. Layer 4: The firewall (deny incoming)
  5. Layer 5: Encrypted DNS with malware blocking
  6. Layer 6: Network privacy
  7. Layer 7: VPN with a kill switch
  8. Layer 8: Network protection (OpenSnitch), the outbound app firewall
  9. Layer 9: Flatpak sandboxing and Flatseal
  10. Layer 10: Automatic updates
  11. Layer 11: Kernel hardening
  12. Layer 12: Secure Boot, kept on
  13. Layer 13: ClamAV antivirus
  14. Layer 14: Lynis security audits
  15. Layer 15: Bitwarden and two-factor authentication
  16. Layer 16: Backups
  17. Extra locks you can add
  18. How the layers fit together
  19. What this does NOT protect against

No single tool makes a computer safe. This laptop uses layers. Each layer stops a different kind of problem. If one layer misses something, another often catches it. This chapter explains each layer in plain terms.

Layer 1: Full-disk encryption (LUKS2)

Protects against: someone stealing the laptop, or pulling out the drive, and reading your files.

Everything on the internal drive is encrypted with LUKS2, the Linux equivalent of BitLocker. Without the password you type at power-on, the drive is unreadable noise. This is why the power-on password matters so much. It is the key to everything. Encryption only protects you when the laptop is switched off. Once you've unlocked it, the data is readable by the running system. So shut down (rather than sleep) when travelling or leaving the laptop somewhere risky.

Layer 2: Your login password and sudo

Protects against: someone using the laptop while it is on but locked, and programs quietly changing the system.

You use your login password to unlock the screen and to approve system changes. Any command that starts with sudo needs it. The built-in "root" super-user account is locked, so nobody can log in as root directly. Lock the screen with Meta+L (the Windows key plus L) whenever you step away.

Layer 3: SELinux (enforcing)

Protects against: a program that has been hacked doing damage beyond its own job.

SELinux is a set of strict rules built into Fedora. It says, for example, "the web server may read web files but not your home folder". Even if an attacker takes over a service, SELinux limits what it can touch. It is set to enforcing, which means the rules are applied, not just logged. Never switch it off. Check it with sestatus.

Layer 4: The firewall (deny incoming)

Protects against: other devices on the same network (café Wi-Fi, hotel, a compromised smart TV) connecting to your laptop.

Fedora's usual desktop setting allows many incoming connections. This machine uses the stricter public zone. It blocks everything coming in, except KDE Connect, Syncthing and LocalSend, which need it to talk to your phone. Even those are open only on networks you have marked as home. On every other network (cafes, hotels, airports) the laptop goes quiet: no phone link, no file-sharing announcements. See "Home or away" in the tools chapter. Outgoing connections (you browsing the web) are not affected by this firewall.

Layer 5: Encrypted DNS with malware blocking

Protects against: your internet provider or Wi-Fi owner seeing which sites you look up, tampering with the answers, and you landing on known malware sites.

Before visiting a site, your computer asks a DNS server for its address. Normally that question travels unencrypted, and anyone on the network can read or change it. Here, every lookup goes over an encrypted connection (DNS-over-TLS) to Cloudflare's 1.1.1.2 service. That service also refuses to answer for known malware sites. Quad9 is the backup. When the VPN is connected, the VPN handles DNS too.

Two helpers sit on top. Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login pauses the VPN and encrypted DNS for up to 15 minutes so a public Wi-Fi sign-in page can load, then restores exactly what was on. The family filter swaps in Cloudflare's family DNS (1.1.1.3) to block adult sites for everyone on the computer, even with the VPN on. Both are in "Every Secure Linux tool, A to Z".

Layer 6: Network privacy

Protects against: being tracked as you move between networks.

  • MAC address randomisation. Every network card has a hardware ID, the MAC address. Shops and public Wi-Fi can use it to recognise you on every visit. This laptop shows a different made-up MAC address to each network. On a given network it stays the same, so you don't have to log in again each time.
  • Hostname hiding. The computer doesn't announce its name (which often contains your name) when it joins a network.
  • IPv6 privacy addresses. Your IPv6 address changes regularly, so websites can't use it as a permanent ID.

Layer 7: VPN with a kill switch

Protects against: the Wi-Fi owner or your internet provider seeing what you do, and websites seeing your real location.

NordVPN wraps all your traffic in an encrypted tunnel to a NordVPN server. The kill switch blocks all traffic if that tunnel drops, so nothing slips out unprotected. A VPN moves trust from your internet provider to the VPN company. It does not make you anonymous, and it does not stop websites from tracking you once you log in.

Layer 8: Network protection (OpenSnitch), the outbound app firewall

Protects against: apps quietly sending data out, malware "phoning home", and trackers.

The normal firewall watches traffic coming in. Network protection watches traffic going out. The first time a brand-new app wants to go online it asks you once, and apps that came with the computer are already approved. It also keeps weekly-updated block lists of known malware, phishing, tracking and spying websites, and blocks them for every app. If it ever blocks something you need, you can allow it in one click. It fails safe: if its lists or the program itself break, your internet keeps working. The Network Monitor window shows what connected where. See "Network Monitor: which apps may go online".

Layer 9: Flatpak sandboxing and Flatseal

Protects against: one app reading files or devices it has no business touching.

Most apps here are Flatpaks. Each one runs in a sandbox, a box with limited access to the rest of the system. Each app declares the permissions it needs. Flatseal lets you see and tighten those permissions. For example, you can stop an app from seeing your whole home folder.

Layer 10: Automatic updates

Protects against: attacks on known security holes. These are by far the most common kind.

On the main laptop, system updates download and prepare themselves every day and install while the computer restarts (with a snapshot first), so a restart about once a week is part of staying safe. Apps update daily. Firmware is checked regularly. Old PCs install updates daily. The "What runs automatically" chapter has the details. Restart about once a week so the updates fully take effect.

Layer 11: Kernel hardening

Protects against: attackers who already have a foothold trying to go further, and some network tricks.

  • kptr_restrict and dmesg_restrict hide internal kernel memory addresses and kernel messages from normal programs. Attackers use those to plan exploits.
  • ptrace_scope stops one program from spying on the memory of another program that isn't its own child. For example, it stops malware from reading passwords out of your browser's memory.
  • ICMP redirects are ignored. This stops a device on your network from telling your laptop to route traffic through it.
  • Other settings protect against "SYN flood" network attacks and some file-system tricks in shared folders.

Layer 12: Secure Boot, kept on

Protects against: "bootkits", malware that loads before the operating system and hides from it.

Secure Boot is kept on unless you chose to turn it off in the installer (a choice with pros and cons, because a laptop can only hibernate with Secure Boot off). Fedora is signed, so it starts normally. The one extra key added for the Ventoy USB stick is explained in the "How the automatic USB install works" chapter, and you can remove it afterwards with secure-linux-mok-remove.

Layer 13: ClamAV antivirus

Protects against: known malware arriving in downloads, especially Windows malware you might pass on to others.

Linux malware aimed at desktops is rare, but not zero. ClamAV scans your Downloads and Desktop weekly. If it finds something, the Status window says so and nothing is deleted without you. ClamTk lets you scan any file or folder on demand.

Layer 14: Lynis security audits

Protects against: settings slowly drifting into a weaker state.

Run sudo lynis audit system every few months. It gives a "hardening index" and a list of suggestions. Many are for servers. Don't change anything you don't understand; ask first.

Layer 15: Bitwarden and two-factor authentication

Protects against: stolen or guessed passwords, which is how most accounts get hacked.

Bitwarden creates and remembers a different strong password for every site. Ente Auth provides the six-digit two-factor codes. Even if a password leaks, an attacker without your code can't log in. Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere it is offered, starting with email, Bitwarden itself, and banking.

Layer 16: Backups

Protects against: theft, drive failure, accidental deletion, and ransomware.

Every other layer can fail. A good backup is what lets you recover. See the "Backups" chapter.

Extra locks you can add

These are optional, and your disk password always keeps working beside each of them:

  • A recovery key: a spare long code for the encrypted disk in case you forget your password. Strongly recommended.
  • A security key (YubiKey, Nitrokey and the like) to unlock the disk by touch.
  • A short PIN checked by the laptop's TPM chip. Honestly: on this Ryzen laptop it is a convenience, not extra security.

All three are explained under "Disk unlock extras" in the tools chapter. For Home Assistant, the checker secure-linux-ha-secure grades your smart-home setup from A to F: see "Keep your smart home safe".

How the layers fit together

ThreatMain layers that help
Laptop stolen while offDisk encryption, backups
Snooping on public Wi-FiVPN + kill switch, encrypted DNS, firewall, MAC randomisation
A malicious or tracking websiteEncrypted DNS blocking, Network protection block lists, LibreWolf's ad blocker
A malicious downloadEncrypted DNS blocking, ClamAV, Flatpak sandbox, SELinux, Network protection
A child or visitor on the computerStandard accounts, the family filter, the guest account that wipes itself
A bug in an app or the systemAutomatic updates, SELinux, sandboxing, kernel hardening
Password leak from a websiteBitwarden (unique passwords), Ente Auth (2FA)
Drive dies or a file is deletedBackups, snapshots (for system files)

What this does NOT protect against

Be honest with yourself about these. No software fixes them.

  • Phishing. If you type your password into a fake login page, the attacker has it. Bitwarden helps: it won't auto-fill on a site whose address doesn't match. If Bitwarden doesn't offer your login, stop and check the address.
  • Weak or reused passwords. Let Bitwarden generate them.
  • Physical access while unlocked. Anyone at your unlocked laptop can do anything you can. Lock it (Meta+L) every time you walk away.
  • Sites you choose to trust. Once you log in to a website, it can see what you do there. Encryption and VPNs don't change that.
  • Running random scripts. A command copied from a forum, especially one like curl ... | bash or anything with sudo, can do anything to your system. Every protection here can be undone by a command you choose to run. Only run commands from sources you trust, and ask if unsure.
  • Scams by phone, text or email that persuade you to install "support" software or move money.

Staying safe

Network Monitor: which apps may go online

On this page 10 sections
  1. What it is, in plain words
  2. Why you want it
  3. What you will actually see
  4. The block lists
  5. Review network protection deliberately
  6. Network Monitor: looking around
  7. The command, for when something does not work
  8. If a website or app stops working
  9. Switching it off or back on
  10. Which computers get it

This chapter explains Network protection, the part of this computer that watches which apps connect to the internet. Its window in the app menu is called Network Monitor. Underneath it is a program called OpenSnitch, which is why you will also see that name in the app guides.

What it is, in plain words

Think of a bouncer at the door of a club. Every app that wants to go out onto the internet has to be known to the bouncer first. On the main laptop (the full setup) the bouncer is switched on from the start. You do not have to set anything up.

The ordinary firewall (see "Your security, explained") only guards the incoming door: other devices trying to reach you. Network protection guards the outgoing door: your own apps reaching out. Windows Defender Firewall does very little of this by default, so it is a new idea for most people.

Why you want it

  • A program that quietly sends your data somewhere stands out, because it has to ask first.
  • Malware that "phones home" is stopped at the door if its address is on a known-bad list.
  • Adverts, trackers and "telemetry" (apps reporting on what you do) are blocked for every app, not just in the browser.

What you will actually see

What happensWhat you do
A brand-new app asks to go online for the first time. A small window says "Do you want to let this app connect?" "Always allow" is already picked, so one click on Allow is enough and that app never asks again.Click Allow if you recognise the app. Click Deny if you do not. Nothing is lost by denying: you can change your mind later in Network Monitor.
Apps that came with the computer (your browser, the VPN, updates, the photo app, Syncthing, phone link, and so on) are already approved.Nothing. You will rarely see the window.
Your home network is always fine. Your printer, phone link and home server (Immich) are never blocked.Nothing.
A block list stops something. A message pops up in the corner with three buttons: Allow once, Always allow, Keep blocked. For malware and phishing sites the message adds a warning ("only allow it if you are sure").Read the address. If it is something you asked for and trust, choose Allow once (just this time) or Always allow. If you are unsure, choose Keep blocked.
Once a week a short summary arrives: "Blocked N connections this week".Just read it. A big jump is worth a look in Network Monitor.

The block lists

The computer keeps lists of websites that are known for four things: malware, phishing (fake log-in pages), advertising trackers and spying ("telemetry"). They update by themselves every week. The lists come from two public projects (StevenBlack's hosts list for trackers, and HaGeZi's threat feed for malware and phishing), plus a small list built into this kit. Each new list is checked for sanity before it is used, and the last good copy is kept.

It fails safe. If a list is broken or cannot be downloaded, nothing is blocked because of it and your internet keeps working. If the firewall program ever stops, it restarts by itself. If it cannot, Secure Linux Status shows a message, and your internet still works while it is stopped.

Review network protection deliberately

Read an OpenSnitch question before answering. Choose Deny if you do not recognise the app; you can change the rule later. The current Secure Linux steps do not establish the old claim that an ignored prompt becomes a persistent “always allow” after 60 seconds, so this guide does not rely on that claim. The daemon and graphical prompt are separate pieces of OpenSnitch, and their current upstream behaviour should be checked before documenting a timeout result.

netguard_prompt_duration stores the configured prompt-duration choice (always or restart). Change it only after reading the current helper and prompt settings:

Terminal
sudo secure-linux-choice set netguard_prompt_duration restart

Use always to select the other saved setting. This does not give this guide permission to invent what an unanswered upstream prompt will do.

For a reviewed overview of the firewall, OpenSnitch, DNS, VPN, updates and other protections, open Secure Linux Control Centre. Its Recommended and Stricter presets show exactly what they will change before Confirm. Custom keeps the current settings until you tick or untick an item.

Network Monitor: looking around

  1. Open Network Monitor from the app menu (or the small shield icon in the system tray).
  2. The Events tab lists recent connections: which app, where to, and whether it was allowed.
  3. The Rules tab lists every decision. To change one, double-click it, change Allow to Deny (or the other way round) and save. To make it ask again next time, delete the rule.

Right-click the Network Monitor menu entry for Pause network protection for 15 minutes. There is also Switch network protection back on.

The command, for when something does not work

Type these in the terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T). They ask for your password where needed.

CommandWhat it does
secure-linux-netguard statusIs it on? How many addresses are on each list, and when the lists last updated.
secure-linux-netguard why example.comIs this address blocked, and by which list?
secure-linux-netguard allow example.comLet it through always. Add --once 15 for 15 minutes, or --for /usr/bin/curl to allow it for one program only.
secure-linux-netguard unallow example.comUndo that.
secure-linux-netguard exceptionsList the places you have allowed.
secure-linux-netguard pause 15Let everything through for 15 minutes to find out whether the firewall is the problem. It switches itself back on.
secure-linux-netguard resumeSwitch it back on now.
secure-linux-netguard update-listsDownload the newest block lists now.

If a website or app stops working

  1. Run secure-linux-netguard pause 15 and try again. If it works now, the firewall was the cause. (If it still fails, the problem is somewhere else: see Troubleshooting.)
  2. Run secure-linux-netguard resume, then secure-linux-netguard why the-address.com to see which list has it.
  3. If you trust the address, run secure-linux-netguard allow the-address.com.
  4. If you answered Deny to an app by mistake: open Network Monitor, go to the Rules tab, and delete or change that app's rule.

If it asks about an app you do not recognise: choose Deny. Nothing is lost, and you can allow it later.

Switching it off or back on

  • Off: sudo secure-linux-choice set opensnitch no, then run the repair once (sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair, or "Repair setup" in Secure Linux Status). Back on: set it to yes and repair again.
  • Stop the corner messages about blocked sites but keep the blocking: sudo secure-linux-choice set netguard_notify no.

Pros of leaving it on: you see what your apps do, and known-bad places are blocked everywhere. Cons: the odd question in your first days, and now and then a site on a list that you need (the three buttons fix that in one click).

Which computers get it

  • Full setup (the main laptop): everything above.
  • Lite setup (older PC) with 3 GB of memory or more: only the quiet part runs. The block lists work, but it never asks questions. With less memory it is left out, and you are told once.
  • Atomic setup and the Debian versions: not included. The ordinary firewall and encrypted DNS still protect you.

Honest limit: this watches by program and by website name. A program that is already allowed, and that has been taken over by an attacker, can still use its permission. Network protection is one layer of many, not a guarantee.
