Staying safe

Your disk-encryption password

On this page 8 sections
  1. Why there is a password at power-on
  2. How strong should it be?
  3. Where to keep it
  4. What happens if you lose it
  5. Adding a backup passphrase
  6. Changing your passphrase
  7. Spare ways in (optional)
  8. Safety tips for these commands

This is the most important chapter in the guide. Please read all of it.

Why there is a password at power-on

The whole internal drive is encrypted. When the computer is off, every file is scrambled. The password you type at power-on is what unscrambles it. Without the password, nobody can read your files. Not a thief, not a repair shop, not someone who pulls the drive out and connects it to another computer.

This password is separate from your login password. You type the disk password first, on a plain screen, before Fedora starts. Then you type your login password on the login screen. You can choose to make them the same, but a different, stronger disk password is safer.

How strong should it be?

Someone who steals the laptop can try guessing your disk password as many times as they like, with powerful computers. So it must be much stronger than a typical password. The best kind is a passphrase:

  • At least 4 random words, preferably 5 or more.
  • At least 16 characters in total.
  • The words must be truly random. Don't use a phrase, a song lyric, a quote, or anything about you (names, birthdays, pets, places).

The installer enforces a floor: at least 12 characters, plain English-keyboard characters only (no accents or emoji, because the power-on screen cannot type them). Or press G and it generates five random words for you, shows them in a box, and makes you type them back so you know you can. The guidance above is what we recommend; the 12 is only the minimum it will accept.

An example of the style (do not use this one): granite-velvet-orbit-lantern-pickle. Bitwarden's password generator has a "Passphrase" option that creates these for you. Five random words are far harder to crack than something like P@ssw0rd2026!, and much easier to type and remember.

Where to keep it

Keep two copies:

  1. In Bitwarden. Save it as a secure note or login item called something like "Laptop disk encryption".
  2. Written on paper, somewhere safe and away from the laptop. A home safe is ideal. Or a sealed envelope with a trusted family member. This copy matters because Bitwarden might be hard to reach if the laptop is your only device and something goes wrong.

Never:

  • write it on a sticky note on or in the laptop, or in the laptop bag;
  • keep it in a plain text file on the same laptop (you can't open that file without the password anyway);
  • send it by email or text message.

What happens if you lose it

This is the hard part. If you forget the disk password and have no copy, your data is gone. That is not a bug. It is the whole point of encryption. There is no "forgot password" link and no back door. Nobody can unlock it: not Fedora, not a computer shop, not the police.

The only way forward would be to wipe the drive, reinstall from the USB stick, and restore your files from a backup. This is why the backup chapter matters and why you keep a paper copy.

Adding a backup passphrase

LUKS2 encryption has several "key slots". Each slot can hold a different password, and any one of them unlocks the drive. You can add a second passphrase as a spare. For example, a very long one that lives only in the safe.

Step 1: find the encrypted partition. Open the terminal and run:

Terminal
lsblk -f

Look for the line whose FSTYPE column says crypto_LUKS. On this laptop it is usually something like nvme0n1p3. On older PCs with SATA drives it may be sda3. Put /dev/ in front to get the full name, for example /dev/nvme0n1p3.

Step 2: add the new passphrase.

Terminal
sudo cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/<partition>

For example: sudo cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/nvme0n1p3. It asks for three things in order:

  1. your login password (for sudo);
  2. an existing disk passphrase (to prove you're allowed);
  3. the new passphrase, twice.

Restart and test the new passphrase at the power-on screen before you rely on it.

Changing your passphrase

To replace a passphrase with a new one:

Terminal
sudo cryptsetup luksChangeKey /dev/<partition>

It asks for the passphrase you want to change, then the new one twice. Afterwards, update the copy in Bitwarden and the paper copy. Then restart to check it works.

To see how many key slots are in use, run sudo cryptsetup luksDump /dev/<partition> and look at the "Keyslots" section. To remove a passphrase you no longer want, use sudo cryptsetup luksRemoveKey /dev/<partition> and type the passphrase to remove. Never remove your last working passphrase.

Spare ways in (optional)

Three extras make a locked-out disk less of a disaster. All three add to your password; none replaces it.

  • A recovery key. Run secure-linux-recovery-key. It shows a long code once. Write it down or print it, keep it away from the laptop, and put a copy in Bitwarden. Strongly recommended: do it today.
  • A security key (secure-linux-fido2). Touch a YubiKey or similar at power-on. Register two.
  • A short PIN (secure-linux-tpm-pin), only with Secure Boot on. The honest warning is in the tools chapter: it is a convenience, not extra security.
  • A header backup (secure-linux-recovery-key header-backup /path/on/a/USB) rescues a disk whose first few megabytes get damaged. It keeps old passwords valid in that file, so make a new one after changing passwords.

Details for each are in "Disk unlock extras" in the tools chapter. Your Emergency Kit page records where each of these is kept.

Safety tips for these commands

  • Make sure your backup is up to date before changing passphrases.
  • Type slowly. The keyboard layout at the power-on screen is the one chosen during installation. If your passphrase uses symbols, check they are where you expect on that layout.
  • Don't run these commands on a partition that isn't crypto_LUKS.

Staying safe

Backups

On this page 9 sections
  1. The 3-2-1 rule
  2. Pika Backup: your main backup tool
  3. Syncthing is sync, not backup
  4. Snapshots are not backups
  5. Clonezilla: full-disk images
  6. Immich for photos
  7. What to back up
  8. Nagging you, kindly: the daily backup check
  9. Test your restores

Every other protection on this laptop can fail. Drives die. Laptops get stolen, dropped or soaked in coffee. Files get deleted by mistake. A backup is what turns a disaster into an inconvenience.

The 3-2-1 rule

The standard advice is easy to remember:

  • 3 copies of your important data (the original plus two backups);
  • on 2 different devices (for example, the laptop and an external drive);
  • with 1 copy off-site (somewhere else: your home server at a different location, a drive kept at a relative's, or encrypted cloud storage).

A practical version for this laptop: Pika Backup to an external drive at home, plus Pika Backup to your home server over the network.

Pika Backup: your main backup tool

Pika Backup makes regular backups of your home folder. It uses BorgBackup under the hood. Each backup only stores what changed since the last one, so they are quick and small. You can open any past backup and copy files back out.

Backing up to an external drive

  1. Plug in an external USB drive. Ideally use one just for backups.
  2. Open Pika Backup and choose to set up a new backup.
  3. Choose the location on the external drive.
  4. Turn on encryption and choose a password. Store it in Bitwarden and on paper with your disk password. Without it, the backup can't be opened.
  5. Check which folders are included. Your home folder is the default. You can exclude big folders you don't need, like Steam games, which can be downloaded again.
  6. Run the first backup. It takes the longest; later ones are much faster.
  7. Open the Schedule section and turn on automatic backups, for example daily. Pika runs the backup whenever the drive is plugged in and a backup is due.

Backing up to your home server over SSH

Pika Backup can also save to a remote computer over SSH, which is ideal for your off-site copy. When adding a location, choose the remote option and enter an address such as ssh://<user>@<server-address>/<path>. The server needs SSH access and BorgBackup installed. If NordVPN's kill switch blocks your home network, allow your home subnet first (see Troubleshooting).

Syncthing is sync, not backup

Syncthing keeps folders identical across devices. That is great for convenience, but it is not a backup. If you delete or damage a file on one device, Syncthing faithfully deletes or damages it everywhere. The same is true if ransomware encrypts it. Syncthing does have optional "file versioning" per folder, which keeps old copies for a while. That helps, but it isn't a substitute for Pika Backup.

Snapshots are not backups

The hourly Btrfs snapshots let you undo a bad system update. But they:

  • live on the same drive as everything else, so a dead or stolen drive takes them too;
  • don't include your home folder (your documents, photos and so on).

Use them for what they are good at: rolling back the system.

Clonezilla: full-disk images

The USB stick includes Clonezilla. It copies an entire drive, every partition, into image files on another drive. Use it:

  • to keep a full image of the old Windows drive before it was wiped (if one was made);
  • before a risky job like replacing the laptop's SSD;
  • to restore a whole machine exactly as it was.

Start from the USB stick, pick Clonezilla in the Ventoy menu, and choose the "device-image" mode to save a drive to image files. Clonezilla is text-based and asks many questions; the default answers are usually right. Read each screen carefully, especially when choosing the source and target drives. Choosing the wrong target overwrites it. An image of an encrypted drive stays encrypted, so you still need the disk password to use it.

Immich for photos

If you run Immich on your home server, it is your own private Google Photos. The phone app uploads new photos automatically. On the laptop, immich-go uploads big batches, including your Google Takeout zips (see the Welcome chapter). Remember that the server needs its own backup too. Immich holding your only copy of your photos is still only one copy.

What to back up

  • Your home folder (Documents, Pictures, Desktop, and so on). Pika does this.
  • Photos (Immich and/or Pika).
  • Your Bitwarden vault. It is stored in the cloud, but you can also export an encrypted copy now and then from Bitwarden's settings.
  • Your Ente Auth codes. Ente syncs them. You can also make an encrypted export from its settings.
  • Your passwords on paper: disk encryption, backup encryption, Bitwarden master password. Keep these in the safe. The Emergency Kit page (app menu) is a printable form for exactly this.
  • The recovery key for your encrypted disk (secure-linux-recovery-key), on paper and in Bitwarden.

You don't need to back up the system or apps. They can be reinstalled from the USB stick in under an hour.

Nagging you, kindly: the daily backup check

A quiet check runs once a day (secure-linux-backup-check). It warns if there has been no backup for 7 days, if backups were never set up, or if your home-server backup is too old, and gives a monthly "try restoring a file" reminder. It also saves the list of installed apps into your backups so a restore can reinstall them. The Status window shows "Backups are set up" in green when all is well. If you back up to your home server, the server's own nightly backup is described in "Your home server".

Test your restores

A backup you have never restored from is only a hope. Every few months:

  1. Open Pika Backup and browse an archive (Pika lets you open one like a folder).
  2. Copy a few files back to a temporary folder.
  3. Open them and check they work: a photo, a document, a spreadsheet.

Also check that the scheduled backups are actually running. Pika shows when the last backup finished. If it says weeks ago, plug in the drive.

Staying safe

Your home server: photos, Pi-hole and reaching home

On this page 7 sections
  1. Home & Server Helper and Docker
  2. Whole-home Pi-hole
  3. The VPN switch: private, home or off
  4. Reach home without router port forwarding
  5. Immich, Caddy and server scripts
  6. Home Assistant container kit
  7. Looking after the family's other computers

A home server is an always-on computer that can hold photos and backups, run Home Assistant or answer DNS for your home. Everything here is optional. Start with Home & Server Helper (secure-linux-home-server-gui) for the reviewed desktop menu; the command-line helper is secure-linux-home-server.

Home & Server Helper and Docker

The helper opens existing Home Assistant tools, reviewed server-kit actions over SSH, an external unRAID server and safer Docker setup. unRAID is a separate proprietary operating system on another server; it is not bundled or installed here. Changes require review and the exact confirmation Confirm. secure-linux-home-server --dry-run explains an action without connecting or changing anything.

The on-demand page 81-docker, Docker and home-server tools, explains optional Docker installation. Choosing it takes effect through Repair setup. You are deliberately not added to the docker group, which is effectively administrator access; the helper offers a separate rootless Docker context instead. Control Centre's Docker button opens this same helper.

Whole-home Pi-hole

Open Whole-home Pi-hole or run secure-linux-pihole. Pi-hole can answer DNS for devices on your home network and block names on its configured lists. It does not guarantee that every advert disappears, that every device will use it, or that DNS never stops.

The local CLI covers assessment, installation, health, backup, restore, update, rollback, repair, DHCP, sleep and export. Router guidance covers generic, asus, tplink, fritzbox, opnsense and per-device. Read secure-linux-pihole --help for the current subcommands and review before changing your router.

Using an existing unRAID server

  • The helper manages an existing server over BatchMode SSH. It never installs unRAID.
  • Prepare root SSH keys, Docker and Compose, free TCP/UDP 53 and TCP 80, at least 1 GiB RAM, at least 2 GiB free on /mnt/user, and a reserved exact IP address. Acknowledge that the server must stay on.
  • An existing pihole container blocks installation. The helper does not adopt or replace it.
  • Remote confirmation is exactly Confirm. The admin password travels over standard input, not in process arguments.
  • Backup briefly stops and restarts DNS. Health requires the container, a real LAN DNS answer and a LAN web response.

Reserve the Pi-hole address in the router and decide what clients should do if that server is off. Test a real LAN DNS lookup and the admin page after any change. Keep a reviewed backup before updates or rollback.

The VPN switch: private, home or off

secure-linux-vpn is one switch. NordVPN and Cloudflare WARP are not used at the same time. The choice is saved as vpn_mode. App-menu entries are Secure Linux VPN, Private (NordVPN on), Home access (reach your home server) and VPN off.

ModePurposeRemember
Private — secure-linux-vpn privateNordVPN private mode for untrusted networks.Trust moves to the VPN provider; local devices may need reviewed allow rules.
Home — secure-linux-vpn homeReach your own home services using the configured private route.Requires the corresponding account/configuration on both ends.
Off — secure-linux-vpn offDisconnect the managed VPN mode.No VPN privacy protection.

First-time setup is secure-linux-vpn setup; status is secure-linux-vpn status. Use Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login for a captive portal rather than disabling protection indefinitely.

Reach home without router port forwarding

The existing helper supports NordVPN Meshnet where the installed NordVPN version provides it. On this computer use secure-linux-vpn meshnet on and secure-linux-vpn meshnet status. Configure and permit each device deliberately, then use the server's private name and actual service port. Current upstream account and client behaviour is not re-verified by this guide.

A Cloudflare Tunnel with an Access login is another separate configuration. Do not reuse historical upload-limit or plan claims as current facts. Never forward Immich or Home Assistant ports directly on the router.

Immich, Caddy and server scripts

The maintained source is linux/server/. These scripts run on the server after review, not as installed desktop commands. Copy the relevant folder to the server and read linux/server/README.md and each script's help.

ScriptPurpose
install-caddy.shPrivate CA and HTTPS name for an existing Immich service.
setup-backup.shNightly encrypted Borg/borgmatic backup of the Immich library and database.
immich-backup.shThe installed backup job and manual run.
setup-fleet-server.shHome-only RustDesk relay pair on the main family computer.

For Caddy, verify the private CA fingerprint before trusting it and configure the local hostname separately. For backups, store the Borg passphrase and repository key independently. The desktop can watch the server's health file after:

Terminal
sudo secure-linux-choice set server_health_url https://immich.home/.secure-linux/backup-health.txt

A health timestamp is not a restore test. Restore sample files into a separate folder regularly and keep an independent copy away from the server.

Home Assistant container kit

The source is linux/server/homeassistant/. Home Assistant OS on its own device is a separate option; this container route does not provide the OS add-on store.

ScriptPurpose
install-ha-container.shPinned, non-privileged Home Assistant stack and selected extras.
safe-update.shBackup, review and update one component with rollback state.
firewall-lan-only.shRestrict service access to the LAN.
lib.shShared functions, not a standalone task.
add-caddy.shPrivate HTTPS through the existing Caddy configuration.
usb-passthrough.shPass one stable serial device to one container without privileged mode.
harden-host.shSecurity updates and Fail2ban on the host.
ha-backup.sh, setup-ha-backup.shHome Assistant backup job and its setup.
setup-mosquitto.shAuthenticated MQTT with ACLs and no anonymous users.

Desktop Home Assistant commands include:

Terminal
secure-linux-ha open
secure-linux-ha status
secure-linux-ha doctor
secure-linux-ha backup
secure-linux-ha update-check
secure-linux-ha validate
secure-linux-ha snapshot
secure-linux-ha rollback
secure-linux-ha starter
secure-linux-ha token-set
secure-linux-ha discover
secure-linux-ha local

Use Home Assistant in Setup Hub or the app menu for the fixed graphical journey. Keep MQTT, Home Assistant and Docker management off public router port forwarding.

Looking after the family's other computers

secure-linux-fleet manages reviewed connections to other Secure Linux PCs. secure-linux-fleet add HOST [NAME] enrols one, status shows health, upgrade NAME requests an upgrade, and list or remove NAME manages the saved list. Protect the main computer: its SSH key can administer the others.

Join from the other PC

  1. On the main computer run secure-linux-fleet pair and keep the displayed address and six words available.
  2. On the other PC run secure-linux-fleet-join, or use the on-demand 85-fleet page, Join your home fleet?.
  3. Check the six words match exactly before accepting. A mismatch means stop.

Optional screen help uses setup-fleet-server.sh on the main home computer. It points RustDesk at that private relay, not the public relay pair, and opens firewall ports only in the home zone. The person at the other computer still approves screen sharing where the desktop requires it.

Repair and health

Is every part of my computer OK?

On this page 9 sections
  1. Secure Linux Status & Fixes: the green, orange and red list
  2. Hardware Health Check: every part, in plain English
  3. Hardware Check (the 2-minute friendly version)
  4. Software for the parts that need it
  5. Drivers: graphics cards, Wi-Fi chips and Macs
  6. Firmware updates (BIOS, SSD, docks)
  7. Create Diagnostics File: a report to send to a helper
  8. Battery care
  9. Sleep or hibernate

This chapter is about looking: the Status window that watches the whole computer, the Hardware Health Check that tests every part, and the tools that make sure each new gadget has the software it needs. Nothing in this chapter changes anything on your drives unless it says so. The next chapter, "My computer is broken: how do I fix it?", is about fixing.

Secure Linux Status & Fixes: the green, orange and red list

What it is. A window with one line per check (disk encryption on, firewall on, updates working, backups set up, antivirus, VPN, battery health, SSD wear and more). Each line has a dot: green is fine, orange needs a look, red needs fixing. Pick an orange or red line and press Fix it.

Why you want it. It is the one place to look when you wonder "is my computer OK?". Problems are turned into plain sentences, and the fix is one click, not a web search.

  1. Open Secure Linux Status & Fixes from the app menu.
  2. Read the list. The worst lines are at the top.
  3. Click a line, then Fix it. Typical fixes are "Install updates now", "Restart the computer", "Repair setup", "Check again", "Update firmware (BIOS, SSD)", "Make a disk recovery key" and "Hotel / cafe Wi-Fi login".
  4. For a text version, open Terminal view from the menu, or type secure-linux-status in a terminal. Typed into a terminal it always answers in text (a window never pops up over your terminal); from anywhere else secure-linux-status --terminal forces the text view. secure-linux-status --refresh runs the checks again straight away.

The window is run by secure-linux-status-gui (it uses KDE's own dialogs on KDE and a simple window elsewhere). Every Fix it button, and what it does:

ButtonWhat it does
Install updates nowDownloads and installs system updates right away (a restart may be needed before the newest versions, such as a new kernel, are in use). It runs the small helper secure-linux-update-now for you; you never need to type it yourself.
Restart the computerRestarts so waiting updates take effect. Save your work first.
Repair setupRuns the setup again in repair mode: adds only what is missing and puts settings back. Safe to repeat.
Check againRuns all the checks again now.
Update firmware (BIOS, SSD)The guided firmware tool (below).
Upgrade FedoraThe guided upgrade to the next Fedora version ("Upgrades and apps from outside Fedora").
Create a diagnostics fileA zip on your Desktop to send to a helper (below).
Update apps from outside FedoraUpdates Network protection, ArtCraft and immich-go, with checksums verified.
Show antivirus findingsLists what the weekly virus scan found.
Mark antivirus findings as dealt withHides the latest findings once you have handled them. Nothing is deleted.
Free space from old snapshotsRemoves old system snapshots when the disk is getting full.
See what's using disk spaceOpens a disk-usage view (Filelight, or Baobab) so you can see the big folders.
Set up VPNSigns in to NordVPN and asks simple yes/no questions.
Renew VPN subscriptionOpens your NordVPN account page when the subscription has run out (a kill switch with a lapsed account would cut your internet).
Hotel / cafe Wi-Fi loginPauses the VPN and encrypted DNS so a sign-in page can load.
Make a disk recovery keyA spare long code for your encrypted disk.
Remove the setup's Secure Boot keyRemoves the USB stick's key after installation.
Welcome & setup choicesOpens the welcome wizard again.
Check backupsRuns the backup check (and the wizard's backup page if backups are not set up).
Battery careThe battery charge-limit page.
Local AI assistantThe private AI page.
Open the START-HERE guideOpens this guide.
Hibernate settingsChoose what closing the lid does.
Care calendarSee your renewal reminders.
Run hardware checkRuns the hardware health check of every part (below) without leaving the Status window.
Install software for my hardwareInstalls the programs your hardware needs (a scanner's drivers, a printer's printing system and so on; see "Software for the parts that need it" below).

A notification also appears (once a day at most, per problem) when something needs you. Click Open Secure Linux Status on it. The checks run 10 minutes after start and every 6 hours (secure-linux-check); a virus scan of Downloads and Desktop runs weekly and a disk data check monthly.

If it fails. If the window will not open, type secure-linux-status in a terminal: there it always answers with the text view of the same list. If a fix says "not available", the tool it needs is missing: run Repair setup (or sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair), which only adds what is missing. To send someone a report, use Create Diagnostics File (see below).

Hardware Health Check: every part, in plain English

What it is. It looks at every part of your computer and says whether it is healthy: the drive, memory, processor, fans and temperatures, battery, screen, graphics, sound, microphone, camera, keyboard, touchpad and mouse, USB ports, CD/DVD drive, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, the security chip (TPM), the card reader, the fingerprint reader, printers and scanners, and more. Parts your computer does not have are shown as not present. That is normal, not a fault. It only looks: it never changes anything on your drives.

Why you want it. Hardware usually gives warning signs before it dies (a drive reporting errors, a swollen battery, a hot processor). Finding them early means you can back up and replace the part on your own terms.

How to use it.

  1. Open Hardware Health Check from the app menu (about a minute). It asks for your password so it can read drive health and memory details.
  2. For the thorough version, open Hardware Test (full, 5 minutes). It adds a stress test and tests where you listen or look (speakers, microphone, camera, screen colours, keys).
  3. Read the result. Each line starts with a tag:
    • [OK] fine.
    • [WARN] works, but needs a look.
    • [FAIL] broken or about to break: back up your files now.
    • [NOT-PRESENT] your computer does not have this part (or it is switched off in the BIOS).
    • [SKIPPED] it could not be checked: a tool is missing (the report names the package) or it needs administrator rights. Use the menu entry (it asks for your password) or run secure-linux-health --elevate.
  4. Every WARN and FAIL line says what to do.

From the terminal:

CommandWhat it does
secure-linux-healthStandard check, about a minute.
secure-linux-health --quickUnder a minute: no speed tests and no 3D or video probes.
secure-linux-health --fullEverything, including the stress test, a memory test on free memory, drive self-tests and the "does it work for you" tests.
secure-linux-health --part batteryOne part only (for example storage, cpu, ram, audio, graphics, wifi). --list shows all the names.
secure-linux-health --guiShow the result in a window.
secure-linux-health --jsonA file a program can read (for people who tinker).

Every week a quick check runs by itself. If a part needs a look, a notification appears and the part shows in Secure Linux Status. Reports are kept in /var/lib/secure-linux/health/ (latest.txt and latest.json).

Things it cannot do on its own.

  • A complete memory test needs a restart: choose Memtest86+ in the USB stick's boot menu (an hour or more). The health check only does a quick pass over free memory.
  • A screen defect (dead or stuck pixels) can only be seen by you. That is what the colour test in the full check is for.
  • It cannot repair hardware. A failing drive, swollen battery or broken fan needs replacing. For a failing drive, copy your files off first (Repair This Computer, then "Rescue my files").

Honest note. The health check was tested against recorded and simulated hardware information, not on a wide range of real machines yet. If a result looks wrong for your computer (for example a part reported missing that you can see), trust your eyes and send the diagnostics file to whoever helps you. The check works on the installed system and from the USB stick's rescue system, with or without the internet.

If it fails. "smartctl is not installed" (or a similar message): run sudo secure-linux-parts --install (below). A line you do not understand: run secure-linux-diag and send the file to whoever helps you; it includes the latest report.

Hardware Check (the 2-minute friendly version)

What it is. A short, friendly test with dialogs: speakers, microphone, camera, the brightness and volume keys, the Wi-Fi band, and (only if you agree) one sleep and wake cycle. It also runs the quick health check of the drive, memory, temperatures, battery and the other parts, and offers a touchpad, mouse and screen-colour test (you move the pointer, click, and look at full-screen colours to spot dead or stuck pixels). At the end it offers the full check, which takes about 10 minutes. If the detailed health tool is missing it says so, and still does the sound, camera, key and Wi-Fi tests. The welcome wizard offers it on your first day, so a problem shows up now rather than when you need it.

  1. Open Hardware Check from the app menu, or type secure-linux-hwtest.
  2. Follow the prompts: listen, look, press the keys it asks for.
  3. See the last results any time: secure-linux-hwtest --show.

If it fails. If the Wi-Fi drops after sleep, the check notes it (through a small helper, secure-linux-hwtest-marker, which asks for your password once; you never run it yourself) and the setup applies a known fix automatically. For other problems, see "Sound problems" and "No Wi-Fi" in Troubleshooting.

Software for the parts that need it

What it is. Some hardware needs a program before it is useful: a DVD burner needs a burning program, a scanner needs scanner drivers, a printer needs the printing system, a fingerprint reader needs its software, a drawing tablet needs its driver. secure-linux-parts finds what hardware you have and makes sure the software to use it is installed.

  1. secure-linux-parts --check shows every device found and what is installed or missing. It changes nothing.
  2. sudo secure-linux-parts --install installs what is missing (the internet is needed).
  3. Plug in a new device (printer, scanner, Bluetooth adapter) and a notification says "New device found: X. Installing software to use it." Only programs from Fedora's own software sources are installed this way, nothing from anywhere else.
  4. To switch the automatic part off: sudo secure-linux-choice set parts_autoinstall no (then use --install yourself).

If it fails. No internet: it says so and tries again next time you run --install while connected. A package "not available for this Fedora release" is skipped, never fatal.

Drivers: graphics cards, Wi-Fi chips and Macs

What it is. A few parts need a driver that must be built into the system, needs a restart and, with Secure Boot on, a one-time key approval. That is handled by secure-linux-drivers instead of the automatic helper above.

CommandWhat it does
secure-linux-drivers (or status)What hardware this is, which drivers are in use, anything waiting.
secure-linux-drivers checkThe full compatibility report (the same one the installer shows).
sudo secure-linux-drivers installInstall whatever drivers are missing.
sudo secure-linux-drivers reinstallRebuild the NVIDIA or Broadcom drivers for every installed kernel, then install. Use it if the screen goes wrong after an update.
sudo secure-linux-drivers enroll-keyAsk Secure Boot to approve the driver key again, with a password you choose. After a restart a blue screen asks for that password: choose Enroll MOK, Continue, Yes, type the password, Reboot.

If it fails. A black or garbled screen after a driver change: see "Black or garbled screen" in the repair chapter. Details of which computers work: see "Starting the USB stick on any computer".

Firmware updates (BIOS, SSD, docks)

What it is. Firmware is the small program inside a part (BIOS or UEFI on the motherboard, SSD, dock, keyboard). Updates fix bugs and security holes. They are never installed behind your back: they are risky if the power fails halfway, so the tool goes step by step and asks first.

  1. secure-linux-firmware status shows what can be updated.
  2. Plug in the charger. Run secure-linux-firmware update (or choose Update firmware (BIOS, SSD) in Secure Linux Status). Add --dry-run first to see what it would do.
  3. Answer each question. The main source is LVFS (the official firmware service); some Western Digital SSDs and ASUS BIOS updates have guided steps of their own.

If it fails. Do not switch off the computer during a flash. If it will not start afterwards, see "Computer won't start" in the repair chapter, and for an ASUS BIOS the maker's EZ Flash rescue (F2, Advanced) from a FAT32 stick.

Create Diagnostics File: a report to send to a helper

What it is. One click makes a zip file on your Desktop with system information and recent error messages, including the latest hardware health report and the parts list (which programs your hardware needs and which are installed). Your user name, the computer name, Wi-Fi names, hardware (MAC) addresses, serial numbers, email addresses and IP addresses are blanked out. No passwords or files of yours are included.

  1. Open Create Diagnostics File from the app menu (or type secure-linux-diag). Type your password once.
  2. Find the zip on your Desktop and send it to whoever is helping you.

Still check it before sending. Open the zip and glance at it. The tool blanks the obvious private details but it cannot know everything about you.

Battery care

What it is. A battery that sits at 100% wears out faster. This keeps it at 80% by default (if your laptop supports it), which can add years of life. The trade-off: a bit less time away from a charger.

  • secure-linux-battery status shows the charge, your limit, whether you are plugged in, and the battery's health.
  • secure-linux-battery limit 80 (or 90, or 100) sets the limit. KDE's own setting (System Settings, Power Management) changes the same thing.
  • Going on a trip? Choose Charge to 100% for a Trip in the app menu (or secure-linux-battery travel). It charges fully once, then goes back to your limit when you unplug or restart.

The Status window shows "Battery health" and "SSD wear" rows, and a monthly wear log is kept, so slow decline gets noticed.

If it fails. "Not supported" means your laptop's firmware does not allow a charge limit. Nothing is wrong; the battery simply charges to 100%.

Sleep or hibernate

What it is. Closing the lid can either sleep (quick wake, small battery drain) or hibernate (everything is saved to the encrypted disk and the laptop switches fully off; opening it asks for your disk password and you carry on where you left off).

Pros and cons. Hibernate gives the best protection against a thief and uses no battery, but waking takes longer and it only works with Secure Boot off (Fedora's rule). With Secure Boot off you lose protection against someone secretly changing the laptop's start-up files; your files stay encrypted either way. Sleep works with Secure Boot on.

  1. The welcome wizard page "Sleep or hibernate" follows what you chose when installing.
  2. To change your mind, run secure-linux-hibernate. It explains, shows the state and asks what you want. The modes are on-lid (lid closed means hibernate) and sleep-then-hibernate (sleep first, hibernate after 30 minutes). secure-linux-hibernate disable goes back to plain sleep.

If it fails. If the laptop does not come back properly, choose sleep again with secure-linux-hibernate disable. The Status window row "Hibernate when the lid closes" tells you what is missing.

Repair and health

My computer is broken: how do I fix it?

On this page 9 sections
  1. The Secure Linux Toolbox: one place that checks, fixes and rescues
  2. What the stick can fix
  3. Two ways in
  4. Not sure what is wrong?
  5. The menu
  6. The safety rules it follows
  7. Pros and cons of the big choices
  8. If a repair does not work
  9. Other emergency tools on the stick

This chapter is about fixing. The repair tool is a guided menu: it explains each step in plain English, shows you what it is about to do, and waits for your yes. You cannot break anything by only looking around, and the dangerous steps need you to type a whole sentence. To check the computer without fixing anything, see the previous chapter.

The Secure Linux Toolbox: one place that checks, fixes and rescues

What it is. The Toolbox is the single front door of Secure Linux, on the installed computer and on the USB stick. Open Secure Linux Toolbox from the app menu (or type secure-linux-toolbox in a terminal; the short name toolbox works too). It first runs a quick check that only looks, shows a simple green, amber or red summary, and then offers one step at a time in plain English.

Its shortcuts. Next to the Toolbox in the app menu you may see three one-tap shortcuts: Look after my computer checks the computer, fixes the safe things, installs updates and tidies up, then checks again — you say yes once, and anything risky still gets its own separate question. (On some computers the same shortcut is called Look After My Computer.) Rescue my files goes straight to copying your files off a failing drive, and Check my hardware goes straight to the hardware health check.

How it works. The Toolbox does not invent fixes. It asks the problem finder, secure-linux-diagnose, what is wrong (that tool only looks), then uses the repair menu below to fix what you approve and the hardware health check for the parts. From the terminal, secure-linux-diagnose lists what is wrong in plain English and how each thing can be fixed, and secure-linux-diagnose --plan shows one ordered plan of fixes to approve once. Careful people can run secure-linux-toolbox --dry-run first: it shows what every step would do and changes nothing.

What the stick can fix

  • A computer that will not start ("no boot device", a GRUB prompt, "emergency mode").
  • A damaged disk or a disk that has gone read-only.
  • A bad update that broke things (go back to an earlier snapshot, or start with an older kernel).
  • A black or garbled screen after an update or a graphics change.
  • Broken software (the package database, half-finished updates) and Flatpak apps.
  • No Wi-Fi or internet.
  • A Windows copy that will not start, or a forgotten local Windows password on your own computer.
  • A forgotten Linux login password (you still need the disk password or recovery key).
  • Virus worries, copying files off a failing drive, cloning a whole drive, factory reset, and wiping before you sell.

What it cannot fix. It cannot bring back a disk-encryption password you have lost (see "Your disk-encryption password"), it cannot repair broken hardware, and it cannot touch an Apple Silicon Mac's firmware. The tool was tested on simulated broken systems here, not yet on many real ones, so read each step before you say yes.

Two ways in

1. The computer still starts

  1. Open Repair This Computer from the app menu, or type secure-linux-repair in a terminal.
  2. A numbered menu appears. Pick the item that matches your problem (the table below).

2. The computer will not start: use the USB stick

  1. Plug in the stick. Switch on while tapping the boot-menu key (ASUS Esc or F8, Dell F12, HP Esc then F9, Lenovo F12, Acer F12; on a Mac hold Option). The full list is in "Starting the USB stick on any computer".
  2. Choose the stick, then SystemRescue in the menu.
  3. At the text prompt, type these two lines (press Enter after each):
    Terminal
    mkdir -p /mnt/usb ; mount /dev/disk/by-label/Ventoy /mnt/usb
bash /mnt/usb/linux-setup/rescue/secure-linux-rescue.sh
  4. The same numbered menu appears. It also works on a computer that only has Windows on it (data rescue and Windows help).

There is also a folder called SecureLinux-Rescue at the top of the stick with the same scripts, easy to find when nothing else will start. The tool works on the installed system, from SystemRescue, and from the Fedora installer's rescue shell. It needs no internet for most steps.

If the stick cannot be found: at the prompt run lsblk -f to see the drives, find the one labelled Ventoy, and mount that name instead. If the SystemRescue keyboard layout is wrong, type loadkeys us (or your layout's code).

Not sure what is wrong?

Choose Find out what is wrong (or run secure-linux-repair --auto-diagnose). It only looks: start-up entries, boot files, the drive list, the last start-up's errors, drive health, free space, network and the software database. Then it tells you which menu item fixes the problem. If a drive is failing it always says "rescue your files first".

The menu

Choice (as shown)Use it whenWhat it does
Find out what is wrongYou do not know where to startLooks only, then recommends a menu item.
Check the health of every partSomething feels wrongThe hardware health check.
Rescue my filesA drive is failing, or before any repairCopies files to another drive (rsync), images a failing drive (ddrescue), recovers deleted files (PhotoRec and TestDisk).
Computer won't start: repair the boot loader"No boot device", a GRUB prompt, emergency modePuts the boot loader back, rebuilds the boot menu and boot images, fixes the drive list (the fstab file that says which drives to use at start-up), and adds Fedora to the firmware list.
Check and repair a diskFile-system errors, a read-only diskfsck (the standard file-system check) for ext4, xfs, btrfs, f2fs, exFAT and FAT; a light NTFS fix. BitLocker drives are never touched without their key.
Go back to an earlier snapshotA bad update broke thingsSnapper undo. A snapshot of "now" is kept first.
Start with an older kernelThe newest kernel misbehavesMakes an older kernel the default. Nothing is deleted.
Black or garbled screen: safe graphicsBlack screen after an update or driver changeSafe graphics mode (nomodeset), back to the open-source NVIDIA driver, forget a bad saved screen layout.
Repair softwareUpdates fail, "rpmdb" errorsRebuild the package database, refresh lists, a preview-first distro-sync, finish a half update, undo the last change, check files, repair Flatpak.
Fix Wi-Fi / internetNo connectionRadios on, restart the network service, clear the DNS cache, reinstall Wi-Fi firmware, forget a network.
Windows on this computerDual-boot trouble, a forgotten local Windows passwordFinds Windows, adds it to the boot menu, sets the firmware entry, resets a local password (your own computer only), and points to Windows' own repair.
Forgot my Linux login passwordLocked outUses the stick's script. You still need the disk password or recovery key.
Scan for virusesWorried about malwareClamAV and rkhunter. Nothing is deleted.
Back up or clone a whole driveMoving to a new driveClonezilla on the stick is the easy way; a straight copy with safety checks is here.
Reset to factory stateYou want a clean startRe-applies Secure Linux's settings, or moves your desktop settings aside, or shows how to reinstall.
Wipe before sellingYou are selling the computerErases the internal drive for good. You must type ERASE and the drive's name.

For scripts and curious people, secure-linux-repair --list prints the short names (diagnose health data boot fs snapshot kernel gpu packages network windows password malware clone factory wipe) and secure-linux-repair --action boot jumps straight to one.

The safety rules it follows

  • Every step that changes something shows what it will do and waits for your explicit yes. The dangerous ones need a typed sentence. There are no timeouts that decide for you.
  • A safety copy of the boot files is made first (and a snapshot when snapper exists).
  • Before anything writes to a drive it asks the drive about its health (SMART is the drive's own built-in health report). If the drive says it is failing, you get a loud warning and must type that your files are backed up.
  • secure-linux-repair --dry-run shows everything a repair would do without changing anything. Try it first.
  • A forgotten local Windows password can be cleared only after you confirm the computer is yours. Microsoft-account passwords cannot be reset this way (use account.live.com/password/reset). BitLocker drives are never opened without their key.
  • Every command it runs is printed on screen, so nothing is hidden.

Pros and cons of the big choices

ChoiceProsCons
Go back to an earlier snapshotFast; undoes a bad update; your home files are not touched.Snapshots live on the same drive, so a dead drive takes them too. They cover the system, not /home or some app folders.
Start with an older kernelSafe, reversible, nothing deleted.You may miss the newest fixes until a better kernel arrives (usually within days).
Reset to factory stateA clean start with your files kept.You lose your own desktop tweaks (they are moved aside, not deleted).
Wipe before sellingNobody can read your old data.Permanent. Test a restore of your backup first.

If a repair does not work

  1. Run Find out what is wrong again after each step.
  2. If the computer still does not start, run secure-linux-diag (or copy /var/lib/secure-linux/health/latest.txt and the diagnosis text) and ask for help. See "How to get help" in Troubleshooting.
  3. If the drive is failing, rescue your files first, then replace the drive and restore from your backup.
  4. Last resort: reinstall from the USB stick and restore your files from the backup (the "Backups" chapter). A reinstall erases the drive, so only do it once your files are safe.

Other emergency tools on the stick

  • Clonezilla: save a whole drive as an image, or clone one drive to another ("Backups" chapter).
  • Memtest86+: test the memory properly (let it finish at least one full pass; any error means faulty memory).
  • Forgot-login-password script (inside SystemRescue) and wipe-before-selling script. The repair menu uses both, so you rarely need to run them yourself.

Starting the USB stick on any computer

On this page 9 sections
  1. What the stick starts on
  2. The boot menu (it waits for you)
  3. If the computer will not start from the stick
  4. Old and 32-bit PCs
  5. Macs
  6. The rescue folder
  7. Other situations
  8. How the Debian entries are made trustworthy
  9. Make another USB: exact clone or portable copy

The stick provides Fedora and Debian installation routes plus rescue tools for a range of BIOS/UEFI PCs and Intel Macs. Compatibility is not universal: firmware, CPU architecture, memory and individual devices matter. Read each screen, keep a backup and stop before any erase confirmation if you are unsure.

Honest note. Source and simulated-hardware checks do not establish a successful install on your computer. Current upstream support and physical boot, driver, suspend and peripheral behaviour need separate evidence.

What the stick starts on

Ventoy provides the menu for supported legacy BIOS and UEFI configurations. The 64-bit Fedora entry, 64-bit Debian entry and 32-bit Debian entry have different architecture and memory routes. Apple Silicon Macs use Fedora Asahi Remix from macOS instead of this PC-oriented stick. Specialist firmware such as Chromebooks and some tablets is not covered by a blanket promise.

The boot menu (it waits for you)

Nothing in this menu has a countdown. It waits until you choose, so a stick left in a computer can never start wiping it by itself.

Menu entryWho it is for
SET UP THIS COMPUTER - Complete Secure LinuxSupported 64-bit PCs that meet the installer's checks (installs Fedora); compatibility is not universal.
SET UP THIS OLD OR SMALL COMPUTER - Debian 13Small or older 64-bit PCs with less than about 1.7 GB of kernel-visible memory. See the "The Debian version for old and small computers" chapter.
SET UP THIS VERY OLD 32-BIT COMPUTER - Debian 12 32-bitVery old PCs with a 32-bit-only processor. See the "The Debian version for old and small computers" chapter.
SystemRescue, Clonezilla, Memtest86+Repair, back up or clone a drive, test the memory.

F6 starts the computer normally (without the stick). Esc goes back.

You do not have to work out which entry suits your computer. If you pick Fedora on a computer that is too small or too old, the setup screen says so in plain words, names the exact menu entry to restart into, and offers R (restart) or P (power off). Nothing is changed first. Nothing is erased until you type ERASE on a later screen.

If the computer will not start from the stick

The stick has a file at its top level called START-HERE-IF-IT-WONT-BOOT.txt. You can open it on any computer (it is plain text). The builder also prints its key steps at the end of the build. The steps below are the same, in the order that sorts most people out.

Step 1: use the boot-menu key

Tap the key again and again from the moment you press the power button.

MakeKey
DellF12
HPEsc, then F9 (some: F10 for the BIOS)
LenovoF12 (or the small "Novo" button or pinhole beside the power button)
ASUSEsc or F8
AcerF12 (if nothing happens, press F2 and turn "F12 Boot Menu" on)
Toshiba / DynabookF12 (some: F2)
MSIF11
Gigabyte / ASRockF12
SamsungEsc or F10
Microsoft SurfaceSwitch off, hold Volume-Down, press power, let go when the logo shows
Apple Mac (Intel)Hold Option (Alt) from the moment you press power; pick "EFI Boot"
Apple Mac (Apple chip, M1 and later)This stick cannot start these Macs. See the Apple Silicon chapter.

A list of drives appears. Pick the stick. If it shows up twice, one name says "UEFI": try the UEFI one first. If you only see a black screen, restart and try the other one.

Step 2: the blue screen (Secure Boot asks about the stick's key), once per computer

If you see a blue screen saying "Verification failed", "Security Violation" or "Perform MOK management", that is normal the first time. The computer is asking whether to trust the stick's boot loader (Ventoy's is not signed by Microsoft). Do this:

  1. Press any key. The screen only waits a few seconds, so be quick.
  2. Choose Enroll key from disk (on some: "Enroll MOK", then "Enroll key from disk").
  3. Choose the drive called VTOYEFI, then the file ENROLL_THIS_KEY_IN_MOKMANAGER.cer.
  4. Choose Continue, then Yes (enroll the key), then Reboot.
  5. Start from the stick again (Step 1). The menu now appears.

Missed the blue screen, or it shows an error and goes back? Restart and try again, or use Step 4 (turn Secure Boot off). The key stays in that computer; you do not repeat this there. It is not tracking: it is one more name on the list of trusted boot loaders. After your install you can remove it again (see "Remove the installer's Secure Boot key" in the tools chapter).

The blue screen uses a US keyboard layout, whatever your keyboard says.

Step 3: turn off Fast Boot

In the BIOS (F2 or Del at power-on), under Boot, set Fast Boot / Ultra Fast Boot / Quick Boot to Disabled (it skips looking for USB sticks). Also check that "Boot from USB" and "Legacy USB Support" are enabled. Save with F10.

Step 4: Secure Boot on or off

The stick works with Secure Boot on (after Step 2) and with it off. If Step 2 keeps failing, turn it off: BIOS, Security or Boot, Secure Boot, Disabled (some need a BIOS password first, or "Custom" or "Other OS" mode). Windows is not harmed, but if the computer uses BitLocker, Windows may ask for its recovery key next time it starts. Find it at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey before you change the setting.

Secure BootProsCons
On (kept)Protects against malware that loads before the system; the PIN unlock and key-removal tools apply.The blue-screen key step; laptops cannot hibernate.
OffThe stick just starts; hibernation works.You lose that start-up protection (your files stay encrypted either way).

Step 5: old computers (before about 2012) and "Legacy" mode

Old computers start from USB in Legacy (BIOS) mode. In the boot menu pick the USB entry without the word "UEFI". If the BIOS has "Boot mode: UEFI / Legacy / Both", choose Both (or Legacy for a computer with no UEFI). If it is a 32-bit-only machine it may be too old for the Fedora entry: use the Debian entries (the setup screen tells you which entry suits it).

Step 6: Windows "Fast Startup"

If the computer boots Windows and ignores the stick, Windows may only be hibernating instead of shutting down fully. Shut down properly (hold Shift while you click Shut down or Restart), or turn it off for good: Control Panel, Power Options, "Choose what the power buttons do", "Change settings that are currently unavailable", untick "Turn on fast start-up". Then use the boot-menu key again.

Step 7: the stick and the port

  • Plug the stick straight into the computer, not through a hub or dock.
  • Try a different port. USB 2.0 ports (usually black inside) are the most reliable on old machines.
  • Wait for the stick's light to stop flashing before you restart.
  • Try the stick on another computer, to see whether the stick itself is fine.

Step 8: what you should see

A menu (usually blue or black) with entries that start "SET UP THIS COMPUTER". If only the Ventoy logo shows and nothing happens for a minute, restart and try the other boot-menu entry for the stick. If it happens on every computer, rebuild the stick on the Windows PC by double-clicking BUILD-USB.cmd. Follow its device-selection and confirmation screens carefully, and keep a separate backup of anything you need; do not assume that every update preserves every file on the stick.

Old and 32-bit PCs

  • 64-bit PC with 3 GB or more of kernel-visible memory: the Fedora entry, with a recommended Full or Lite profile.
  • 64-bit PC with about 1.7 GB to less than 3 GB: the Fedora entry, with the recommended M / Min profile (LXQt).
  • 64-bit PC with less than about 1.7 GB: the Debian 13 entry.
  • 32-bit-only processor (roughly before 2005 to 2008): the Debian 12 32-bit entry, with an honest warning about web browsers. See the "The Debian version for old and small computers" chapter.
  • 32-bit UEFI (some 2010 to 2013 tablets, Atom netbooks, early Intel Macs): the stick carries the files for it. Turn Secure Boot off, and use a USB keyboard through an adapter.
  • Less than 512 MB of memory, or older than a Pentium Pro: no supported route in this kit.

What is limited on a 32-bit machine. The 64-bit rescue system (SystemRescue) cannot run on a 32-bit processor, so for rescue on such a machine the practical option is the Debian installer's own rescue mode. The builder includes separate 64-bit and 32-bit (i586) Memtest86+ entries. Neither has been tried on a real 32-bit computer in this project.

Macs

The stick has a folder called FOR-MACS at its top. Its README.txt tells you which Mac you have and which sub-folder to open.

Your MacWhat to do
Intel Mac before 2018Hold Option at power-on, choose "EFI Boot". If the Ventoy menu hangs at the logo, the stick can be rebuilt with Secure Boot support off (a builder switch, -NoSecureBootSupport).
Intel Mac with the T2 chip (2018 to 2020)Open FOR-MACS\T2-Macs\READ-ME-FIRST-T2-Mac.txt. In macOS, run get-apple-firmware.sh first (it saves the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth firmware to the stick). Then in Startup Security Utility set No Security and Allow booting from external media. Use a USB keyboard and a network cable for the install. Pick Fedora; the first-start setup swaps in the t2linux kernel (needs the internet) and one restart finishes it.
Apple Silicon (M1 and later)The stick cannot start these Macs (Apple's start-up chip only runs macOS or Asahi's own chain). Use the sub-folder Apple-Silicon-Macs: Fedora Asahi Remix, installed from macOS. See the "Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and M2)" chapter.

The Mac tools are on the stick only; they are not installed on the computer. On a T2 Mac the built-in keyboard and trackpad do not work in the rescue system until the t2linux kernel is installed, so bring a USB keyboard and mouse.

The rescue folder

SecureLinux-Rescue at the top of the stick holds the rescue menu scripts (the same files as in linux-setup\rescue). If the computer will not start: boot SystemRescue, mount the stick, and run bash secure-linux-rescue.sh. Details in the repair chapter.

Other situations

SituationWhat to do
No internet during installUse a network cable or phone USB tethering. The installer needs the internet to download packages.
No usable graphics driverAll the repair and health tools have a text mode. For a black screen see "Black or garbled screen" in the repair chapter.
Tiny text on a high-resolution screenIn the rescue system type setfont ter-v32n. The installed desktop has a Scale setting (150 to 200 per cent on screens of 2560 pixels or more).
Odd keyboard layoutSystemRescue's boot menu has a keymap choice; loadkeys us works at the prompt.
Less than 2 GB of memory in SystemRescueStay in the text menu. SystemRescue itself needs about 1 GB; the smallest class of computer is Debian-only.

How the Debian entries are made trustworthy

When the stick is built on Windows, the builder finds the current Debian 13 (64-bit) and the newest Debian 12 (32-bit) installers by itself. It checks Debian's signature on the list of checksums (three Debian signing keys whose fingerprints are built into the builder), then checks each installer against that list. If anything does not match, that entry is left off the stick and the build says so; the Fedora entry is not affected.

  • If gpg is missing on the Windows PC, the signature cannot be checked. The builder then checks the checksum from Debian's website only, says so loudly, prints the three key fingerprints (compare them with debian.org/CD/verify), and marks the entry "HASH ONLY" in linux-setup\debian-verification.txt on the stick.
  • -NoDebian leaves both Debian entries off (saves about 1.5 GB).
  • If the build says a Debian entry was not added, read the line after "NOT added to the stick" (no internet, Debian changed its website layout, or a check failed) before running the builder again later. Keep a separate backup of anything you need on the stick.

Make another USB: exact clone or portable copy

On an installed Secure Linux computer, open Linux USB Installer Creator - Turn any blank USB into a Linux installer. The graphical launcher is secure-linux-usb-creator-gui; the command is secure-linux-usb-creator. It supports list, create, clone, portable, measure, verify, status and an interactive menu.

MethodWhat it writes and verifies
Exact cloneThe complete raw master image. The target must have room for that entire image. On a larger target only the master-sized beginning is overwritten and verified; old data may remain in the unused tail.
Portable copyA separate genuine Ventoy installation and the saved file tree. Every copied file is verified. This is not the same operation or evidence as an exact raw clone.

The required size is calculated from content, allocation, Ventoy/filesystem overhead and a safety margin. Recommendations such as 64 GB or 128 GB are headroom, not universal minimums. A nominally 32 GB stick is accepted only if its enumerated bytes meet the calculated requirement.

  1. Use secure-linux-usb-creator list and compare the model, exact capacity and serial/WWN. Disconnect drives you do not need.
  2. Use measure to review the requirement and status to inspect saved state.
  3. Choose clone or portable deliberately. Erase confirmation waits for ERASE SERIAL-OR-WWN; there is no timeout.
  4. Let the operation finish and run verify. Interrupted output remains incomplete and not verified; do not boot an important recovery from it until verification succeeds.

For a failing USB, Secure Linux USB Fixer first captures an image and works on a disposable copy. Formatting is a separate destructive action, not a secure erase.

The USB stick

On this page 5 sections
  1. What's on it
  2. Using the stick on a machine that already runs Fedora
  3. Rebuilding or updating the stick from Windows
  4. Before you wipe Windows: the pre-flight checklist
  5. Security: keep the stick safe

The USB stick that installed this laptop is a toolkit worth keeping. It can reinstall this laptop, set up other PCs (new, old, 32-bit and many Macs), and rescue a computer that won't start.

What's on it

The stick uses Ventoy, which shows a menu of everything on it when you boot from it.

ItemWhat it is for
SET UP THIS COMPUTER - Complete Secure LinuxInstalls Fedora with encryption and runs the full or lite setup by itself. See "How the automatic USB install works". Erases the internal drive (only after you type ERASE).
Debian 13 and Debian 12 (32-bit) entriesFor small and very old computers. See "The Debian version for old and small computers". (Left off if you built the stick with -NoDebian.)
SystemRescueA complete Linux system that runs from the stick. Use it to fix a PC that won't start. The Secure Linux repair menu runs from here (see "My computer is broken").
ClonezillaSaves a whole drive as an image, restores it, or clones one drive to another. See "Backups".
Memtest86+Tests a PC's memory (RAM). Run it if a computer crashes or freezes at random. Let it run at least one full pass. Any errors mean faulty RAM.
linux-setup folderThe setup files, the Windows backup scripts, the Flipper script, the server kit, the Apple Silicon installer and more (see below).
START-HERE-IF-IT-WONT-BOOT.txtA plain-text checklist you can open on any computer: boot-menu keys by make, the blue Secure Boot screen, Fast Boot, Legacy mode and more. Same content as "Starting the USB stick on any computer".
FOR-MACS folderA README for Macs, the T2-Mac helper and the Apple Silicon installer.
SecureLinux-Rescue folderThe rescue-menu scripts, easy to find when nothing starts.
SAVE-THIS-PC.cmdOpens the same Setup App in collect-only mode for reviewed health, backup, Wi-Fi, browser-password and app-list collection without the later USB-writing stages. SAVE-APPS.cmd runs only the read-only app scanner.

Each rescue tool was downloaded from its own project and checked against the official checksum when the stick was built.

Inside the linux-setup folder

  • linux: the whole Secure Linux package (the same files built into the installed system at /usr/local/lib/secure-linux).
  • install-on-existing-fedora.sh: for a machine that already runs Fedora (see below).
  • rescue: the rescue menu scripts.
  • server: the optional home-server kit (see "Your home server").
  • asahi: the installer for Apple Silicon Macs (see the Apple Silicon chapter).
  • flipper: a Flipper Zero BadUSB script, repair_setup.txt (see below).
  • debian-verification.txt: which Debian check each entry passed.
  • kit: everything needed to rebuild the stick from Windows, including BUILD-USB.cmd, make-usb.ps1, this guide's sources, and the Windows scripts that back up and check a PC before you wipe it (backup-windows.ps1, preflight-windows.ps1, save-wifi.ps1).

There is a Flipper Zero BadUSB script (repair_setup.txt). If you own a Flipper Zero, copy it to its SD card in the badusb folder using qFlipper. When you plug the Flipper into a machine and run it, it opens a terminal and types sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair. You then type your password. Only use it on your own machines.

Using the stick on a machine that already runs Fedora

If a PC already has Fedora but wasn't installed from this stick, you can still apply the setup. Plug the stick in, open a terminal, and run:

Terminal
sudo bash /run/media/<your-username>/Ventoy/linux-setup/install-on-existing-fedora.sh

This doesn't erase anything. It adds apps and protections. It does not add disk encryption; that can only be set up during installation.

Rebuilding or updating the stick from Windows

Rebuild the stick when you want the newest Fedora version, a changed password, a different Wi-Fi network, or an updated app list. You need a Windows PC.

  1. Connect the stick and a separate backup drive if requested, then double-click BUILD-USB.cmd and approve the Windows administrator prompt. The graphical Setup App opens.
  2. Review the ticked health, backup, Wi-Fi, browser-password, app-list, download, USB-write, rescue, Debian and offline-pack steps. Untick anything you do not want. Nothing downloads or writes while you review.
  3. If you request a backup, choose a separate drive and wait for every indexed file's size and full SHA-256, the counts and the manifest to verify. Browser CSV export is a separate action; private key folders and saved Wi-Fi passwords are skipped by the ordinary backup.
  4. On the final review, check the disk number, friendly name, exact byte size and stable ID. Tick the checkbox and choose Confirm. The builder checks that identity again before writing.

Interruption recovery keeps only explicit non-secret state. Secrets and erase consent are cleared, a backup is verified again, and the combined download/build stage restarts. See Prepare Windows and build the USB with Setup App. Advanced maintainers can still use make-usb.ps1 -DryRun for a non-writing preview.

Useful switches for make-usb.ps1: -DryRun (preview without touching a drive), -KeepBuild, -NoDebian, -NoRescueTools, -DownloadOnly, -AiModel, -HomeSubnet, -Regdom and -NoSecureBootSupport (only if a Mac hangs at the Ventoy logo).

Before you wipe Windows: the pre-flight checklist

Setup App's read-only health scan reports Windows, CPU, RAM, disks and health, Secure Boot, battery, internet and disabled Wi-Fi. Separately save your BitLocker recovery key, export Clipchamp/CapCut projects and Anaconda environments, sign out of Adobe/Office and release any MATLAB licence as needed. The app-list scan contains app names, publishers and sources, not documents, passwords or licence keys. Browser-password export is a separate reviewed action. Read the backup manifest and verification result rather than assuming a folder copy is enough.

Security: keep the stick safe

The stick holds two sensitive things:

  • Your Wi-Fi passwords, in plain text, if you chose to include them. Anyone who plugs the stick into a computer can read them. (Networks you protected with a PIN are locked by that PIN instead.)
  • A hash of your login password. A hash isn't the password itself. But with a weak password, a determined attacker could crack it offline by trying billions of guesses. A strong login password makes this impractical.

So:

  • Store the stick somewhere safe at home, ideally with your paper passwords. Don't leave it in the laptop bag or lend it out.
  • If you lose it, change your Wi-Fi password and your login password (passwd), then rebuild a new stick.
  • To make a stick you can lend or carry, rebuild it without Wi-Fi details.
  • Remember that the installer on the stick erases drives. Label the stick clearly, for example "LINUX INSTALLER: ERASES PCs".

The stick does not hold your disk-encryption password, your files, or any of your app accounts.

How the automatic USB install works

On this page 6 sections
  1. Step 1: Boot from the USB stick
  2. Step 2: The Ventoy menu
  3. Step 3: Secure Boot and the MOK key (once per PC)
  4. Step 4: The installer's setup screen
  5. Step 5: The automatic install
  6. Step 6: The first-boot setup

This chapter explains what happened when this computer was installed from the USB stick. Read it if you ever need to reinstall this laptop, or set up another PC. How to start the stick on different kinds of computer, and what to do when it will not start, is in "Starting the USB stick on any computer".

Step 1: Boot from the USB stick

A computer normally starts from its internal drive. To install, it must start from the USB stick instead. There are two ways:

  • One-time boot menu. Plug in the stick. Power on and immediately tap the boot-menu key over and over. On an ASUS Zenbook this is Esc. On most other PCs it is F12, F11 or F8. A list of drives appears. Pick the USB stick.
  • Change the boot order. Enter the BIOS/UEFI setup (usually F2 or Del at power-on) and move USB to the top of the boot order. The PC then starts from the stick whenever it is plugged in. Without the stick, it starts from the internal drive as usual.

The key for each make, Macs, old PCs and the other things that get in the way are in the "if the computer will not start" checklist.

Step 2: The Ventoy menu

The stick uses a tool called Ventoy. Ventoy shows a menu of everything on the stick. Nothing is chosen for you. The menu waits until you pick something with the arrow keys and Enter. This is deliberate. It means a forgotten stick can never start wiping a computer on its own. The entries are:

  • SET UP THIS COMPUTER - Complete Secure Linux: Fedora for supported 64-bit PCs that meet the installer's checks; compatibility is not universal.
  • SET UP THIS OLD OR SMALL COMPUTER - Debian 13 and SET UP THIS VERY OLD 32-BIT COMPUTER - Debian 12: see "The Debian version for old and small computers".
  • SystemRescue, Clonezilla and Memtest86+: repair, copy a drive, test the memory.

F6 starts the computer normally. If you choose the wrong entry for your computer, the setup screen says so and offers to restart into the right one before anything is changed.

Step 3: Secure Boot and the MOK key (once per PC)

Secure Boot is a feature of modern PCs. At power-on, the firmware checks that the first program it runs is signed by someone it trusts. Out of the box, PCs trust Microsoft's signature. Fedora's own boot loader is signed through Microsoft, so an installed Fedora starts normally with Secure Boot switched on.

Ventoy's boot loader, however, is not signed by Microsoft. So the first time you start the stick on a PC with Secure Boot on, you see a blue screen saying the verification failed. That is expected. Ventoy then lets you add its key to the PC's own allow-list. This allow-list is called the MOK list (Machine Owner Key). It is stored in the PC's firmware.

What to do on that screen:

  1. Press a key or choose OK when the verification message appears.
  2. In the MOK manager (a plain blue screen), choose Enroll key from disk.
  3. Pick the Ventoy partition (named VTOYEFI), then the file ENROLL_THIS_KEY_IN_MOKMANAGER.cer.
  4. Choose Continue, then Yes, then Reboot.
  5. Start from the stick again. The Ventoy menu now appears.

Things worth knowing:

  • You do this once per PC. The key stays in that PC's firmware.
  • It is not tracking of any kind. It is just one more name on a list of trusted boot loaders.
  • You do not need to turn Secure Boot off. Keeping it on protects against malware that tries to load before the operating system. (The setup screen also lets you choose to turn it off; see below.)
  • After the install you can remove the key again with secure-linux-mok-remove (the welcome wizard offers it, and it is described under "Remove the installer's Secure Boot key" in the tools chapter). Afterwards the stick only starts with Secure Boot off, or after you enrol its key again.

Step 4: The installer's setup screen

When you choose the Fedora entry, a plain text screen appears before anything is touched. Every question waits for you; nothing has a timer. In order:

  1. Hardware compatibility report. It detects the computer, shows the model and memory, and says whether it is a good match. If the computer is too small or too old, it tells you which menu entry to restart into.
  2. Profile: F, L, M or A. Full (F) is KDE Plasma with the full application set. Lite (L) uses Xfce with fewer apps. Min (M) uses LXQt for the wrapper's lower-memory Fedora tier. Atomic (A) is the experimental Fedora Kinoite route with fewer extras. A recommendation is explained; accept it or pick another after reading the compatibility report.
  3. Which drive (only if there are several). The biggest SSD is suggested. USB sticks and memory cards are never offered.
  4. Backup check. The builder recorded whether this computer had been backed up. If no backup is recorded, you choose to stop and back up first, or to continue.
  5. Wi-Fi networks from Windows (if you ran SAVE-THIS-PC.cmd or the builder saved them): A for all, C to choose, N for none. Networks protected by a PIN ask for it. If there is no Wi-Fi driver and no cable, it asks you to plug in Ethernet or use phone USB tethering.
  6. Secure Boot: keep it on or turn it off, with pros and cons. On keeps the strongest protection against start-up malware but a laptop cannot hibernate; off allows hibernation (lid closed saves to the encrypted disk) but gives up that protection. Your files are encrypted either way.
  7. Optional unfiltered AI model (full only), with an honest explanation of what it can and cannot do.
  8. ERASE. It shows the drive and warns that everything on it will go: Windows, files, everything. To continue you must type ERASE in capital letters. Anything else cancels. This is your last chance to back out. If in doubt, pull out the stick and hold the power button.
  9. The encryption password. Either type your own (12 or more characters, plain English-keyboard characters only; accents and emoji are refused because the power-on screen cannot type them), or press G and it makes five random words for you, shows them in a box, and asks you to type them back. See "Your disk-encryption password".

Old or low-memory PCs get a text-mode installer. The Debian entries have their own, very similar screens.

Step 5: The automatic install

After that you can walk away. The installer:

  • connects to the internet (using the Wi-Fi saved on the stick, or a network cable);
  • erases the drive and creates an encrypted (LUKS2) partition with the Btrfs file system inside;
  • downloads and installs Fedora, creates your user account, and locks the separate "root" administrator account;
  • turns on SELinux and the firewall;
  • turns the computer off.

Remove the USB stick, switch the computer on, and type the disk-encryption password at the first screen.

Step 6: The first-boot setup

On the first start, a background service called firstboot-setup runs by itself. It waits until the internet is reachable (a small message shows "Waiting for the internet" until you connect). Then it runs the Secure Linux setup script, /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh. That script:

  • updates everything to the latest version;
  • adds RPM Fusion (for full video codecs) and Flathub (the main app store for Flatpak apps);
  • applies all the protections: firewall rules, encrypted DNS, network privacy, kernel hardening, automatic updates;
  • installs the VPN apps and every app for the chosen profile;
  • on the full setup, also sets up ClamAV, Network protection (OpenSnitch), system snapshots and Cloudflare WARP;
  • installs the helper tools described in "Every Secure Linux tool, A to Z";
  • writes SETUP-REPORT.txt and this guide to your Desktop.

The duration depends on the computer, network, packages and any offline content; the setup report and logs are the evidence of completion rather than a fixed estimate. You can log in and watch while it runs; the five-screen welcome opens at your first login. To see what the setup is doing, open the terminal and run journalctl -fu firstboot-setup (press Ctrl+C to stop watching). It runs only once on its own; a marker file stops it running again. The full log is kept in /var/log/secure-linux/setup.log, and anything that failed in /var/log/secure-linux/failures.log.

Once SETUP-REPORT.txt appears on your Desktop, setup is complete. Go back to the "Welcome" chapter and do the ten first-hour tasks.

To run the setup again, choose Repair setup in Secure Linux Status & Fixes, or type sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair. Repair is designed to retry missing setup work; review its report and logs rather than assuming that every local file or setting will be preserved.

The Debian version for old and small computers

On this page 7 sections
  1. Which one is mine?
  2. What you will see, and what to do
  3. The honest 32-bit warning
  4. What is the same as the Fedora setup and what is not
  5. Everyday tools on Debian
