Most computers get Fedora from the USB stick. Computers with less than about 1.7 GB of kernel-visible memory, or with a 32-bit-only processor, get Debian instead: a very steady, long-lived Linux that runs well on weak hardware. It has a light desktop (Xfce, or LXQt on tiny PCs), the same kind of "Secure Linux Status" window, and the same protections where they fit.

Which one is mine?

Your computerPick this entry in the USB menuYou get
64-bit PC with 3 GB or more of kernel-visible memorySET UP THIS COMPUTER - Complete Secure Linux, then the recommended Full or Lite profileFedora with KDE Plasma or Xfce
64-bit PC with about 1.7 GB to less than 3 GB of kernel-visible memorySET UP THIS COMPUTER - Complete Secure Linux, then the recommended M / Min profileFedora with LXQt, the lightest Fedora desktop in this kit
64-bit PC with less than about 1.7 GB of kernel-visible memorySET UP THIS OLD OR SMALL COMPUTER - Debian 13, 64-bitThe kit's Debian 13, 64-bit route
32-bit-only processor (very old: roughly before 2005 to 2008)SET UP THIS VERY OLD 32-BIT COMPUTER - Debian 12, 32-bitThe kit's Debian 12, 32-bit route
Less than 512 MB of memory, or older than a Pentium Pro / Pentium IInoneNo supported route in this kit

You do not have to work it out yourself. Each entry checks the computer first and says, in plain words, if the other entry would suit it better. Nothing is erased until you type ERASE.

What you will see, and what to do

  1. A check of your computer. It shows the make, processor and memory. If it says the computer is strong enough for Fedora, it asks whether to stop and use the Fedora entry (usually best) or go on with Debian.
  2. (32-bit only) A warning page you must read (below). Type C to continue.
  3. A name for the computer. A suggestion is shown (the model plus the end of its serial number). Press Enter to accept, or type another (letters, numbers and dashes only).
  4. Your saved Wi-Fi networks from Windows (only if you ran SAVE-THIS-PC.cmd on that computer). Choose A (all), C (one by one) or N (none). If you protected them with a PIN, they are added after the install instead. The installer needs the internet to download Debian, so plug in a cable if you can.
  5. The installer's own questions: the keyboard (Australian is pre-selected) and the password you will log in with.
  6. Which drive? With one internal drive it is used. With several, you type the number of the one to erase; the others are not touched. USB sticks and memory cards are never offered.
  7. Backup check. If no backup was recorded for this computer it says so and waits for you: B to stop and back up first, C to carry on without one.
  8. ERASE. Type ERASE in capitals. Anything else cancels and nothing is changed.
  9. The disk-encryption passphrase. Same rules as Fedora: G makes five random words for you (write them on paper, then type them back) or O lets you type your own: 12 or more characters, plain English-keyboard characters only (no accents or emoji). You type it every time the computer starts. If it is lost, the files are gone.
  10. The installer then runs by itself and turns the computer off. The duration depends on the computer, network and packages. Take the stick out, turn it on, type the passphrase and log in. A small window shows the rest of the setup (it needs the internet).

Every question waits for you; nothing has a countdown. Before you confirm ERASE, pressing Q leaves the installation without applying the erase. After that confirmation, do not assume that stopping or restarting will preserve the old system.

The honest 32-bit warning

Your computer has an older, 32-bit-only processor, so this kit uses its Debian 12 route. This documentation update has not rechecked Debian's current upstream support dates or architectures.

Web browser support is a separate risk. Do not assume that a 32-bit browser will keep receiving security fixes for the whole life of the operating system. Check the browser's actual update status. If it is no longer supported, do banking and shopping on a newer device and use this computer only for tasks you understand to be lower risk.

There is no Flatpak or Flathub for 32-bit, so a few newer apps are not available.

The Status window keeps a permanent amber line about this ("Web browser on a 32-bit computer"). It is a reminder, not an alarm: it does not pop up every day.

Another idea for very old computers: antiX Linux (antixlinux.com), an even lighter system. The stick does not install it and it has not been tried here; it is only an idea if Debian feels too heavy or the browser problem worries you.

What is the same as the Fedora setup and what is not

Debian versionCompared with Fedora
Disk encryptionYes (LUKS), same passphrase rulesSame
Automatic updatesYes, every day (unattended-upgrades); a restart reminder after 7 daysSame idea
Optional automatic restart at 4 amYes: secure-linux-choice set lite_auto_reboot yes, then "Repair setup"Same choice
FirewallYes (ufw): blocks everything from outside; SSH only from the home networkSame idea
Encrypted DNSYes (Cloudflare 1.1.1.2 and Quad9 over TLS)Same
"Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login"Yes, in the app menuSame
Random Wi-Fi addresses (MAC), Wi-Fi country AUYesSame
BrowsersFirefox ESR; LibreWolf too on 64-bitLibreWolf only
OfficeLibreOffice; under 1 GB of memory: AbiWord and GnumericLibreOffice
Video, emailVLC, ThunderbirdSame
PasswordsBitwarden desktop app only on 64-bit with 1.5 GB or more; otherwise the Bitwarden browser extensionDesktop app
Memory helpYes: compressed memory (zram) under 2 GBNot needed
Remote login (SSH) with fail2banYes, home network onlySame
VPN apps (NordVPN, WARP), welcome wizardYes, simpler versions: the same one-switch VPN tool and a short first-login wizard that asks at most 3 questionsYes
The app firewall (OpenSnitch)NoYes
Virus scanner, system snapshotsYes: a weekly virus scan (on computers with 1.5 GB of memory or more), and automatic system snapshots before updatesYes
Gaming, AI helper, art toolsNo (too heavy)Full setup only

Everyday tools on Debian

  • Secure Linux Status & Fixes (app menu): the green, orange and red list with a "Fix it" button. In a terminal: secure-linux-status.
  • Secure Linux Guide (START-HERE) in the app menu, or secure-linux-guide: opens this guide.
  • Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login (app menu), or secure-linux-dns open: pauses encrypted DNS for 15 minutes so a sign-in page can load. It switches back on by itself.
  • secure-linux-choice set default_browser firefox (or librewolf), lite_auto_reboot yes, ssh_server no, family_dns yes, and then Repair setup in the Status window.
  • secure-linux-browser: which web browser opens your links. secure-linux-browser get shows the current one; secure-linux-browser set firefox (or librewolf) changes it everywhere, and the choice is remembered if you ever run Repair setup.
  • secure-linux-scan: the weekly virus scan of your files (on computers with 1.5 GB of memory or more). secure-linux-scan status shows when it last ran and secure-linux-scan findings lists what it found. Nothing is ever deleted or moved; a suspicious file is listed and you decide.
  • secure-linux-snapshot: automatic system snapshots, taken before updates and repairs. secure-linux-snapshot list shows them; secure-linux-snapshot rollback takes the system back to one at the next restart (your own files are not changed). The retention rule keeps at most two and none older than 14 days; still check free disk space because snapshot sizes vary.
  • secure-linux-wifi-import: adds the PIN-protected Wi-Fi networks saved from Windows.
  • On the first start, secure-linux-firstboot waits for the internet and runs the rest of the setup, and secure-linux-progress shows its small progress window. You do not run either yourself.

If something goes wrong

  • "Waiting for the internet" never finishes after the first start. Click the network icon (top right) and connect to Wi-Fi, or plug in a cable. The setup carries on by itself.
  • No Wi-Fi at all (some Broadcom chips). Use a cable or phone USB tethering for the install. Some old Broadcom chips need a driver Debian keeps in its "non-free" section; or use a cheap USB Wi-Fi adapter (most work without extra drivers).
  • The installer says it cannot download. Check the cable or Wi-Fi before starting the entry again. If you already confirmed ERASE, assume that the old system may be lost and do not retry without a backup.
  • "Setup finished (a few items need a retry)". Open the Status window and choose Repair setup. It is designed to retry missing work; read the resulting report and logs.
  • Forgot the encryption passphrase. There is no reset. Restore from your backup.
  • A website will not load on hotel or cafe Wi-Fi. Use "Hotel / Cafe Wi-Fi Login".
  • The computer is slow. Close extra browser tabs; 1 GB computers run best with a few tabs. The installer chose the lightest desktop for your memory size.

Support and update caution

  • Check Debian's current release and LTS information, including 32-bit architecture support, before relying on this route for a computer that must remain supported.
  • A support-date warning in the Status window is wrapper-maintained information, not live proof of upstream support.
  • Check browser security updates separately: operating-system support does not establish that every application remains supported.

Honest note. This documentation update has not rechecked current upstream support. The Debian installer files were checked on Windows but have not been run through a real Debian installation here. The "if something goes wrong" steps above still need physical-installer verification. Upstream starting point: wiki.debian.org/LTS.

Repair and health

Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and M2)

On this page 6 sections
  1. The short version
  2. Installing it, step by step (30 to 60 minutes)
  3. What is the same and what is different
  4. Apps that only exist for Intel and AMD
  5. Steam on an Apple Silicon Mac
  6. What to do if an app you want is missing

This chapter is for you if your Mac has an Apple chip (M1, M2 and later) rather than an Intel chip. If you are not sure: Apple menu, About This Mac. If it says "Chip: Apple M1" (or similar), this chapter is yours. Intel Macs follow the "Starting the USB stick on any computer" chapter instead.

The short version

  • The USB stick cannot start an Apple Silicon Mac. Apple's start-up system only runs operating systems prepared for it.
  • Instead you install Fedora Asahi Remix (made by Fedora and the Asahi Linux project) from inside macOS, then run this package's setup on top. You get the same KDE desktop, apps and security settings as on other computers, minus a few things listed below.
  • macOS stays on the Mac and keeps working. You choose which one to start by holding the power button at start-up.
ChipStatus (as checked in November 2026)
M1, M1 Pro / Max / UltraSupported
M2, M2 Pro / Max / UltraSupported
M3 familyNot ready for daily use (starts on some models, no graphics acceleration). Keep macOS and check asahilinux.org before trying.
M4 and newerNot supported

Installing it, step by step (30 to 60 minutes)

  1. Back up the Mac with Time Machine. Update macOS (13.5 or newer) and make sure at least 60 GB is free: the installer shrinks macOS to make room.
  2. Open Terminal (Applications, Utilities) and run the official installer: curl https://alx.sh | sh. (This is the Asahi project's own installer. Running a program straight from the internet is something this guide normally warns against: here it is the project's documented method, and you can read what it does at asahilinux.org first.)
  3. Choose Fedora Asahi Remix with KDE Plasma, give it the space you want, and follow the prompts. When it says so, shut down, then hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears. Choose the new system and follow the Apple security steps (it asks for your macOS password).
  4. Fedora's first-start screens ask for language, user name and password. Use the same login name you used when building the stick, so everything lines up.
  5. Connect to Wi-Fi and plug in the USB stick. Open its linux-setup/asahi folder in the file manager, right-click in the folder and choose Open Terminal Here, then type:
    Terminal
    sudo bash install-secure-linux-on-asahi.sh --profile full
    It copies the package to /usr/local/lib/secure-linux and runs the setup. Leave it running (30 to 90 minutes), then restart.

Getting back to macOS: hold the power button at start-up and choose macOS. To remove Linux later, use the Asahi documentation's "Uninstalling" steps (done from macOS Disk Utility).

What is the same and what is different

The same: KDE Plasma, the Flathub apps that are built for ARM (most are), LibreWolf, the privacy settings, the firewall, encrypted DNS, updates and snapshots, backups, the welcome wizard and Secure Linux Status, and the private AI (on the processor; graphics acceleration is experimental).

ItemOn Apple Silicon
Secure Boot key, PIN unlock, TPMNot applicable: Apple has its own start-up security and no TPM.
Full-disk encryptionNot set up by the Asahi installer. FileVault keeps macOS encrypted but your Linux files are not. The Asahi documentation describes manual encryption. Until then treat the Mac as "not encrypted"; Secure Linux Status shows this.
NVIDIA and Broadcom driversNot applicable.
HibernateNot supported. Sleep works well.
NordVPN, Cloudflare WARP, cloudflaredInstalled only if their makers offer an ARM version. Otherwise skipped and shown in Secure Linux Status. Use WireGuard or another VPN in the meantime.
Network protection (OpenSnitch)On by default as on other computers, but from Fedora's own package. If there is none for this Mac it is skipped with a one-off notice.
Touch ID, Thunderbolt and USB4 displaysDepend on Asahi's progress (asahilinux.org feature pages).

Apps that only exist for Intel and AMD

Some programs are made only for ordinary Intel and AMD computers (called "x86"). An Apple Silicon Mac uses a different kind of chip (called "ARM" or "aarch64"), so those programs cannot run. Instead of trying and showing errors, the setup checks first:

  • If the program's makers publish an ARM version (for example the immich-go photo uploader), setup downloads that version, checks its fingerprint (checksum) exactly as on other computers, and installs it.
  • If there is no ARM version, setup leaves that program out, says so in the setup log, and carries on. Nothing is marked as broken.

Programs usually left out on a Mac: the Flathub versions of Steam, Heroic Games Launcher, ProtonUp-Qt, Bottles and Upscayl, plus ArtCraft and immich-go if their makers have no ARM download yet. The list is decided live by asking Flathub when the Mac is online; offline, a short built-in list is used. The Status window shows each one as a calm blue line, for example "Not available on this computer: NordVPN, because NordVPN doesn't offer a version for this type of computer (Apple Silicon / ARM)". It is only information: nothing is wrong, there is nothing to fix, and it is never red or orange. The line disappears by itself once the program is installed (for example after its makers publish an ARM version and you run Repair setup). On a Mac this usually includes NordVPN and its window app, Cloudflare WARP and Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared), as well as the games and art apps above.

Steam on an Apple Silicon Mac

Flathub's Steam does not work on ARM. Fedora Asahi has its own steam package that runs Windows and x86 games inside a small virtual machine (using FEX). It needs a lot of memory, so setup installs it only if the Mac has 16 GB of memory or more. With less, Steam is skipped; you can try sudo dnf install steam yourself. Pros: many games work. Cons: games run slower than on a PC, and not all will start.

What to do if an app you want is missing

  1. See why it was left out: the list is in /var/lib/secure-linux/skipped-apps (one line per app, "app|reason"), or look at the setup log, or the Status window.
  2. For a Flathub app, check yourself: flatpak remote-info --arch=aarch64 flathub APP-ID. If it prints details, install it with flatpak install flathub APP-ID.
  3. Later, run Update apps from outside Fedora in Secure Linux Status (or secure-linux-outside-apps --update): it picks up an ARM download once the makers publish one, and the app's line is removed from the skipped list.
  4. Many Intel-only programs can still be tried through Asahi's x86 support (FEX): docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/fedora-asahi-remix/x86-support/.

Honest note. The Apple Silicon path was written against Asahi's documentation and tested with simulated ARM systems here. It has not been run on a real Mac yet. Whether NordVPN, WARP and OpenSnitch have ARM packages was not confirmed.

Smart home

Home Assistant for complete beginners

  7. The secure-linux-ha command, in one table
  8. Keep passwords out of your files
  9. Add the starter kit (ten minutes, no typing)
  10. Safe testing in a copy
  11. Presence by phone (who is home)
  12. Notifications to your phone

  15. Using your Android phone and Flipper Zero

This is the first of four smart-home chapters. This one explains what Home Assistant is, the words you need, your first 30 minutes, and how to set up a home server for it. The next three are "Ten starter automations", "Keep your smart home safe" and "Advanced, made easy". If you have no smart-home gadgets and no plans for any, you can skip all four: nothing here is installed that you have to use.

What it is, in one paragraph

Home Assistant is free, open-source software that becomes the brain of your smart home. Lights, plugs, heaters, door sensors, cameras and speakers from many brands all show up in one place, and you can make them work together ("when the front door opens after dark, turn on the hall light"). It runs on a small always-on computer at home, so it keeps working when the internet is down and nobody's cloud company sees when you come and go.

Home Assistant is server software: it does not run "on" this laptop. This laptop has a Home Assistant window in the app menu that opens its web page, and your phone has the Home Assistant app.

Where does it run?

WayGood forProsCons
Home Assistant OS on its own small computer (Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, or a mini PC)Almost everybody (recommended)One-click updates, backups and add-ons. Least to go wrong.A new box to buy (about A$120 to A$300) and keep powered.
Container on your existing home server (next to Immich)You like tinkering and already have a serverNo new hardware. Our server kit sets up the extras safely.No add-on store; more do-it-yourself; you look after updates.
Practice copy on this laptop (secure-linux-ha local start)Learning safelyPrivate to this laptop, off until you start it; nothing at risk.Not your real house. Downloads about 1.5 GB the first time. Full and atomic setups only.

The words you need

  • Entity: one thing Home Assistant can see or control (a light, a temperature reading). Named like light.lounge.
  • Device: the physical gadget. One device can have several entities (a motion sensor also reports its battery).
  • Integration: the "driver" for a brand or standard (Hue, Zigbee, Matter, ESPHome).
  • Area: a room. Put devices in areas and you can say "turn off the kitchen".
  • Automation: "when this happens (trigger), and only if this is true (condition), do that (action)".
  • Script: a saved list of actions you run on demand, like a macro.
  • Scene: a saved look, like "Movie night".
  • Helper: a small switch, number or text box you create (great for modes like Away mode).
  • Blueprint: a ready-made automation recipe. You only choose the sensor and lights from lists.
  • Dashboard: the pages you look at.
  • Add-on: extra software beside Home Assistant (only on Home Assistant OS). Mosquitto and ESPHome are add-ons there.

More words (YAML, MQTT, Zigbee, Matter, Thread, ESPHome, Node-RED, Assist, Whisper, Piper, long-lived access token, reverse proxy, VLAN, Meshnet, restore point, rollback and others) each have a one-line meaning you can look up: secure-linux-ha-learn glossary WORD.

Your first 30 minutes

  1. Open it from the app menu ("Home Assistant"). First time only: create the owner account. Use a long, unique password from Bitwarden. This account is the administrator.
  2. Make a second, normal account for everyday use: Settings, People, Add person.
  3. Turn on two-step login: your name (bottom-left), Security, Multi-factor Authentication. Do it for every account.
  4. Set your home: Settings, System, General. Location, time zone (Australia/Melbourne), units, currency AUD. Sunrise and sunset automations depend on the location being right.
  5. See what it found: Settings, Devices & services. Lights, speakers and TVs often appear by themselves. Click Configure.
  6. Add your phone (Android: Play Store or F-Droid): install "Home Assistant", sign in with your address. You now get notifications and presence.
  7. Turn on automatic backups: Settings, System, Backups. Keep encryption on and save the key in Bitwarden.
  8. Run the security check: secure-linux-ha-secure --guided (or "Security check (grade A to F)" in the app menu).

Stop there. Everything else can wait for another day.

The Home Assistant entries in the app menu

Menu entryWhat it does
Home AssistantOpens your dashboard in its own window (secure-linux-ha open). The address comes from your saved choice ha_url.
Security check (grade A to F)The friendly security walk-through. See "Keep your smart home safe".
Learn Home Assistant (beginner lessons) and Home Assistant: Learn the BasicsEight short lessons in a terminal window (secure-linux-ha-learn).
Is it working? (status)Is Home Assistant answering, what is installed, and when was the last security check (secure-linux-ha status).

Setting up a home server for Home Assistant

What it is. secure-linux-ha-setup is a guided set-up of Home Assistant on your home server, one question at a time. Every question waits for you and nothing happens until you say yes. It helps you choose between the two real ways: (A) Home Assistant OS on its own small computer (the recommended way), or (B) the Container version on the home server you already have (the one running Immich).

  1. Run secure-linux-ha-setup (or say yes when the welcome wizard's Home Assistant page offers it). Add --dry-run first to see what it would do without connecting anywhere.
  2. For A it guides you through writing Home Assistant OS to a memory card or drive and first start-up.
  3. For B it copies the server kit (the server/homeassistant folder on your stick) to your server over SSH and, if you say yes, runs it there. The main script is install-ha-container.sh. It asks which extras you want (Mosquitto for MQTT with a password, Zigbee2MQTT, ESPHome, Node-RED, a Matter server, local voice with Whisper and Piper), and writes a tidy stack folder, locked down.
  4. Tell the laptop where Home Assistant lives: the welcome wizard page "Home Assistant (smart home)" can look for homeassistant.local for you, or you can type the address (for example http://10.0.30.50:8123). It is saved as the choice ha_url.

What the server kit never does: open anything to the internet, install an auto-updater (Watchtower), mount the Docker socket anywhere, or run anything "privileged". Updates are your decision: safe-update.sh backs up first and updates one thing at a time. The other kit scripts are add-caddy.sh (HTTPS at home), firewall-lan-only.sh, harden-host.sh, setup-ha-backup.sh, setup-mosquitto.sh and usb-passthrough.sh (for a Zigbee or Z-Wave dongle). "Keep your smart home safe" explains what each does for security.

If it fails. If the laptop cannot reach the server, check you are on your home Wi-Fi (or Meshnet), then run secure-linux-ha doctor, which explains each step. If SSH asks for a password and you have not set a key, that is normal the first time. Nothing in the set-up is irreversible: you can stop at any question.

The secure-linux-ha command, in one table

CommandWhat it does
secure-linux-ha openOpen Home Assistant in its own window.
secure-linux-ha statusIs it answering? What is installed? When was the last security check?
secure-linux-ha doctorFind problems and say how to fix each one, in plain English.
secure-linux-ha backup [--api]Save a copy of your Home Assistant settings (--api asks Home Assistant to make its own). Copies go in ~/HomeAssistant-backups/ (private; they contain secrets).
secure-linux-ha update-checkIs a newer Home Assistant out? What to do before updating.
secure-linux-ha validate [FOLDER]Check your YAML files for mistakes before you restart Home Assistant.
secure-linux-ha snapshot [FOLDER]Save a restore point of your settings (Git; secrets left out).
secure-linux-ha rollback [FOLDER]Go back to an earlier restore point (shows the list, asks first).
secure-linux-ha starter list | install [NAME|all] | dashboardReady-made automations, safe to add.
secure-linux-ha token-set [--delete]Save a Home Assistant access token in a private (root-only) file for the security check. The token is read silently and never shown or logged.
secure-linux-ha discover [--save]Look for homeassistant.local on your network.
secure-linux-ha local enable | start | stop | status | open | logs | update | relax | resetThe private practice copy on this laptop only.

Keep passwords out of your files

Anything secret goes in secrets.yaml (same folder as configuration.yaml) and is used by name, so a screenshot of your settings never shows it:

Terminal
# in secrets.yaml
camera_password: "a-long-unique-password"

# in any other file
camera:
  - platform: generic
    still_image_url: http://10.0.30.50/snap.jpg
    username: viewer
    password: !secret camera_password

secure-linux-ha-secure --check finds secrets typed straight into your files, and --apply moves them for you.

Add the starter kit (ten minutes, no typing)

secure-linux-ha starter list shows the ready-made automations. secure-linux-ha starter install all --dir <your config folder> adds them. It makes a restore point first, checks the result loads, and undoes itself if not. The next chapter shows each one. Then set your phone once: Settings, Devices & services, Helpers, Phone notify service, and type the name that looks like notify.mobile_app_pixel_8. Every alert the kit sends goes through that one box.

Safe testing in a copy

Never try risky things on the real house. Three safety nets:

  1. Restore points (secure-linux-ha snapshot, then secure-linux-ha rollback to go back): a Git history of your settings that keeps your passwords out.
  2. Check before you restart (secure-linux-ha validate): finds YAML mistakes, duplicate keys and missing files before Home Assistant chokes on them.
  3. A practice copy: secure-linux-ha local start runs a separate Home Assistant on this laptop only (reachable only from this computer, sandboxed). Copy an automation in, try it, throw the copy away with secure-linux-ha local reset. To test a backup of your real setup, restore it into the practice copy first.

Presence by phone (who is home)

Install the Home Assistant app on each phone, allow location "all the time", and sign in. Home Assistant creates a device tracker per phone and a Person you link them to (Settings, People). The built-in Home zone then counts how many people are home, which is what the Away mode blueprint uses. Tips: turn off battery optimisation for the app (Android), keep location accuracy on, and give it a Wi-Fi name to confirm "home" (Companion app, Settings, Sensors, Wi-Fi connection). Privacy: location stays on your own server; that is the point of running it at home.

Notifications to your phone

With the app installed, Home Assistant adds a notify service named notify.mobile_app_<your phone>. Test it in Developer tools, Actions: choose it, message "Hello", Perform action. The starter kit's "Notify me" script wraps this so you set the phone once. For urgent alerts (leak, smoke) the kit sets high priority so they ring through. Allow the app to bypass Do Not Disturb for those.

Energy dashboard

Settings, Dashboards, Energy. Add your grid consumption (a smart meter integration or a plug with power monitoring), solar if you have it, and each big appliance. Enter your electricity price in AUD per kWh (find it on your bill; time-of-use tariffs are supported). Give it a week to show patterns. Quick wins people find: the standby power of TVs and the hot-water system's schedule.

Voice (Assist) that stays at home

Assist is Home Assistant's built-in voice assistant. Typed commands work straight away (the speech-bubble icon): "turn on the hall light". For voice, run speech engines on your own server so nothing leaves the house: Whisper (speech to text) and Piper (text to speech). The server kit has them as an option (install-ha-container.sh --with voice); on Home Assistant OS install the "Whisper" and "Piper" add-ons. Then Settings, Voice assistants, your assistant, and pick them. Start with the small Whisper model; a Raspberry Pi manages "tiny" fine. The phone app can use Assist too (the microphone button).

Using your Android phone and Flipper Zero

  • Android phone: the Companion app gives presence, notifications, battery and Wi-Fi sensors, voice, and quick tiles. NFC tags can start automations: Settings, Tags, write one with the app, stick it on the door ("goodnight").
  • Flipper Zero (sub-GHz radio, NFC, RFID, infrared, Bluetooth LE): safe, useful ideas are recording your own TV or air conditioner's infrared codes as a reference for a cheap IR blaster, and reading the frequency of your own garage remote to choose a compatible relay. Only capture signals from devices you own. Do not use it to copy anyone else's cards or remotes. For a bridge to Home Assistant, a small ESP32 running ESPHome is the clean way ("Advanced, made easy").
  • Together: an NFC tag on the nightstand starts the "Goodnight" routine.

Learn by listening

secure-linux-ha-learn has eight short lessons (a menu that waits for you). secure-linux-ha-learn tour shows them in order. secure-linux-ha-learn explain sl_battery_alerts reads any ready-made file out loud in plain English ("It starts when the clock reaches 09:00. Then it will send you a notification..."), and --speak says it aloud if a speech program is installed. secure-linux-ha-learn files lists the files it can explain.

Desktop tools on this laptop

  • Home Assistant (app menu): your dashboard in its own window.
  • Butler (from Flathub, GPL-3.0): an optional native window for a dashboard. It does not give location, notifications or sensors: that is what the phone app is for. Not verified: how to set its address (it asks on first run).
  • hass-cli (command line): hass-cli state list. It needs a token in the environment (HASS_TOKEN) and HASS_SERVER; do not type the token on a command line you keep in history.
  • esphome (optional, off by default): build your own sensors.

There is no official Home Assistant desktop app for Linux. The web window and Butler are the trustworthy options found. LNXlink (publishes this laptop to Home Assistant over MQTT) exists but asks for broad permissions, so it is not installed by default.

When something goes wrong

ProblemWhat to try
The Home Assistant window shows "can't connect"Is the server on? Are you on your home Wi-Fi or Meshnet? secure-linux-ha doctor explains each step.
homeassistant.local does not workSome routers hide .local names. Use the server's number: secure-linux-choice set ha_url http://10.0.30.50:8123.
"400: Bad Request" after adding CaddyAdd use_x_forwarded_for: true and trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1, ::1] (the server kit's add-caddy.sh does it).
Home Assistant will not start after I edited YAMLRestore: secure-linux-ha rollback. Next time run secure-linux-ha validate before restarting.
An automation never runsSettings, Automations, open it, Traces: it shows exactly which step stopped it.
A device keeps going "unavailable"Wi-Fi range, a flat battery, or a USB dongle on a USB 3 port (use an extension cable). The offline watchdog tells you.
No phone notificationsCheck the helper "Phone notify service" holds the right name; allow notifications and disable battery optimisation in Android.
The practice copy will not startsecure-linux-ha local logs; if it complains about permissions, secure-linux-ha local relax removes the extra sandbox settings.
I forgot the admin passwordOn Home Assistant OS use the console or ha auth reset; on a container, docker exec -it homeassistant hass --script auth -c /config change_password <user> <new>. Then change it to something long again.

The saved choices behind it

The welcome wizard (or secure-linux-choice set KEY VALUE) saves these. You rarely need them by hand.

ChoiceMeaning
ha_urlWhere the menu entry and the checker look (default http://homeassistant.local:8123).
ha_localyes sets up the practice copy (never started until you run secure-linux-ha local start).
ha_token_fileThe path of the private file holding an access token (never the token itself).
ha_remote_modeHow you reach Home Assistant from away: meshnet, wireguard, tailscale, cloudflare, nabucasa, none, portforward (graded as a serious failure) or other.
ha_sshThe home server login (user@host) used by the security check and the set-up.
ha_have_serverWhat the wizard learned: yes, no, or no-os-appliance.
ha_esphomeyes installs the esphome command-line tool (large; off by default).
ha_config_dirWhich config folder the validate, snapshot, rollback, starter and backup commands use by default.

Your own answers (like "does my router forward ports?") are kept in ~/.config/secure-linux/ha-attest, and the last security grade in ~/.local/state/secure-linux/ha-last-check. Neither holds any password.
