Smart home

Ten starter automations

On this page 13 sections
  1. First: the shared switches and the one messenger
  2. 1. Lights on when there is motion
  3. 2. Lights on at sunset
  4. 3. Away mode (everyone out)
  5. 4. Low-battery warning for every battery
  6. 5. Door left open
  7. 6. Leak, smoke, gas or carbon-monoxide alarm (urgent)
  8. 7. Goodnight
  9. 8. Vacation simulation
  10. 9. Device offline watchdog
  11. 10. Failed login alert (your smoke alarm for the login page)
  12. Also in the kit
  13. After adding or changing anything: check, then restart

An automation is "when this happens (the trigger), and only if this is true (the condition), do that (the action)". You do not have to type any of the ten below: they are already in the kit. secure-linux-ha starter list shows them and secure-linux-ha starter install all adds them to your config safely (it makes a restore point first, checks the result loads, and undoes itself if not).

Each one below shows what it does, how to use it, what to do if it does not work, and the exact file from the kit, so you can read how simple an automation is and copy the idea. The files are copied into this guide when it is built, so they cannot drift from the real ones. Hear any file explained in everyday words: secure-linux-ha-learn explain sl_battery_alerts.

Two kinds of file. A blueprint is a recipe: you do not edit it, you pick your sensors and lights from drop-down lists in Settings, Automations & scenes, Blueprints. A package is a ready-made feature file in your config's packages folder that switches itself on, with nothing to set up. All of them send alerts through the same "Notify me" messenger, so you set your phone once.

First: the shared switches and the one messenger

Every package sends alerts through one script called Notify me, and three on/off switches (Away mode, Vacation mode, Goodnight) are shared. They live in sl_helpers.yaml. Until you type your phone's notify name into the helper Phone notify service (Settings, Devices & services, Helpers), alerts still appear in the bell icon inside Home Assistant.

The exact file: sl_helpers.yaml (switches and Notify me)
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_helpers.yaml  -  the "switches and one messenger" that all the other Secure Linux packages share
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   Creates a few on/off switches (Away mode, Vacation mode, Goodnight) and ONE script called
#                "Notify me". Every other package sends its alerts through "Notify me", so you only set
#                up your phone once.
# WHY            If each automation had its own phone settings, you'd have to change them everywhere when
#                you buy a new phone. Here you change ONE box.
# HOW TO USE     1. Install the Home Assistant app on your phone (Android: Play Store or F-Droid) and sign in.
#                2. In Home Assistant: Settings > Devices & services > Mobile App > your phone. Note the
#                   "notify" name, it looks like:  notify.mobile_app_pixel_8
#                3. Settings > Devices & services > Helpers > "Phone notify service" > type that name into it.
#                4. Test it: Developer tools > Actions > script.sl_notify > Perform action.
#                Until you do step 3, alerts still appear in the bell icon (bottom-left) inside Home Assistant.
# SAFE TO EDIT   Names and icons. Please leave the ids (the part after the dot) alone: other files use them.

input_boolean:
  sl_away_mode:
    name: "Away mode"
    icon: mdi:home-export-outline
  sl_vacation_mode:
    name: "Vacation mode (pretend someone is home)"
    icon: mdi:airplane
  sl_goodnight:
    name: "Goodnight (turn on to run the routine)"
    icon: mdi:weather-night

input_text:
  # Where phone alerts go. It keeps what you type, even after a restart.
  sl_notify_service:
    name: "Phone notify service"
    icon: mdi:cellphone-message
    max: 100

script:
  sl_notify:
    alias: "Notify me"
    description: "Sends a message to the bell in Home Assistant and (if you filled in the helper) to your phone."
    icon: mdi:bell-ring
    mode: queued
    fields:
      title:
        description: "Short headline"
        example: "Low battery"
      message:
        description: "The details"
        example: "Front door sensor is at 12%"
      urgent:
        description: "true makes the phone alert loud and immediate"
        example: false
    sequence:
      # 1. Always put it in the bell inside Home Assistant (works even before the phone is set up).
      - action: persistent_notification.create
        data:
          title: "{{ title | default('Home Assistant') }}"
          message: "{{ message | default('') }}"
          notification_id: "sl_{{ (title | default('note')) | slugify }}"
      # 2. If a phone is configured, send it there too.
      - if:
          - condition: template
            value_template: "{{ states('input_text.sl_notify_service') | length > 0 }}"
        then:
          - action: "{{ states('input_text.sl_notify_service') }}"
            data:
              title: "{{ title | default('Home Assistant') }}"
              message: "{{ message | default('') }}"
              data:
                ttl: "{{ 0 if urgent | default(false) else 3600 }}"
                priority: "{{ 'high' if urgent | default(false) else 'normal' }}"

1. Lights on when there is motion

What it does. When the hall motion sensor sees movement (after dark, if you tick "only when it's dark"), the lights come on. They go off again after nobody has moved for a while (120 seconds unless you change it).

How to use it (blueprint). Settings, Automations & scenes, Blueprints, Lights on when there is motion, Create automation. Pick your motion sensor and lights from the lists. No typing.

If it does not work. Lights never come on: check the sensor reports its type as motion, and that "only when it's dark" is not blocking your daytime test. Lights go off too soon: raise the "Switch off after" number.

The exact file: motion_light.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# Blueprint: Lights on when there is motion
# =====================================================================================================
# A blueprint is a RECIPE. You don't edit this file. In Home Assistant go to
#   Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints > "Lights on when there is motion" > Create automation
# and pick your motion sensor and lights from the drop-down lists. Done: no YAML typing.
#
# WHAT IT DOES   Motion seen -> lights on. No motion for the wait time -> lights off.
# OPTION         "Only when it's dark" stops daytime switching (uses the sun).
blueprint:
  name: "Lights on when there is motion"
  author: Secure Linux
  description: >
    Turns lights on when a motion sensor sees movement and off again after nobody has moved for a while.
    Tick "only when dark" so it does nothing in daylight.
  domain: automation
  min_version: 2024.10.0
  input:
    motion_sensor:
      name: Motion sensor
      description: The sensor that sees movement.
      selector:
        entity:
          filter:
            - domain: binary_sensor
              device_class: motion
    lights:
      name: Lights
      description: Which lights to switch (pick lights, a room or a floor).
      selector:
        target:
          entity:
            domain: light
    wait_seconds:
      name: Switch off after
      description: How long with no movement before the lights go off.
      default: 120
      selector:
        number:
          min: 10
          max: 3600
          step: 10
          unit_of_measurement: seconds
    only_dark:
      name: Only when it's dark
      description: When on, nothing happens while the sun is up.
      default: true
      selector:
        boolean:

mode: restart
max_exceeded: silent

variables:
  only_dark: !input only_dark

triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: !input motion_sensor
    from: "off"
    to: "on"

conditions:
  - condition: or
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ not only_dark }}"
      - condition: state
        entity_id: sun.sun
        state: below_horizon

actions:
  - action: light.turn_on
    target: !input lights
  - wait_for_trigger:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: !input motion_sensor
        from: "on"
        to: "off"
        for:
          seconds: !input wait_seconds
  - action: light.turn_off
    target: !input lights

2. Lights on at sunset

What it does. Half an hour before sunset your chosen lights come on, so the house is never dark when you walk in, and they go off at bedtime. Home Assistant knows when the sun sets at your address, so it follows the seasons by itself.

How to use it (blueprint). Blueprints, Lights on at sunset, off at bedtime, Create automation. The "Sunset offset" box uses hours:minutes:seconds with a minus sign: -00:30:00 is 30 minutes before sunset; 00:15:00 is 15 minutes after.

If it does not work. Lights come on at the wrong time: check your location and time zone in Settings, System, General.

The exact file: sunset_lights.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# Blueprint: Lights on at sunset, off at bedtime
# =====================================================================================================
# Create it from: Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints > "Lights on at sunset, off at bedtime" > Create automation.
#
# WHAT IT DOES   Lights come on a little before the sun sets (so the house is never dark), and go off at your
#                chosen bedtime. Home Assistant knows when the sun sets at YOUR address (set in Settings >
#                System > General), so it follows the seasons by itself.
# THE "BEFORE SUNSET" BOX  Type it as hours:minutes:seconds with a minus sign, for example -00:30:00 means
#                30 minutes BEFORE sunset. 00:15:00 (no minus) means 15 minutes after.
blueprint:
  name: "Lights on at sunset, off at bedtime"
  author: Secure Linux
  description: >
    Switches your chosen lights on around sunset and off at a set time every night.
  domain: automation
  min_version: 2024.10.0
  input:
    lights:
      name: Lights
      selector:
        target:
          entity:
            domain: light
    sunset_offset:
      name: Sunset offset
      description: "-00:30:00 = half an hour before sunset. 00:00:00 = exactly at sunset."
      default: "-00:30:00"
      selector:
        text:
    bedtime:
      name: Off at
      description: Time the lights go off.
      default: "23:00:00"
      selector:
        time:

mode: single

triggers:
  - trigger: sun
    event: sunset
    offset: !input sunset_offset
    id: "on"
  - trigger: time
    at: !input bedtime
    id: "off"

actions:
  - choose:
      - conditions:
          - condition: trigger
            id: "on"
        sequence:
          - action: light.turn_on
            target: !input lights
      - conditions:
          - condition: trigger
            id: "off"
        sequence:
          - action: light.turn_off
            target: !input lights

3. Away mode (everyone out)

What it does. The built-in Home zone counts the people at home. When it stays at zero for five minutes (you choose), Away mode switches on, your chosen lights go off and your chosen locks lock. When someone comes back, Away mode switches off. Locks are only ever locked, never unlocked, by this recipe.

How to use it (blueprint). Needs the Home Assistant app on each phone with location on (see "Presence by phone" in the first chapter). Blueprints, Away mode, Create automation, then choose lights, locks and (optionally) an alarm panel.

If it does not work. It switches on while you are home: a phone's location is jumping about. Raise the wait, and turn off battery optimisation for the app.

The exact file: away_mode.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# Blueprint: Away mode (everyone out: switch off and lock up; someone home: switch back)
# =====================================================================================================
# Create it from: Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints > "Away mode" > Create automation.
#
# HOW IT KNOWS NOBODY IS HOME  The built-in "Home" zone counts how many People are there. For this you
#                need the Home Assistant app on each phone with location turned on (see the guide chapter
#                "Presence by phone"). When the count stays at 0 for 5 minutes, everyone is out.
# WHAT IT DOES   Everyone out: turns on the "Away mode" switch (from sl_helpers.yaml, or pick your own), turns off the
#                lights you choose and locks the locks you choose. Someone comes home: Away mode goes off.
#                Optional: arm an alarm panel if you have one.
# SAFETY         Locks are only LOCKED, never unlocked, by this blueprint.
blueprint:
  name: "Away mode"
  author: Secure Linux
  description: >
    When the last person leaves, switch off lights and lock the doors. When someone comes home, go back to normal.
  domain: automation
  min_version: 2024.10.0
  input:
    away_switch:
      name: Away mode switch
      description: The on/off helper that other automations can look at.
      default: input_boolean.sl_away_mode
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: input_boolean
    wait_minutes:
      name: Wait before deciding nobody is home
      description: Stops false alarms when a phone's location jumps for a moment.
      default: 5
      selector:
        number:
          min: 1
          max: 60
          unit_of_measurement: minutes
    lights:
      name: Lights to switch off
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: light
          multiple: true
    locks:
      name: Locks to lock
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: lock
          multiple: true
    alarm:
      name: Alarm panel to arm (optional)
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: alarm_control_panel
          multiple: true

mode: single

variables:
  lights: !input lights
  locks: !input locks
  alarm: !input alarm

triggers:
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id: zone.home
    below: 1
    for:
      minutes: !input wait_minutes
    id: left
  - trigger: numeric_state
    entity_id: zone.home
    above: 0
    id: arrived

actions:
  - choose:
      - conditions:
          - condition: trigger
            id: left
        sequence:
          - action: input_boolean.turn_on
            target:
              entity_id: !input away_switch
          - if:
              - condition: template
                value_template: "{{ lights | count > 0 }}"
            then:
              - action: light.turn_off
                target:
                  entity_id: !input lights
          - if:
              - condition: template
                value_template: "{{ locks | count > 0 }}"
            then:
              - action: lock.lock
                target:
                  entity_id: !input locks
          - if:
              - condition: template
                value_template: "{{ alarm | count > 0 }}"
            then:
              - action: alarm_control_panel.alarm_arm_away
                target:
                  entity_id: !input alarm
      - conditions:
          - condition: trigger
            id: arrived
        sequence:
          - action: input_boolean.turn_off
            target:
              entity_id: !input away_switch

4. Low-battery warning for every battery

What it does. A morning list at 9am of anything under 20 per cent, with nothing to set up, because it asks for every sensor of type "battery". A second automation warns straight away when anything falls under 10 per cent. New gadgets are covered automatically.

How to use it (package). Nothing to configure. secure-linux-ha starter install sl_battery_alerts adds it. To change the limits, edit the numbers 20 and 10 in the file, run secure-linux-ha validate, then restart.

If it does not work. No message ever arrives: set "Phone notify service" (see the first 30 minutes) and check the bell icon in Home Assistant, where every alert also appears.

The exact file: sl_battery_alerts.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_battery_alerts.yaml  -  tells you about EVERY low battery in the house (nothing to set up)
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   Warns you about every low battery in the house. Every morning at 9 it looks at all battery sensors (door sensors, motion sensors, remotes,
#                phones, temperature gadgets...) and sends you one message listing any under 20%.
#                Also warns straight away if any drops under 10%.
# WHY            Flat batteries are the number one reason a smart home "stops working". This finds them first.
# HOW IT FINDS THEM  Home Assistant labels battery sensors with device_class "battery". We ask for all
#                of those, so new gadgets are covered automatically.
# CHANGE THE LIMITS  Edit the two numbers: 20 (daily digest) and 10 (urgent). Save, then run
#                secure-linux-ha validate before restarting.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Batteries: daily low-battery list"
    id: sl_battery_daily
    description: "At 9am, lists every battery under 20% in one message."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: time
        at: "09:00:00"
    variables:
      # Build a list like "Front door (12%)" from every battery sensor under 20.
      low: >
        {% set ns = namespace(items=[]) %}
        {% for s in states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined') | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery') %}
          {% if s.state | float(100) < 20 %}
            {% set ns.items = ns.items + [s.name ~ ' (' ~ (s.state | float | round(0) | int) ~ '%)'] %}
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
        {% for s in states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined') | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery') | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') %}
          {% set ns.items = ns.items + [s.name ~ ' (low)'] %}
        {% endfor %}
        {{ ns.items }}
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ low | count > 0 }}"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Low batteries"
          message: "{{ low | join(', ') }}"

  - alias: "Batteries: urgent when one gets very low"
    id: sl_battery_urgent
    description: "Warns straight away when any battery drops under 10%."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: template
        value_template: >
          {{ states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined') | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery')
             | selectattr('state', 'search', '^[0-9.]+$') | map(attribute='state') | map('float') | select('lt', 10) | list | count > 0 }}
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Battery almost flat"
          message: >
            {% set ns = namespace(items=[]) %}
            {% for s in states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined') | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery') %}
              {% if s.state | float(100) < 10 %}{% set ns.items = ns.items + [s.name ~ ' (' ~ (s.state | float | round(0) | int) ~ '%)'] %}{% endif %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ ns.items | join(', ') }}
          urgent: false

5. Door left open

What it does. If any door, window or garage-door sensor stays open for ten minutes, you get a message naming it. It speaks up once per open period; to be told again, close everything and reopen.

How to use it (package). Nothing to configure. Change 00:10:00 (hours:minutes:seconds) for another time, such as 00:05:00 for five minutes.

If it does not work. A sensor that never triggers: set its "device class" to door, window or garage door in that entity's settings.

The exact file: sl_door_left_open.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_door_left_open.yaml  -  "the garage / front door has been open for 10 minutes"
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   If any door, window or garage-door sensor stays open for 10 minutes, you get a message
#                naming it.
# WHY            Doors left open waste heating, let bugs in, and are a security risk.
# CHANGE THE TIME  Change "00:10:00" (hours:minutes:seconds). Try "00:05:00" for 5 minutes.
# NOTE           It speaks up once per open period. To be told again, close everything and reopen.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Doors: left open for 10 minutes"
    id: sl_door_open
    description: "Tells you when a door, window or garage door has been open for 10 minutes."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: template
        value_template: >
          {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
             | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
             | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}
        for: "00:10:00"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Still open"
          message: >
            {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
               | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
               | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }}
            open for 10 minutes or more.

6. Leak, smoke, gas or carbon-monoxide alarm (urgent)

What it does. Any water-leak, smoke, gas or carbon-monoxide sensor turning "on" sends a loud, immediate phone alert naming the sensor. Doing it by sensor type means a new leak sensor is protected the moment you add it.

How to use it (package). Nothing to configure. Allow the Home Assistant app to bypass Do Not Disturb so urgent alerts ring through.

If it does not work. Important: this is an extra alert. Smoke and carbon-monoxide safety must still come from proper, certified alarms. If no alert arrives, check the phone notify service and that the sensor's device class is moisture, smoke, gas or carbon monoxide.

The exact file: sl_leak_smoke.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_leak_smoke.yaml  -  water, smoke, gas and carbon monoxide alarms: loud phone alert, nothing to set up
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   If ANY sensor of type moisture (leak), smoke, gas or carbon monoxide turns "on", you get an
#                urgent message on your phone and in Home Assistant, naming the sensor.
# WHY            These are the alerts you never want to miss. Doing it by sensor TYPE means a new leak sensor
#                is protected the moment you add it.
# IMPORTANT      This is an EXTRA alert. Smoke and CO safety must still come from proper, certified alarms.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Safety: leak, smoke or gas alarm"
    id: sl_leak_smoke
    description: "Urgent phone alert when any leak, smoke, gas or carbon monoxide sensor goes on."
    mode: queued
    triggers:
      - trigger: template
        value_template: >
          {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
             | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['moisture', 'smoke', 'gas', 'carbon_monoxide'])
             | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "ALARM: leak, smoke or gas"
          message: >
            {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
               | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['moisture', 'smoke', 'gas', 'carbon_monoxide'])
               | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }} - go and check now.
          urgent: true

7. Goodnight

What it does. Turn on the Goodnight switch (on your dashboard, by voice, or with an NFC tag) and: lights go off, doors lock, heating can be turned down, and you are warned if a door or window is still open. The switch turns itself off again, ready for tomorrow. You can also pick a bedtime so it runs by itself.

How to use it (blueprint). Blueprints, Goodnight routine, Create automation. Choose lights, locks and optional heating.

If it does not work. The routine runs but a light stays on: that light was not in your list. Edit the automation and add it.

The exact file: goodnight.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# Blueprint: Goodnight routine
# =====================================================================================================
# Create it from: Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints > "Goodnight routine" > Create automation.
#
# HOW YOU START IT   Turn on the "Goodnight" switch (it appears on your dashboard and works with voice:
#                "turn on goodnight"). Or pick a time and it runs by itself each night.
# WHAT IT DOES   Lights off, doors locked, optional heating setback, then tells you if a door or window is
#                still open. The switch turns itself off again, ready for tomorrow.
blueprint:
  name: "Goodnight routine"
  author: Secure Linux
  description: >
    One switch (or a bedtime) that turns off lights, locks doors, and warns you about anything left open.
  domain: automation
  min_version: 2024.10.0
  input:
    trigger_switch:
      name: Goodnight switch
      default: input_boolean.sl_goodnight
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: input_boolean
    use_bedtime:
      name: Also run automatically at bedtime
      default: false
      selector:
        boolean:
    bedtime:
      name: Bedtime
      default: "22:30:00"
      selector:
        time:
    lights:
      name: Lights to switch off
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: light
          multiple: true
    locks:
      name: Locks to lock
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: lock
          multiple: true
    heating:
      name: Heating or cooling to turn down (optional)
      default: []
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: climate
          multiple: true
    night_temperature:
      name: Night temperature
      default: 17
      selector:
        number:
          min: 10
          max: 26
          unit_of_measurement: "°C"

mode: single

variables:
  lights: !input lights
  locks: !input locks
  heating: !input heating
  use_bedtime: !input use_bedtime

triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: !input trigger_switch
    to: "on"
  - trigger: time
    at: !input bedtime

conditions:
  - condition: or
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ trigger.platform == 'state' }}"
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ use_bedtime }}"

actions:
  - if:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ lights | count > 0 }}"
    then:
      - action: light.turn_off
        target:
          entity_id: !input lights
  - if:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ locks | count > 0 }}"
    then:
      - action: lock.lock
        target:
          entity_id: !input locks
  - if:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ heating | count > 0 }}"
    then:
      - action: climate.set_temperature
        target:
          entity_id: !input heating
        data:
          temperature: !input night_temperature
  - if:
      - condition: template
        value_template: >
          {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
             | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
             | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}
    then:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Goodnight: still open"
          message: >
            {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
               | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
               | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }}
  - action: input_boolean.turn_off
    target:
      entity_id: !input trigger_switch

8. Vacation simulation

What it does. While the "Vacation mode" switch is on, at dusk (a random few minutes after sunset so it never looks the same) one of your chosen lights comes on for a random one to three hours, then goes off. A different light most nights, so the house looks lived in.

How to use it (blueprint). Create it once from Blueprints, Vacation simulation, and choose lights that can be seen from outside. Flip "Vacation mode" on when you leave and off when you are back. Do not post on social media that you are away.

If it does not work. Nothing happens: Vacation mode must be on, and the list of lights must not be empty.

The exact file: vacation_simulation.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# Blueprint: Vacation simulation (looks like someone is home)
# =====================================================================================================
# Create it from: Settings > Automations & scenes > Blueprints > "Vacation simulation" > Create automation.
#
# WHAT IT DOES   While the "Vacation mode" switch is ON, at dusk (a random few minutes after sunset so it never looks
#                the same) it turns on ONE of your chosen lights, leaves it a random 1 to 3 hours, then turns
#                it off. Different light most nights. Burglars watch for houses that stay dark.
# TO USE         Create the automation once, then just flip "Vacation mode" on when you leave and off when
#                you're back. Tell nobody on social media you are away.
blueprint:
  name: "Vacation simulation"
  author: Secure Linux
  description: >
    While Vacation mode is on, turns a random light on at dusk and off a few hours later so the house looks lived in.
  domain: automation
  min_version: 2024.10.0
  input:
    vacation_switch:
      name: Vacation mode switch
      default: input_boolean.sl_vacation_mode
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: input_boolean
    lights:
      name: Lights to use
      description: Lights that can be seen from outside (lounge, hallway, bedroom).
      selector:
        entity:
          domain: light
          multiple: true

mode: single

variables:
  lights: !input lights

triggers:
  - trigger: sun
    event: sunset

conditions:
  - condition: state
    entity_id: !input vacation_switch
    state: "on"
  - condition: template
    value_template: "{{ lights | count > 0 }}"

actions:
  - delay:
      minutes: "{{ range(0, 31) | random }}"
  - variables:
      chosen: "{{ lights | random }}"
  - action: light.turn_on
    target:
      entity_id: "{{ chosen }}"
  - delay:
      minutes: "{{ range(60, 181) | random }}"
  - action: light.turn_off
    target:
      entity_id: "{{ chosen }}"

9. Device offline watchdog

What it does. If any device has been "unavailable" for 30 minutes, you get a message listing up to ten. Gadgets quietly drop off the network (a Wi-Fi hiccup, a flat battery, unplugged). A device offline for days can also mean a network problem.

How to use it (package). Nothing to configure. If a device you switch off on purpose (a TV) nags you, disable that entity: Settings, Devices & services, Entities, the entity, Settings, Disable.

If it does not work. Too many alerts: raise 00:30:00, or disable the nagging entities.

The exact file: sl_offline_watchdog.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_offline_watchdog.yaml  -  "something has dropped off the network"
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   If any device has been "unavailable" for 30 minutes, you get a message listing up to 10.
# WHY            Smart gadgets quietly go offline (Wi-Fi hiccup, flat battery, unplugged). You would otherwise
#                find out when the light does not come on. A device that stays offline for days can also mean
#                a problem on your network.
# TIPS           A device you switch off on purpose (a TV) will show up here. If it nags you, disable that
#                entity: Settings > Devices & services > Entities > the entity > Settings > Disable.
# CHANGE THE TIME  Edit "00:30:00".
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Watchdog: devices offline for 30 minutes"
    id: sl_offline
    description: "Messages you when something has been unavailable for 30 minutes."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: template
        value_template: >
          {{ states | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'unavailable')
             | rejectattr('domain', 'in', ['automation', 'script', 'scene', 'update', 'event', 'button', 'input_button'])
             | list | count > 0 }}
        for: "00:30:00"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Offline devices"
          message: >
            {% set bad = states | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'unavailable')
               | rejectattr('domain', 'in', ['automation', 'script', 'scene', 'update', 'event', 'button', 'input_button']) | list %}
            {{ bad[:10] | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }}{{ ' and ' ~ (bad | count - 10) ~ ' more' if bad | count > 10 else '' }}

10. Failed login alert (your smoke alarm for the login page)

What it does. Home Assistant already notices failed logins and puts a notice in the bell icon. This sends that notice to your phone in seconds. The same file has two quiet extras: an urgent alert if a door or window opens while Away mode is on, and a note each time Home Assistant restarts (so an unexpected restart or update is noticed).

How to use it (package). secure-linux-ha starter install sl_security_watch. One mistyped password is normal; a string of them from a strange address means someone is guessing.

If it does not work. If it fires and it was not you: check your router has no port-forward, turn on two-step login for every account, and look in Settings, System, Logs for the address.

The exact file: sl_security_watch.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_security_watch.yaml  -  "somebody got a password wrong": a phone alert in seconds
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   Home Assistant already notices failed logins and puts a message in the bell icon. This
#                package sends that same message to your phone straight away.
# WHY            One mistyped password is normal. A string of them from a strange address means someone is
#                guessing. You want to know in minutes. (Combined with ip_ban_enabled in the secure defaults,
#                repeat guessers get blocked automatically.)
# WHAT TO DO WHEN IT FIRES  If it was you, ignore it. If not: check Settings > System > Logs for the address,
#                make sure nothing is port-forwarded on your router, turn on two-step login for every account.
# VERIFY         It listens for the notification id "http-login", which Home Assistant's web server uses
#                (checked in Home Assistant's source). The message fields available inside are
#                trigger.notification.title / message; if a future version renames them the alert still
#                arrives, with plain wording.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Security watch: failed login"
    id: sl_login_alert
    description: "Sends Home Assistant's failed-login notice to your phone."
    mode: queued
    max: 5
    triggers:
      - trigger: persistent_notification
        update_type:
          - added
          - updated
        notification_id: http-login
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Failed login to Home Assistant"
          message: "{{ trigger.notification.message | default('Someone used a wrong password. Check Settings > System > Logs.') }}"
          urgent: true

  # Two more watchers that need no setup:
  # - a door or window opens while Away mode (everyone out, see the Away mode blueprint) is on
  - alias: "Security watch: door opened while Away mode is on"
    id: sl_away_door
    description: "Urgent alert if a door or window opens while nobody is meant to be home."
    mode: queued
    triggers:
      - trigger: template
        value_template: >
          {{ is_state('input_boolean.sl_away_mode', 'on')
             and (states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
                  | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
                  | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count > 0) }}
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Opened while you're away"
          message: >
            {{ states.binary_sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
               | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'in', ['door', 'window', 'garage_door', 'opening'])
               | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }} opened while Away mode is on.
          urgent: true

  # - Home Assistant itself restarted (so an unexpected restart or update doesn't go unnoticed)
  - alias: "Security watch: Home Assistant restarted"
    id: sl_restart_notice
    description: "A quiet note each time Home Assistant starts, so an unexpected restart is noticed."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: homeassistant
        event: start
    actions:
      - delay: "00:01:00"
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Home Assistant started"
          message: "It started at {{ now().strftime('%H:%M') }}. If you didn't restart or update it, look at Settings > System > Logs."

Also in the kit

Three more packages, with nothing to set up except where they say so: backup failed or too old (turn on automatic backups first), certificate expiring in 14 days (add the "Certificate Expiry" integration for each certificate; nothing is checked until you do), and a weekly "updates waiting" digest on Sundays. There is also a starter dashboard called "Home (starter)" that works out what needs attention by itself, and a secure-defaults configuration.yaml you can read line by line.

The exact file: sl_backup_alert.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_backup_alert.yaml  -  "your backup failed" or "your backup is too old"
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   1. Alerts you when an automatic backup fails.
#                2. Every morning checks the last good backup is less than 36 hours old; alerts if not.
# WHY            Backups fail silently. The day you need one is the wrong day to find out.
# BEFORE USING   Switch on automatic backups: Settings > System > Backups > Set up automatic backups.
# VERIFY         The entity names below (event.backup_automatic_backup and
#                sensor.backup_last_successful_automatic_backup) are Home Assistant's built-in backup
#                entities in recent versions. If yours differ, check Settings > Devices & services >
#                Entities, search "backup", and change the names here.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Backup: failed"
    id: sl_backup_failed
    description: "Tells you when Home Assistant's automatic backup fails."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: event.backup_automatic_backup
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ trigger.to_state is not none and trigger.to_state.attributes.get('event_type') == 'failed' }}"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Backup FAILED"
          message: "Home Assistant's automatic backup failed. Open Settings > System > Backups to see why."
          urgent: true

  - alias: "Backup: too old"
    id: sl_backup_old
    description: "Every morning, alerts if the last good backup is older than 36 hours."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: time
        at: "08:30:00"
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: >
          {% set last = states('sensor.backup_last_successful_automatic_backup') %}
          {{ last in ['unknown', 'unavailable', 'none', ''] or (now().timestamp() - as_timestamp(last, 0)) > 36 * 3600 }}
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Backup is out of date"
          message: "No successful automatic backup in the last 36 hours. Settings > System > Backups."
The exact file: sl_cert_expiry.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_cert_expiry.yaml  -  "your HTTPS certificate expires soon"
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   Each morning checks every "Certificate Expiry" sensor and warns when one has under 14 days left.
# WHY            An expired certificate stops your phone app and browsers connecting, usually at a bad time.
#                (Caddy renews its own certificates, so this is your early warning if renewal quietly breaks.)
# ONE-TIME SETUP Settings > Devices & services > Add integration > "Certificate Expiry". Enter your
#                Home Assistant address (for example ha.home) and port 443. Add one per certificate.
#                Nothing is checked until you do that: no sensors, no alerts.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Certificates: expiring within 14 days"
    id: sl_cert_expiry
    description: "Warns when a Certificate Expiry sensor has fewer than 14 days left."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: time
        at: "09:05:00"
    variables:
      soon: >
        {% set ns = namespace(items=[]) %}
        {% for s in states.sensor | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined') | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'timestamp') | selectattr('entity_id', 'search', 'cert_expiry') %}
          {% set left = ((as_timestamp(s.state, 0) - now().timestamp()) / 86400) | int %}
          {% if s.state not in ['unknown', 'unavailable'] and left < 14 %}
            {% set ns.items = ns.items + [s.name ~ ' (' ~ left ~ ' days)'] %}
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
        {{ ns.items }}
    conditions:
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ soon | count > 0 }}"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Certificate expiring"
          message: "{{ soon | join(', ') }}"
          urgent: true
The exact file: sl_update_digest.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# sl_update_digest.yaml  -  one weekly message: "these updates are waiting"
# =====================================================================================================
# WHAT IT DOES   Sunday 10am: lists everything with an update available (Home Assistant itself, add-ons,
#                ESPHome devices, integrations, firmware) and reminds you of the safe routine.
# WHY            Security fixes only help once installed. A weekly nudge beats forgetting for six months.
# THE SAFE ROUTINE  1) make a backup, 2) read the release notes (link in the Updates page),
#                3) update ONE thing at a time, 4) check it works.  The server kit's safe-update.sh does step 1 for you.
# NEEDS          sl_helpers.yaml (for script.sl_notify)

automation:
  - alias: "Updates: weekly digest"
    id: sl_update_digest
    description: "Sunday 10am: lists all available updates and the safe update routine."
    mode: single
    triggers:
      - trigger: time
        at: "10:00:00"
    conditions:
      - condition: time
        weekday:
          - sun
      - condition: template
        value_template: "{{ states.update | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count > 0 }}"
    actions:
      - action: script.sl_notify
        data:
          title: "Updates waiting"
          message: >
            {{ states.update | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | map(attribute='name') | join(', ') }}.
            Back up first, read the release notes, then update one at a time.
The exact file: secure-defaults/configuration.yaml
Terminal
# =====================================================================================================
# configuration.yaml  -  SECURE DEFAULTS for Home Assistant (a starting point you can read line by line)
# =====================================================================================================
# HOW TO USE   If you are starting fresh, this can be your configuration.yaml. If you already have one,
#              DON'T replace it: copy only the parts you want (the comments say what each does), or let
#              secure-linux-ha-secure --apply add the safe bits for you (it shows you first and can undo).
#              Always run   secure-linux-ha validate   before restarting Home Assistant.
# SECRETS      Passwords and keys go in secrets.yaml (see secrets.yaml.example), written here as:
#                  password: !secret my_password

# ---- the basics ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
homeassistant:
  name: Home
  # Packages = ready-made feature files. Anything you drop into the 'packages' folder is loaded.
  packages: !include_dir_named packages
  # Tell Home Assistant its web addresses if you use HTTPS (otherwise leave commented out):
  # internal_url: "https://ha.home"
  # external_url: "https://ha.home"
  # SECURITY: do NOT add an 'auth_providers: - type: trusted_networks' block. It lets devices skip the password.

default_config:

# ---- the web server: this is the part that faces your network -----------------------------------------
http:
  # Block an address after too many wrong passwords. The ban is OFF unless you give a number.
  ip_ban_enabled: true
  login_attempts_threshold: 5
  # Only if a reverse proxy (Caddy) sits in front of Home Assistant on the SAME computer:
  # use_x_forwarded_for: true
  # trusted_proxies:
  #   - 127.0.0.1
  #   - ::1
  #   - 172.16.0.0/12      # Docker's private network, if Caddy runs in a container
  # Never use 0.0.0.0/0 here: that trusts the whole world to claim any address it likes.
  # cors_allowed_origins: leave it unset. Never use "*".

# ---- keep logs useful but quiet -----------------------------------------------------------------------
logger:
  default: warning
  logs:
    homeassistant.components.http.ban: warning   # failed logins show up here

# ---- keep the database a sensible size -----------------------------------------------------------------
recorder:
  purge_keep_days: 14

# ---- your own automations, scripts and scenes (the UI writes these files) ----------------------------------
automation: !include automations.yaml
script: !include scripts.yaml
scene: !include scenes.yaml

# ---- the starter dashboard ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
lovelace:
  dashboards:
    sl-starter:
      mode: yaml
      title: Home (starter)
      icon: mdi:home-heart
      show_in_sidebar: true
      filename: dashboards/sl_starter.yaml

After adding or changing anything: check, then restart

  1. secure-linux-ha snapshot (a restore point).
  2. Make your change.
  3. secure-linux-ha validate (finds mistakes before they bite).
  4. Restart Home Assistant.
  5. If an automation does not run: Settings, Automations, open it, Traces shows which step stopped it. Change one thing at a time. If the whole thing will not start, secure-linux-ha rollback.

Honest note. The automations were checked with a YAML checker and Home Assistant's documentation, but not yet against a running Home Assistant. Two details are marked unverified in the files themselves: the exact names of the backup entities (event.backup_automatic_backup and sensor.backup_last_successful_automatic_backup) and the message field inside the failed-login notice. If yours differ, the files tell you where to look.

Smart home

Keep your smart home safe

On this page 8 sections
  1. The one command: the security check
  2. What it checks, in plain English
  3. Reach it from anywhere
  4. The two lines that switch on the login ban
  5. Your first-day security checklist
  6. Passwords, secrets and tokens
  7. The server
  8. If something looks wrong

Home Assistant can unlock doors, open garages and see your cameras. That makes it worth protecting properly. The good news: a handful of habits do almost all the work, and Secure Linux has a checker that grades you from A to F and fixes the safe things for you.

The one command: the security check

Terminal
secure-linux-ha-secure --guided

Or open Security check (grade A to F) in the app menu. It asks how to look, reads your setup, and gives a grade from A to F with a plain-English line for every problem: what is wrong, why it matters and exactly how to fix it. It only looks. Nothing changes unless you say yes later. Nobody's passwords or tokens appear in the result or the report.

What the grades mean

GradeScoreIn plain words
A90 to 100Well protected. Keep your monthly routine.
B80 to 89Good. Fix the few items listed when you have a spare half hour. This is the target.
C65 to 79Fair. Real gaps. Work through the list, worst first.
D50 to 64Weak. Fix the top items soon.
Funder 50Poor. Do the "first-day checklist" below before anything else.

A serious problem holds the grade at D, however good the rest looks. Serious problems are: an open MQTT broker (anyone can control your gadgets), a router port-forward, a login bypass, or an account with a guessable password.

The score also shows a coverage figure: how many of the checks it could actually see. Looking at a copy of your config folder sees less than looking over SSH, so a grade is only as good as what it could see.

Three ways to look, one score

  • A copy of the config folder: secure-linux-ha-secure --check --config /path. Easiest, nothing leaves your computer.
  • Your server over SSH: secure-linux-ha-secure --check --ssh matt@10.0.30.42. Only yes/no facts come back, never passwords.
  • Home Assistant's own API: secure-linux-ha-secure --check --api. Needs an access token in a private file (secure-linux-ha token-set, which reads it silently).

Some things only you know (does your router forward ports? is there an off-site backup?). secure-linux-ha-secure --checklist asks those 20 questions once and remembers the answers (secure-linux-ha-secure attest KEY VALUE records a single one).

secure-linux-ha-secure --list shows every check, and --explain ip-ban (or any other id) says why one matters. --report saves the findings as a file you can keep.

Letting it fix the safe things

secure-linux-ha-secure --apply --config /path fixes the safe problems automatically. It shows you each change as a before-and-after, waits for you to type yes, saves a restore point, checks the result still loads, and undoes itself if it does not. One exception: moving a typed-in password into secrets.yaml does not make a Git restore point first (that would copy the password into the history). If you committed that file earlier, change that password.

Pros of --apply: quick, safe, reversible. Cons: it only handles the safe fixes. Things like your router, VLANs and off-site backups are yours to do; the checker tells you how.

What it checks, in plain English

GroupThe checkWhy it matters
Reaching it from awayNo router port-forward, no UPnP; a good remote methodBots find an exposed login within hours. Safe by design beats safe by effort.
EncryptionHTTPS wherever it leaves home; trusted_proxies tight; certificate not expiringPasswords in clear text can be read; a loose proxy list lets strangers fake their address.
Logging inip_ban_enabled and login_attempts_threshold; no wildcard cors_allowed_origins; no trusted_networks bypassThe automatic ban is OFF unless you set a number.
AccountsTwo-step login for everyone; no shared admin; a normal daily account; no default usernames or common passwords; few, recent, used long-lived tokensOne stolen password should never be enough.
SoftwareFew add-ons; SSH or Terminal add-on locked down; "run a command" features only if needed; debug logging offEvery extra program is extra risk.
MQTTLogin required, encrypted or loopback-only (reachable only from the same computer), per-user permissions (ACLs)An open broker lets anyone control your gadgets.
SecretsNo passwords typed into YAML or dashboards (use secrets.yaml); secrets never in Git; files not world-readable; long random webhook idsSecrets leak through backups, screenshots and forum posts.
BackupsA recent one; encrypted; one copy outside the house; a restore actually testedA backup you never restored is a hope.
UpdatesNot far behind; a monthly routine with release notesSecurity fixes only help once installed.
PrivacyFew cloud integrationsEach is a company that can be breached or switched off.
NetworkGadgets on their own VLAN or IoT Wi-Fi; local-only gadgets blocked from the internet; Wi-Fi client isolation; cameras local-only with no UPnP; Zigbee network key not the defaultA hacked cheap gadget must not reach your computers.
The serverFirewall on; only 443/8123 (and SSH) reachable; containers not privileged, no Docker socket; automatic OS updates; physically safeHome Assistant can be perfect and still lose to an old kernel.
Detecting troublePhone alert on a failed login; no failed logins from outside; you read the logs now and thenA smoke alarm for your login page.

Reach it from anywhere

Never forward port 8123 (or 443, or 1883) on your router. Not "temporarily", not "just for the phone app". It is graded as a serious failure.

The options, ranked for you (best first):

#OptionProsCons
1NordVPN Meshnet (or your own WireGuard)You already pay for NordVPN. Phone and server join a private network; nothing at all is opened on your router. Best safety, no extra cost.Both ends need the NordVPN app signed in. If Meshnet is not on your plan, Tailscale (free for personal use) works the same way.
2Cloudflare Tunnel plus Zero Trust AccessThe server connects out to Cloudflare, so no router port is opened. An Access rule (for example "only my email, with a one-time code") puts a login in front of Home Assistant's own login. Free for a few users.Needs a domain on Cloudflare. The phone app needs a service token to get through Access (the browser uses the email code). Your traffic passes through Cloudflare. Upload limit of 100 MB per request on free plans. The Zero Trust screens change often.
3Nabu Casa (Home Assistant Cloud)The simplest; works with Alexa and Google; your money funds Home Assistant's developers.About US$6.50 a month; your connection passes through their servers (encrypted).
NeverA router port-forwardNone worth the risk.Exposes your login to the whole internet.

Setting up option 1 (Meshnet), about 10 minutes

  1. On the home server, install NordVPN and sign in (a login token from Nord Account, Advanced settings, avoids typing a password on the server), then nordvpn set meshnet on.
  2. On this computer: secure-linux-vpn meshnet on, then secure-linux-vpn meshnet status. It shows the server's Meshnet name (for example something.nord).
  3. On your phone: NordVPN app, Meshnet on.
  4. In the Home Assistant app, add http://<server-meshnet-name>:8123 as an extra address. Away from home it uses that.

Save the choice with the welcome wizard (page "Home Assistant (smart home)") or secure-linux-choice set ha_remote_mode meshnet, and the checker will score it.

The two lines that switch on the login ban

Home Assistant can block an address that keeps getting the password wrong, but only if you give it a number:

Terminal
http:
  ip_ban_enabled: true
  login_attempts_threshold: 5

Behind a reverse proxy such as Caddy on the same computer, also tell Home Assistant to trust that one address (and no other):

Terminal
http:
  use_x_forwarded_for: true
  trusted_proxies:
    - 127.0.0.1
    - ::1

Your first-day security checklist

  1. Make the owner account with a long, unique password (use Bitwarden).
  2. Create a second, normal account for daily use. Keep the admin for changing settings.
  3. Profile, Security: turn on two-step login (an authenticator app such as Ente Auth) on every account.
  4. Add the two http: lines above to configuration.yaml (or let --apply do it).
  5. Settings, System, Backups: automatic daily, encrypted, and keep the key in Bitwarden. Copy one outside the house.
  6. Install the security-watch package so a failed login pings your phone: secure-linux-ha starter install sl_security_watch.
  7. Put smart gadgets on a guest or IoT Wi-Fi (or a VLAN). Block the internet for the ones that work locally.
  8. Run secure-linux-ha-secure --guided and aim for B or better.

Passwords, secrets and tokens

  • Passwords and keys belong in secrets.yaml, referenced as !secret name. The checker finds typed-in secrets and --apply moves them for you.
  • A long-lived access token is a password that never expires and skips two-step login. Make one only when you need it (Profile, Security), name it, and delete it when done. secure-linux-ha token-set stores one for the checker in a root-only file (read silently; never printed, logged or put on a command line). secure-linux-ha token-set --delete removes it.
  • A webhook address is a login-free way to start an automation. Use 24 or more random characters and keep it private.

The server

If you run Home Assistant as a container on your home server, the server kit (server/homeassistant on the stick) does the safe things for you: nothing privileged, no Docker socket, helper services on 127.0.0.1 only, Mosquitto with passwords and ACLs, Zigbee2MQTT with a generated network key, Caddy HTTPS with trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1, ::1], a firewall that lets only your home network in (firewall-lan-only.sh), automatic security updates and fail2ban (harden-host.sh), nightly encrypted backups (setup-ha-backup.sh) and updates with a backup first (safe-update.sh, no Watchtower). Docker bypasses ufw and firewalld for published ports, which is why the helpers are published on 127.0.0.1 only.

If something looks wrong

A phone alert for a failed login, or a failed login in the log from a strange address:

  1. If it was you, nothing to do.
  2. If not: check your router has no port-forward; change the admin password; turn on two-step login for everyone; delete unused tokens.
  3. Run the checker; look at "failed-logins" and "remote-exposure".
  4. fail2ban and the ip_ban setting will already be blocking repeat guessers if you set them up.

Not verified against a real Home Assistant yet: the entity names in the backup alert package, the field inside the failed-login notice, whether your ESPHome and Matter images accept the "listen on 127.0.0.1" options, the Piper voice name, the fail2ban date pattern, and the exact Cloudflare Zero Trust screens (they change often). The checker's grade is a guide, not a guarantee.

Smart home

Home Assistant: advanced, made easy

On this page 12 sections
  1. 1. Templates: let Home Assistant do the thinking
  2. 2. Packages: one file per idea
  3. 3. Git-tracked config: an undo button for everything
  4. 4. Native automations or Node-RED?
  5. 5. Zigbee mesh planning
  6. 6. ESPHome: build your own sensors
  7. 7. VLAN and IoT segmentation
  8. 8. Local-only devices
  9. 9. Reaching it from anywhere
  10. 10. HTTPS at home with your own Caddy
  11. 11. Updates without surprises
  12. 12. Backups that really work

You have the basics. This chapter is the "next level" for people who like to tinker, with the scary parts explained and a safety net under every step. Rule one never changes: snapshot, validate, then restart (secure-linux-ha snapshot, secure-linux-ha validate).

1. Templates: let Home Assistant do the thinking

A template is a small piece of text that Home Assistant works out for you, written between double curly brackets.

  • {{ states('sensor.hall_temperature') }} is the current reading (always text).
  • {{ states('sensor.hall_temperature') | float(0) > 25 }} turns it into a number and compares it (the 0 is a safe fallback when the sensor is offline).
  • {{ now().hour >= 22 }} is true after 10pm.
  • {{ states.light | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count }} is how many lights are on.

A template can also become a sensor of its own. This one counts the lights that are on and shows it on a dashboard:

Terminal
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Lights on
        unique_id: lights_on_count
        icon: mdi:lightbulb-group
        state: "{{ states.light | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'on') | list | count }}"

Try templates in Developer tools, Template: type on the left, the answer appears on the right immediately. Nothing can break there. The starter kit's alert packages are mostly templates; read one aloud with secure-linux-ha-learn explain sl_door_left_open.

2. Packages: one file per idea

A package is a YAML file in config/packages/ that holds everything for one feature: its helpers, scripts and automations together. Delete the file and the feature is gone. Turn the feature on with one line in configuration.yaml:

Terminal
homeassistant:
  packages: !include_dir_named packages

The kit works this way (sl_battery_alerts.yaml, sl_security_watch.yaml and so on). To share a feature with someone, send them one file.

3. Git-tracked config: an undo button for everything

secure-linux-ha snapshot puts your settings under Git (a history of every change), keeps secrets.yaml and the .storage folder out of it (they hold passwords and logins), and secure-linux-ha rollback shows the list and goes back to any point after asking. It always saves your current state first, so you can undo the undo. For more control use plain Git: git -C <config> log, git -C <config> diff. Never push the repository anywhere public. If you want an off-site copy, push to a private repository and keep the .gitignore as written.

4. Native automations or Node-RED?

Home Assistant's own automationsNode-RED
LookMenus and forms (plus YAML)Boxes joined by wires
LearningGentlestA new tool to learn
Complex logic (loops, timers, state machines)Good since 2024 (choose, if/then, repeat, variables)Natural
Share, back up, versionPlain filesA JSON flow file
Extra riskNoneOne more container and web page to secure

Start with native automations. Add Node-RED (a server kit option) only if you keep hitting a wall. Keep its editor on 127.0.0.1 and reach it through an SSH tunnel, because it has no login until you configure one.

5. Zigbee mesh planning

Zigbee gadgets form a mesh: mains-powered devices (plugs, bulbs, in-wall switches) are routers that pass messages on; battery sensors are end devices that talk to the nearest router.

  1. Put the USB dongle on a USB 2.0 port with a short extension cable, away from USB 3 ports, the router and the server's fans.
  2. Pick a Zigbee channel (15, 20 or 25) that avoids your Wi-Fi's channels (Wi-Fi 1, 6 and 11 overlap Zigbee 11 to 24; 15, 20 and 25 are the usual escapes).
  3. Add routers first, spread through the house, then the battery sensors.
  4. Change the network key before you pair anything. Zigbee2MQTT: advanced: network_key: GENERATE (ZHA creates a random key by itself). The default key is public knowledge. Changing it later means re-pairing everything.
  5. Choose one system for the dongle: ZHA (inside Home Assistant, simplest) or Zigbee2MQTT (more devices, a nice web page, needs Mosquitto).
  6. Leave permit_join: false; switch it on only while pairing, then off.

6. ESPHome: build your own sensors

ESPHome turns an A$5 ESP32 board into a Wi-Fi sensor or switch you configure with a few lines of YAML, with no cloud. A temperature sensor:

Terminal
esphome:
  name: shed-temperature
esp32:
  board: esp32dev
wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password
api:
  encryption:
    key: !secret api_key
ota:
  - platform: esphome
    password: !secret ota_password
sensor:
  - platform: dht
    pin: GPIO4
    model: DHT22
    temperature:
      name: Shed temperature
    update_interval: 60s

Use !secret for the Wi-Fi password and keys; put ESPHome devices on the IoT Wi-Fi; the first flash is by USB cable, later updates go over Wi-Fi (OTA). The server kit runs the dashboard on 127.0.0.1 (reach it through an SSH tunnel). The command-line tool is esphome (installed when the choice ha_esphome is yes). Not verified: the exact ota: syntax changes between ESPHome versions; copy the current form from the ESPHome documentation.

7. VLAN and IoT segmentation

Cheap smart gadgets are rarely updated. Put them where a hacked one cannot reach your laptop, phone or photos.

  1. On your router make a separate network for gadgets: a guest or IoT Wi-Fi is the easy version; a VLAN is the proper one.
  2. Simplest rules: gadgets may talk to Home Assistant (and to each other only if they must); your main network may talk to the gadgets; the gadgets may not start connections to your main network.
  3. Block the internet for gadgets that work locally (cameras, plugs, sensors). Allow only what is needed (time server, firmware server) for the rest.
  4. Turn on Wi-Fi client isolation on the IoT network so gadgets cannot talk to each other.
  5. Catch: discovery by mDNS ("shouting") does not cross networks. Either put Home Assistant on both networks, or add an mDNS reflector (your router may call it "mDNS repeater" or "Bonjour"), or add devices by IP address.
  6. Tell the checker: secure-linux-ha-secure --checklist (answers iot_vlan, iot_cloud_blocked, wifi_isolation).

Pros: a hacked gadget is stuck in its box. Cons: some routers cannot do VLANs, and discovery needs the extra step above.

8. Local-only devices

Prefer gadgets that work without the cloud: Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter, ESPHome, and brands with a local API. Signs of a local-only gadget: it keeps working when you unplug the router's internet, and the integration says "local polling" or "local push" in Home Assistant. Then block its internet access on the router. Avoid gadgets that need an account just to switch on, and cameras that use "P2P" or UPnP.

9. Reaching it from anywhere

The ranking and the pros and cons are in "Keep your smart home safe", section "Reach it from anywhere". The short version: Meshnet (or Tailscale), then Cloudflare Tunnel with Access, then Nabu Casa. Never a router port-forward.

10. HTTPS at home with your own Caddy

If you already used install-caddy.sh for Immich, add-caddy.sh adds https://ha.home to the same Caddy (one marked block, # BEGIN secure-linux-ha to # END secure-linux-ha; your Immich block is untouched, and re-running install-caddy.sh later will not remove it; it validates and restores the old file if Caddy refuses it) and sets trusted_proxies so Home Assistant only believes Caddy about who is visiting. Remember to point ha.home at the server (router DNS or /etc/hosts) and trust your home certificate on each device.

11. Updates without surprises

No auto-updater (Watchtower). Use safe-update.sh on the server, or the update button on Home Assistant OS, but always:

  1. Back up.
  2. Read the release notes' "Backward-incompatible changes".
  3. Update one thing.
  4. Look at your key automations.

secure-linux-ha update-check tells you where you stand; the weekly digest package nudges you on Sundays.

12. Backups that really work

Home Assistant's own backups (encrypted), plus the server's nightly Borg backup (setup-ha-backup.sh: the same encrypted repository as Immich, optionally copied to the cloud), plus one test restore a few times a year into the practice copy (secure-linux-ha local). Save the encryption key in Bitwarden: without it the backup cannot be opened.

What runs automatically

On this page 4 sections
  1. The full list
  2. How to see them yourself
  3. Running a job right now
  4. Should I turn any of these off?

A lot happens in the background on this computer, so you don't have to remember it. This chapter lists every automatic job, what it does and how often.

Linux uses systemd to start and manage background programs. A program that runs all the time is a service. A job that runs on a schedule is started by a timer, which works like Windows Task Scheduler.

The full list

WhatName in systemdWhenWhat it does
System updates (main laptop)secure-linux-offline-updates.timerDailyDownloads the day's updates and prepares them, even if nobody is logged in. They install while the computer restarts (Discover calls this "offline updates"), with a snapshot first. It never restarts the computer by itself. Restart when convenient.
System updates (old PCs)dnf5-automatic.timerDailyInstalls all updates. Restarts at 04:00 only if you chose that (lite_auto_reboot).
App updatessecure-linux-flatpak-update.timerDailyUpdates all Flatpak apps: LibreWolf, Signal, Steam, Bitwarden and the rest.
Apps from outside Fedorasecure-linux-outside-apps.timerWeeklyChecks for newer versions of Network protection, ArtCraft and immich-go and raises a notice. You install them (checksums are verified).
Firmware checksfwupd-refresh.timerRegularlyChecks for new firmware. It only checks. You install firmware yourself from the Status window or Discover.
System snapshots (laptop)snapper-timeline.timer and snapper-cleanup.timerHourly, plus clean-upTakes a snapshot of the system (not your home folder) every hour, and one before every update. Use them to undo a bad update.
Status checkssecure-linux-check.timer10 minutes after start, then every 6 hoursTurns problems into the green, orange and red lines in Secure Linux Status & Fixes.
Virus signatures (laptop)clamav-freshclam.serviceSeveral times a dayKeeps ClamAV's list of known malware up to date.
Virus scan (laptop)secure-linux-clamscan.timerWeeklyScans your Downloads and Desktop at low priority. Logs to /var/log/secure-linux/clamscan/ (the 12 newest are kept). It never deletes anything.
Disk data check (laptop)secure-linux-btrfs-scrub.timerMonthlyReads every block of the Btrfs disk to find damage early.
Wear logsecure-linux-wear.timerMonthlyRecords battery and SSD wear so slow decline is noticed.
Hardware healthsecure-linux-health.timer20 minutes after start, then weeklyThe quick hardware check; a notice appears if a part needs a look.
Home server watchdogsecure-linux-server-watch.timerWeeklyChecks your home server's backup health file (if you set one up).
Network protectionopensnitch.service plus secure-linux-netguard-lists.timer (weekly), -summary.timer (Sunday 18:00), -check.timer (every 30 minutes), -watch.serviceAlways running, plus the schedules shownWatches outgoing connections, refreshes the block lists, sends the weekly summary, restarts the firewall if it stops, and shows the Allow once / Always allow / Keep blocked messages.
Encrypted DNS hand-oversecure-linux-dns-sync.pathWhen a VPN connects or disconnectsLets the VPN's DNS win while it is connected, and puts encrypted DNS back afterwards.
Battery limitsecure-linux-battery.serviceAt start-up and when the charger changesApplies your charge limit.
New-device helpersecure-linux-parts-hotplug.serviceWhen you plug in a USB deviceInstalls the software a new device needs (printer, scanner, Bluetooth adapter).
Notificationssecure-linux-notify.timer (your user)At login, then every 15 minutesShows each alert at most once a day, and each one-off event once.
Care calendarsecure-linux-care.timer (your user)DailyReminds you 60, 30 and 7 days before things expire.
Backup checksecure-linux-backup-check.timer (your user)DailyWarns if backups are not happening.
Daily tipssecure-linux-tips.timer (your user)Daily at 11:00 for your first 14 daysOne short tip a day, then it stops by itself.
File syncsyncthing@<your-username>.serviceAlways runningSyncs your chosen folders with your phone and other devices. Control page: http://localhost:8384. Paused away from home.
VPNnordvpnd.serviceAlways runningThe NordVPN background program.
SSH protection (old PCs)fail2ban.serviceAlways runningOnly on lite machines, where remote login (SSH) is switched on, for the home network only. After 5 failed attempts from one address, it blocks that address for an hour.
Firewallfirewalld.serviceAlways runningBlocks incoming connections. Phone-link, file-sharing and printer features are open only on networks you marked as home.
Encrypted DNSsystemd-resolved.serviceAlways runningLooks up website names over an encrypted connection to Cloudflare's malware-blocking DNS (with Quad9 as backup).

"Laptop" means the full profile. The lite profile on old PCs skips snapshots, ClamAV and the question window to stay light (with 3 GB or more of memory it still gets the quiet block lists). The Debian versions have their own, shorter list: see "The Debian version".

How to see them yourself

Open the terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) and try these. None of them change anything.

  • systemctl list-timers lists every timer, when it last ran, and when it runs next. Press q to leave the list. Add --user to see your own.
  • systemctl status <name> shows whether something is running and its latest log lines. For example: systemctl status firewalld or systemctl status secure-linux-flatpak-update.timer. Look for active (running) or active (waiting) in green. Press q to leave.
  • journalctl -u <name> shows the full log for one service. Add -e to jump to the end.
  • systemctl status syncthing@$USER checks your Syncthing service.
  • Or just open Secure Linux Status & Fixes: it shows the result of all these in plain English.

Running a job right now

You don't have to wait for the timer. These run the same job straight away:

  • System updates: click Install updates now in the Status window (they install right away), or Update All in Discover (they install when you restart).
  • App updates: flatpak update.
  • Firmware: secure-linux-firmware update (see "Is every part of my computer OK?").
  • Status checks: secure-linux-status --refresh.
  • Virus scan: sudo secure-linux-check --antivirus-scan, or open ClamTk for a point-and-click scanner.
  • Block lists: secure-linux-netguard update-lists.
  • Hardware check: open Hardware Health Check.

Should I turn any of these off?

No. They are all light. Most only run for a few minutes a day. If one ever seems to be slowing the computer down, open Mission Center to see what is busy. Then ask for help before switching anything off; see the Troubleshooting chapter.
