Phone, sync & devices

Immich tools

fullPhone, sync & devices

Your own private Google Photos-style photo server, plus a tool to bring photos over from Google Photos.

Immich is a self-hosted photo and video library running on your home server at http://10.0.30.42:8080. It works like Google Photos: timeline, albums, search and phone backup, but the photos are stored on your own hardware. The 'Immich' shortcut in the app menu opens it in LibreWolf, and the immich-go command uploads photos from a Google Takeout export.

Why it's here

It keeps your photos private at home and lets you move away from Google Photos.

What to do next

Immich (app launcher, opens in LibreWolf); immich-go in Konsole

What it can do
  • Browse all photos and videos on a timeline
  • Albums and sharing with other Immich users
  • Search by people, places and things
  • Phone backup with the Immich mobile app
  • Upload a Google Photos Takeout export with immich-go
  • Download photos back to the laptop
Getting started
  1. Open Immich from the app menu and sign in.
  2. To get an API key: click your profile picture > Account Settings > API Keys > create a new key. Copy it.
  3. Download your Google Photos from Google Takeout, and save all the takeout-*.zip files in one folder.
  4. Open Konsole and go to that folder, for example: cd ~/Downloads
  5. Run: immich-go upload from-google-photos --server=http://10.0.30.42:8080 --api-key=KEY takeout-*.zip (replace KEY with your key).
  6. Wait for it to finish, then check the photos in the Immich web page.
  7. Install the Immich app on your phone and point it at the same server address to back up new photos.
Everyday tips
  • Keep all Takeout zip files together; immich-go needs every part of the export.
  • Run immich-go --help (or add --help after a command) to see options, such as a test run without uploading.
  • Large libraries take hours; keep the laptop plugged in and awake.
  • Keep your Google Takeout files until you have checked that everything arrived in Immich.
  • The server address only works on your home network unless you have set up a VPN to home.
Privacy & security
  • Photos stay on your home server instead of a big tech cloud.
  • Treat the API key like a password. Do not share it or post it online. Delete it in Account Settings when you no longer need it.
  • Typing the key in a command can leave it in Konsole's history; you can delete the key from Immich after the import.
  • Keep a separate backup of the server; one copy of your photos is not a backup.
If something goes wrong
  • Page will not load: you must be on your home network (or home VPN), and the server must be running.
  • immich-go says unauthorized: the API key is wrong or deleted. Create a new one.
  • Some photos have the wrong date: Google stores dates in separate files; make sure you gave immich-go the full Takeout zip files, not unzipped single photos.
  • Command not found: immich-go lives in /usr/local/bin; open a new Konsole window and try again.

Learn more: https://immich.app  ·  All apps

KDE Connect

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

Links your phone and your computer so they can share notifications, files, the clipboard and media controls over your home Wi-Fi.

KDE Connect is a free app that joins your phone and your Linux computer together. It is a bit like Microsoft's Phone Link on Windows, but it works with both Android and iPhone and does not need an account. Everything travels directly over your own Wi-Fi network, not through the internet.

Why it's here

It makes moving photos and files between your phone and laptop quick and easy. It also lets you see phone notifications on the laptop so you do not have to keep picking your phone up.

What to do next

KDE Connect (also available from the phone icon in the system tray, bottom right)

What it can do
  • Show phone notifications on the computer
  • Send files both ways between phone and computer
  • Share the clipboard (copy on one, paste on the other)
  • Control music and video playing on the computer from your phone
  • Use your phone as a touchpad or remote control
  • Read and reply to text messages from the computer (Android only)
  • Ring your phone to find it
  • See your phone's battery level on the computer
Getting started
  1. Install the free 'KDE Connect' app on your phone (Google Play, F-Droid or the Apple App Store).
  2. Make sure the phone and the laptop are on the same Wi-Fi network.
  3. Open the KDE Connect app on the phone. Your laptop should appear in the list of available devices.
  4. Tap the laptop's name and choose to request pairing.
  5. A pop-up appears on the laptop. Click Accept.
  6. On the phone, allow the permissions it asks for (for example notifications and files), only for the features you want.
  7. On the laptop, open KDE Connect from the system tray to see the phone and switch individual features (plugins) on or off.
Everyday tips
  • To send a file from the laptop, right-click it in Dolphin (the file manager) and look for the KDE Connect 'Send to' option.
  • To send from the phone, use the phone's normal Share button and pick KDE Connect.
  • Received files are saved in your Downloads folder by default (this can be changed in the settings).
  • Use the phone as a remote to pause or skip music when you are across the room.
  • Turn off plugins you never use. Fewer features means fewer things that can go wrong.
  • If you lose your phone around the house, use 'Ring' from the laptop.
Privacy & security
  • Pairing is required before any data is shared, and the connection is encrypted.
  • It only works on your local network. Nothing is sent to a cloud service.
  • The firewall on this laptop is set to allow KDE Connect, so it works out of the box on your home network.
  • Only pair devices you own. On public Wi-Fi, consider turning KDE Connect off or unpairing.
  • Notification sharing can show private messages on the laptop screen. Turn that plugin off if other people use the laptop.
If something goes wrong
  • Phone does not see the laptop: check both are on the same Wi-Fi (not a guest network), then try 'Refresh' or add the laptop's IP address manually in the phone app.
  • Some routers (often on guest or public networks) block devices from talking to each other. Use your normal home network.
  • On iPhone, Apple limits what background apps can do, so fewer features are available and the connection may drop when the app is closed.
  • Android battery saving can stop KDE Connect running in the background. Exclude it from battery optimisation in the phone's settings.
  • SMS features work on Android only.

Learn more: https://kdeconnect.kde.org/  ·  All apps

LocalSend

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

Sends files and text to nearby devices on the same network, like Apple's AirDrop but for every kind of device.

LocalSend is a simple app for sending files between devices on the same Wi-Fi or home network. It works on Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and iPhone, so you can send to almost anyone nearby. It is similar to AirDrop or Windows 'Nearby sharing', but works across brands. No account and no internet connection are needed.

Why it's here

It is the easiest way to move a file to a friend's phone or another computer, even if they do not use Linux. It works without pairing, so it is handy for one-off transfers.

What to do next

LocalSend

What it can do
  • Send files, folders, photos and videos to nearby devices
  • Send a piece of text or a link
  • Receive files from any device running LocalSend
  • Works on Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and iOS
  • No account or internet connection needed
  • Encrypted transfers on your local network
  • Choose to accept or decline each incoming transfer
Getting started
  1. Open LocalSend on the laptop.
  2. Install LocalSend on the other device (it is free in the app stores and at localsend.org).
  3. Make sure both devices are on the same Wi-Fi network.
  4. On the sending device, go to the Send tab and choose files, a folder, text or pasted content.
  5. Pick the receiving device from the 'Nearby devices' list.
  6. On the receiving device, click or tap Accept.
  7. Received files go to your Downloads folder by default. You can change this in LocalSend's Settings.
Everyday tips
  • Each device shows a random friendly name. You can change it in Settings so you recognise your devices.
  • If a device does not appear, press the refresh button in the nearby devices list.
  • LocalSend needs to be open on the receiving device to accept files.
  • You can send several files at once by selecting them all before choosing a device.
  • Use 'Text' to quickly send a link or address from your laptop to your phone.
Privacy & security
  • Files go directly between the two devices on your network. They do not pass through any company's server.
  • The firewall on this laptop allows LocalSend (it uses port 53317), so it works on your home network.
  • Always check who is sending before you press Accept, especially on shared or public Wi-Fi.
  • It is a Flatpak app, so it is sandboxed. Flatseal can change which folders it can reach.
If something goes wrong
  • Devices cannot see each other: check they are on the same network and not on a guest network that keeps devices apart.
  • If auto-discovery still fails, you can usually connect by typing the other device's IP address. Look in the Send tab for a manual option.
  • Cannot save to a certain folder: the Flatpak sandbox may be blocking it. Pick a folder inside your home folder, or adjust permissions with Flatseal.
  • Transfers can be slow on weak Wi-Fi. Move closer to the router for big files.

Learn more: https://localsend.org/  ·  All apps

Syncthing

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

Keeps folders automatically in sync between your own devices, directly, without any cloud company in the middle.

Syncthing copies changes in chosen folders between your devices so they always match. It is like OneDrive or Dropbox, but there is no cloud: your devices talk straight to each other. It runs quietly in the background and you control it through a web page in your browser.

Why it's here

It is a private way to keep things like photos, documents or notes the same on your laptop, phone and other computers. Your files never sit on someone else's server.

What to do next

Open http://localhost:8384 in your web browser (Syncthing already runs in the background)

What it can do
  • Sync folders between computers and phones automatically
  • Peer-to-peer: devices connect directly, no cloud storage
  • Encrypted connections between devices
  • Choose exactly which folders go to which devices
  • Send-only or receive-only folders (for one-way copies)
  • Keep old versions of files (file versioning) if you turn it on
  • Works on Linux, Windows, macOS and Android
  • Runs in the background as a service
Getting started
  1. Open your browser and go to http://localhost:8384 to see the Syncthing control page.
  2. If you are asked about sending anonymous usage reports, choose whichever you prefer (No is fine).
  3. Set a username and password for this page: Actions > Settings > GUI.
  4. On your Android phone, install 'Syncthing-Fork' (from F-Droid or Google Play).
  5. On the laptop, click Actions > Show ID to see the laptop's Device ID and QR code.
  6. In the phone app, add a device and scan that QR code. Then accept the new device on the laptop when it asks.
  7. Click 'Add Folder' on one device, choose the folder, and tick the other device under the Sharing tab.
  8. Accept the folder on the other device and choose where to save it. Syncing then starts by itself.
Everyday tips
  • A green 'Up to Date' status means everything matches.
  • Turn on File Versioning in a folder's settings so deleted or changed files are kept for a while.
  • Use 'Send Only' on the device that holds the master copy if you only want one-way syncing.
  • Syncing only happens when both devices are on and connected. A phone syncs when the app is allowed to run.
  • Add ignore patterns (in folder settings) to skip big or temporary files.
  • Bookmark http://localhost:8384 in your browser.
Privacy & security
  • Your files never go to a company's cloud. Devices only sync with devices you have approved.
  • Connections between devices are encrypted.
  • The firewall on this laptop allows Syncthing, so devices on your network can connect.
  • Set a password on the web control page so other local users cannot change your settings.
  • Sync is not a backup: if you delete a file on one device, it is deleted on the others too. Keep a real backup as well (for example with Pika Backup).
If something goes wrong
  • Devices show 'Disconnected': check both are on and that Syncthing is running on both. On the laptop, run 'sudo systemctl status syncthing@$USER' in a terminal.
  • The web page does not load: Syncthing may not be running. Try 'sudo systemctl restart syncthing@$USER' in a terminal.
  • Conflict files (with 'sync-conflict' in the name) appear when the same file is edited on two devices at once. Open both, keep the right one, delete the other.
  • Android stops syncing in the background: allow Syncthing-Fork to ignore battery optimisation in the phone's settings.
  • The original official Syncthing Android app has been discontinued, which is why Syncthing-Fork is recommended.

Learn more: https://syncthing.net/  ·  All apps

Solaar

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

Manages Logitech wireless mice, keyboards and trackballs, including your MX Ergo, on Linux.

Solaar is a Linux app for Logitech devices that use a Unifying or Bolt USB receiver, and many that use Bluetooth. It does a similar job to Logitech Options+ on Windows, which is not available for Linux. It shows battery levels, pairs devices to receivers and changes device settings.

Why it's here

It replaces Logi Options+ for your MX Ergo trackball and any other Logitech gear. It lets you check the battery and adjust settings without Windows.

What to do next

Solaar

What it can do
  • Show battery level for Logitech devices
  • Pair and unpair devices with Unifying and Bolt receivers
  • Change settings such as pointer speed (DPI) and scroll behaviour, where the device supports it
  • Shows a system tray icon with quick status
  • Warns when a battery is low
  • Rules to make buttons do custom actions (advanced)
  • Works with many Logitech keyboards, mice and trackballs
Getting started
  1. Plug in your Logitech USB receiver, or make sure the device is connected over Bluetooth.
  2. Open Solaar. Its icon also appears in the system tray.
  3. Click your receiver or device in the left list to see its details and battery level.
  4. Look through the settings shown on the right. Only settings your device supports are listed.
  5. To pair a new device to a receiver, select the receiver and click 'Pair new device', then switch the device on or press its connect button.
  6. Close the window: Solaar keeps running in the tray so it can warn you about low battery.
Everyday tips
  • Hover over the tray icon to see the battery level quickly.
  • The MX Ergo has an Easy-Switch button for two connections. Solaar shows the device on whichever connection it is currently using.
  • Change one setting at a time so you know what made a difference.
  • Solaar's 'Rules' editor can remap buttons, but it is advanced. Leave it alone until you are comfortable.
Privacy & security
  • Solaar works offline and talks only to your devices over USB or Bluetooth.
  • Unlike Logitech's own Windows software, it does not need an account.
  • It is installed from Fedora's official repositories.
If something goes wrong
  • Device not shown: unplug and replug the receiver, then reopen Solaar. Make sure the device is switched on.
  • Some settings from Logi Options+ are not available, because Solaar only supports what the device reports.
  • Bolt devices cannot pair to a Unifying receiver, and Unifying devices cannot pair to a Bolt receiver. Use the matching receiver.
  • If Solaar does not start with the computer, open it once from the app launcher. Look in Solaar's options or System Settings > Autostart to add it.

Learn more: https://pwr-solaar.github.io/Solaar/  ·  All apps

qFlipper

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

The official desktop app for the Flipper Zero, used to update its firmware and manage files on its SD card.

qFlipper is made by the Flipper Zero team. You connect your Flipper Zero with a USB cable and qFlipper lets you update its firmware, back it up, and copy files to and from its memory card. It works the same way as the Windows version.

Why it's here

You own a Flipper Zero and need it for firmware updates and file transfers. The USB stick for this laptop also includes a BadUSB script that can repair the laptop setup, and qFlipper is how you copy it onto the Flipper.

What to do next

qFlipper

What it can do
  • Update the Flipper Zero firmware
  • Back up and restore the Flipper's settings and data
  • Browse, copy, rename and delete files on the Flipper's SD card
  • Copy BadUSB scripts to the /badusb folder on the SD card
  • Show the Flipper's screen on your computer and control it
  • Repair a Flipper that will not start normally
Getting started
  1. Connect the Flipper Zero to the laptop with a USB data cable.
  2. Open qFlipper. It should find the Flipper automatically.
  3. If an update is offered, click Update and wait. Do not unplug the Flipper until it finishes.
  4. Open the file manager view in qFlipper to see the SD card.
  5. Open the 'badusb' folder on the SD card.
  6. Drag in the script from the setup USB stick: linux-setup\flipper\repair_setup.txt.
  7. To run a script, on the Flipper go to the Bad USB app, pick the script, plug the Flipper into the target computer and press Run.
Everyday tips
  • Make a backup in qFlipper before big firmware updates.
  • The repair_setup script types 'sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair' into an open terminal. Open a terminal window first and click into it.
  • After the script types the command, you still need to type your password yourself for sudo.
  • Check the keyboard layout setting in the Flipper's Bad USB app matches the computer, or characters may come out wrong.
  • Close qFlipper before using other Flipper tools, as only one app can talk to the Flipper at a time.
Privacy & security
  • Only use BadUSB scripts on computers you own or have clear permission to use. Using them on other people's machines can be illegal.
  • A BadUSB script acts like a fast keyboard. Read any script before running it so you know exactly what it will type.
  • qFlipper downloads firmware from the internet. Network protection may ask whether to allow this the first time.
  • Only install firmware from sources you trust.
If something goes wrong
  • Flipper not detected: try a different USB cable (some are charge-only) or another USB port, and make sure no other app is using the Flipper.
  • Update stuck or failed: qFlipper has a repair option for this. Do not unplug the Flipper during an update.
  • BadUSB typed the wrong characters: change the keyboard layout in the Flipper's Bad USB app to match the computer.
  • BadUSB typed into the wrong window: make sure the terminal is open and focused before you press Run.

Learn more: https://docs.flipper.net/qflipper  ·  All apps

Flipper Zero Backup & Files

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

A guided local tool for Flipper Zero backups, encrypted restores, SD-card files, favourites and customisation.

Flipper Zero Backup & Files is the Secure Linux companion for looking after your Flipper Zero. Its local backup, restore, encryption, SD-card file, favourites and customisation tools work without internet. RogueMaster and firmware downloads are separate online features; releases already downloaded into its local cache can be resumed without downloading them again.

Why it's here

It gives you one clear place to make a safety copy before changing your Flipper, protect that copy with a password or key, and manage the files on the SD card.

What to do next

Flipper Zero Backup & Files (or terminal: secure-linux-flipper menu)

What it can do
  • Back up and restore Flipper Zero data locally
  • Encrypt and decrypt backups with the installed age or GnuPG tools
  • Browse and manage SD-card files, favourites and customisation without internet
  • Prepare device-recovery operations with the installed device tools
  • Download RogueMaster or firmware when internet is available
  • Resume suitable releases that were previously downloaded into the local cache
Getting started
  1. Close qFlipper and any other program that is using the Flipper Zero.
  2. Connect the Flipper with a USB data cable and insert its SD card if you want to manage SD files.
  3. Open Flipper Zero Backup & Files and follow the menu to make a local backup before making changes.
  4. Choose encrypted backup or restore when you want password- or key-based protection, and keep a separate copy of the credentials.
  5. Connect to the internet before choosing a RogueMaster or firmware download; local backup and file tasks do not need a connection.
Everyday tips
  • Keep more than one backup, including one somewhere other than the computer and the Flipper.
  • Only one app can normally use the Flipper at a time, so close qFlipper before starting the companion.
  • Local backup, restore, encryption, SD files, favourites and customisation work offline.
  • A new RogueMaster or firmware download requires internet. The offline app does not include those release files.
  • If a release was downloaded previously, choose the cached release option to resume or reuse it locally.
Privacy & security
  • Local backups and file operations stay on your computer and connected Flipper; the companion does not need an account.
  • Store encryption passwords and keys safely. Without them, an encrypted backup cannot be restored.
  • Download firmware or RogueMaster only from sources you trust, and make a backup before installing it.
  • Use device-recovery and firmware operations only on your own Flipper or one you have clear permission to modify.
If something goes wrong
  • Flipper not detected: try a different USB data cable or port, and close qFlipper and other Flipper tools first.
  • An encryption or device feature is unavailable: the companion checks for its helper program and explains what is missing instead of pretending the operation succeeded.
  • A RogueMaster or firmware download fails offline: connect to the internet, or use a suitable release already present in the local cache.
  • Do not unplug the Flipper or remove its SD card while a backup, restore, file transfer or firmware operation is still running.

Learn more:  ·  All apps

RustDesk

fulllitePhone, sync & devices

Help a family member remotely: they read you a code and you see their screen.

RustDesk is a remote-desktop program. By default connections go through RustDesk's public server (the screen itself is end-to-end encrypted). You can run your own server at home so nothing goes through anyone else.

Why it's here

So you can fix a relative's computer without being there.

What to do next

RustDesk (app launcher)

What it can do
  • See and control a remote screen with permission
  • Connect by a code
  • Run your own server (optional)
Getting started
  1. Install it from "Handy extras" (and ask your helper to install it too).
  2. Read out the ID and one-time password it shows.
  3. They connect; you approve.
Everyday tips
  • Close it when you are done.
Privacy & security
  • Only share the code with someone you trust. Scammers ask for remote access; never give it to an unexpected caller.
  • With the default public server, a third party sees that a connection happened.
If something goes wrong
  • It cannot connect: both computers need the internet; try again with a fresh code.

Learn more: https://rustdesk.com/  ·  All apps

System tools

KDE built-in apps

fullliteSystem tools

The everyday apps that come with the desktop: files, PDFs, images, screenshots, archives, terminal and settings.

On the main laptop the KDE Plasma desktop includes Dolphin (files, like File Explorer), Okular (PDF viewer), Gwenview (image viewer, like Photos), Spectacle (screenshots, like Snipping Tool), Ark (zip files), Konsole (terminal, like Command Prompt) and System Settings (like Windows Settings). The older PCs use the lighter Xfce desktop instead, so the names differ there: Thunar for files, Ristretto for images, and xfce4-screenshooter for screenshots.

Why it's here

These are the basic tools you will use every day, and knowing their names makes everything else easier.

What to do next

App launcher: Dolphin, Okular, Gwenview, Spectacle, Ark, Konsole, System Settings (on old PCs: Thunar, Ristretto, Screenshot, Settings Manager)

What it can do
  • Dolphin: browse, copy, move and rename files, with tabs and split view
  • Okular: read PDFs, highlight, add notes and fill forms
  • Gwenview: view photos, plus quick crop, rotate and resize
  • Spectacle: screenshots of the full screen, a window or a region
  • Ark: open and create zip and other archive files
  • Konsole: the terminal for typing commands
  • System Settings: display, sound, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, default apps and more
  • On Xfce (old PCs): Thunar, Ristretto, xfce4-screenshooter and Settings Manager
Getting started
  1. Open Dolphin to find your Documents, Downloads and Pictures folders.
  2. Double-click a PDF to open it in Okular, or a photo to open it in Gwenview.
  3. Press the Print Screen key to take a screenshot with Spectacle.
  4. Right-click a zip file and use the extract options (Ark) to unpack it.
  5. Open System Settings to change wallpaper, display scaling, sound and Wi-Fi.
  6. On an old PC, use Thunar for files and the Xfce Settings Manager instead.
Everyday tips
  • Dolphin: Ctrl+H shows hidden files; F3 splits the window into two panes; Ctrl+T opens a new tab.
  • Dolphin: F4 opens a small terminal at the bottom, already in the current folder.
  • Konsole: copy and paste use Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V, not Ctrl+C (Ctrl+C stops a command).
  • Okular: use the Annotations tool (Tools menu) to highlight and add notes to PDFs.
  • Spectacle: choose region, window or full screen at the top, then save or copy.
  • Search for any app or setting by pressing the Meta (Windows) key and typing.
  • Deleted files go to the Trash first, so you can restore them.
Privacy & security
  • These apps work offline and come from the system, so they are updated with normal system updates.
  • Be careful in Konsole: commands starting with sudo can change the whole system. Do not paste commands from random websites.
  • Screenshots can capture private notifications or passwords; check them before sharing.
  • System Settings is where you manage Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and screen lock; keep the screen lock on.
If something goes wrong
  • Text and icons too small or too big: change Display Scale in System Settings > Display & Monitor.
  • Wrong app opens a file: right-click the file > Open With > choose the app, and tick the option to remember it.
  • Cannot paste in Konsole: use Ctrl+Shift+V.
  • On an old PC the app names are different: look for Thunar, Ristretto and Screenshot in the Xfce menu. Okular or Ark may not be there; check the menu for the PDF and archive tools that are installed.

Learn more: https://apps.kde.org  ·  All apps

Impression

fullSystem tools

Writes disk images (such as Linux ISO files) to USB sticks to make bootable installers.

Impression is a small, simple app for making bootable USB sticks. You pick an image file, pick the USB stick, and click write. It does the same job as Rufus or balenaEtcher on Windows, with fewer options.

Why it's here

You will sometimes need a bootable USB stick, for example to try another Linux, make a rescue stick or reinstall. Impression makes this hard to get wrong.

What to do next

Impression

What it can do
  • Write .iso and .img files to USB sticks
  • Make bootable Linux installer or live USB sticks
  • Simple drag-and-drop interface
  • Lists only removable drives, to help avoid wiping the wrong disk
  • Shows progress while writing
Getting started
  1. Download the .iso file you want (for example a Linux installer) from its official website.
  2. Plug in a USB stick. Everything on it will be erased, so copy off anything you need first.
  3. Open Impression and drag the .iso file into the window, or click to open it.
  4. Choose your USB stick from the list of drives.
  5. Click Write and confirm.
  6. Wait for it to finish, then safely remove the stick.
Everyday tips
  • Use a stick that is at least as big as the image. 8 GB or more is a safe choice for most Linux images.
  • Check the drive name and size before you click Write.
  • After writing, the stick may look strange or tiny in the file manager. That is normal for a bootable stick.
  • To use the stick as normal storage again, reformat it with KDE Partition Manager.
Privacy & security
  • Writing erases the whole USB stick. Double-check you picked the right one.
  • Only download images from official websites, and check the checksum if the site provides one.
  • Impression is a sandboxed Flatpak app.
If something goes wrong
  • USB stick not listed: unplug it and plug it back in, or try another port.
  • Windows installer ISOs often do not work properly with simple image writers like this. Impression is mainly meant for Linux images.
  • Computer will not boot from the stick: open the computer's boot menu (often F12, F11 or Esc at power-on) and pick the USB stick.

Learn more: https://gitlab.com/adhami3310/Impression  ·  All apps

Discover

fullSystem tools

KDE's app store for installing and removing apps and installing system, app and firmware updates.

Discover is the software centre for KDE Plasma. It works like the Microsoft Store and Windows Update rolled into one. You can search for apps, install them with a click, and update the whole system. It handles both normal Fedora packages and Flatpak apps.

Why it's here

It is the easiest way to find new apps and keep everything up to date without using the terminal. It also offers upgrades to new Fedora versions and firmware updates for supported hardware.

What to do next

Discover

What it can do
  • Search, install and remove apps
  • Install Flatpak apps from Flathub
  • Install Fedora system updates
  • Upgrade to the next Fedora version when it is released
  • Install firmware updates for supported devices
  • Shows screenshots, descriptions and reviews
  • Manage software sources in its Settings
Getting started
  1. Open Discover from the app launcher.
  2. Use the search box at the top to find an app, or browse the categories.
  3. Click an app to see its description and screenshots, then click Install.
  4. Enter your password if asked.
  5. To update, click 'Updates' on the left, then 'Update All'.
  6. Restart the computer when Discover asks, so system updates can be applied.
Everyday tips
  • When an app is offered from more than one source (for example Fedora and Flathub), look for a source selector on the app's page.
  • The 'Installed' page lists everything you have installed and lets you remove apps.
  • System updates are often installed during a restart. Let the computer finish; do not switch it off.
  • A notification icon in the system tray tells you when updates are waiting.
  • When a new Fedora version is out, Discover shows an upgrade offer on the Updates page. It is fine to wait a few weeks after release.
  • Before a Fedora version upgrade, make sure your backups are current.
Privacy & security
  • Install apps from Fedora's repositories or Flathub. Be careful with apps marked as unverified or from unknown sources.
  • Flatpak apps are sandboxed. You can see and change what they can access with Flatseal.
  • Keeping up to date is one of the best ways to stay safe. This computer also installs all updates automatically every day.
  • Network protection already approves Discover and the update tools. If it ever asks, choose Allow, or Discover cannot check for updates.
If something goes wrong
  • Discover is slow or stuck on 'Loading': give it a minute on first launch while it downloads app lists. If it stays stuck, close and reopen it.
  • An update fails: restart the computer and try again. In a terminal, 'sudo dnf upgrade' often shows a clearer error.
  • Can't find an app: it may have a different name on Linux. Search for what it does (for example 'photo editor').
  • Two copies of an app appear: you may have installed both the Fedora and Flatpak versions. Remove one from the Installed page.

Learn more: https://apps.kde.org/discover/  ·  All apps

Mission Center

fullliteSystem tools

Shows what is using your processor, memory, disk, network and graphics card, like the Windows Task Manager.

Mission Center is a system monitor that looks and works much like the Windows Task Manager. It shows live graphs of your computer's performance and a list of running apps and processes. You can also use it to close apps that have frozen.

Why it's here

It gives a familiar, Windows-like way to see why the computer is slow and to close stuck programs.

What to do next

Mission Center

What it can do
  • Live graphs of processor (CPU) use
  • Memory (RAM) use
  • Disk activity
  • Network activity
  • Graphics card (GPU) use, where supported
  • List of running apps and processes
  • End (stop) a frozen app or process
  • View background services
Getting started
  1. Open Mission Center from the app launcher.
  2. The Performance tab shows graphs. Click CPU, Memory, Disk, Network or GPU on the left for more detail.
  3. Switch to the Apps tab to see what is running.
  4. Click a column heading to sort, for example by CPU or memory use, to find what is using the most.
  5. To close a frozen app, select it and use the stop or end option. Save your work in other apps first.
Everyday tips
  • Sort by memory to see which app is using the most RAM.
  • High CPU for a short time is normal, for example while updates install or a web page loads.
  • If one browser tab is heavy, close the tab rather than the whole browser.
  • KDE also has its own 'System Monitor' app that does a similar job. Use whichever you like.
Privacy & security
  • Mission Center only reads information about your own computer. It does not need the internet.
  • Be careful ending processes you do not recognise. Some are part of the system and ending them can log you out or freeze the desktop.
If something goes wrong
  • Graphics card information may be missing or limited for some GPUs. This is a limit of the drivers, not a fault.
  • Some details may show less information because Mission Center runs as a sandboxed Flatpak.
  • Ended the wrong process and the desktop froze: press Ctrl+Alt+Del to get the logout screen, or restart the computer.

Learn more: https://missioncenter.io/  ·  All apps

Pika Backup

fullSystem tools

Makes regular, encrypted backups of your personal files to a USB drive or another computer.

Pika Backup is a simple backup app. It copies your files to a USB drive or a remote computer (such as a home server reachable over SSH). It is built on a trusted tool called BorgBackup, which only stores changes after the first backup, so later backups are fast and small. It does a similar job to Windows 'File History'.

Why it's here

Laptops get lost, stolen or broken, and drives fail. Pika Backup makes it easy to keep a safe, encrypted copy of your files and restore them later.

What to do next

Pika Backup

What it can do
  • Back up your home folder or chosen folders
  • Back up to a USB drive or external disk
  • Back up to a remote computer over SSH, such as a home server
  • Encrypt backups with a password
  • Deduplication: unchanged files are not stored twice
  • Run backups automatically on a schedule
  • Browse old backups and restore individual files
  • Exclude folders you do not want backed up
Getting started
  1. Plug in the USB drive you want to use for backups.
  2. Open Pika Backup and click 'Setup Backup'.
  3. Choose to create a new backup repository on the drive, or on a remote location (for a home server, enter its SSH address).
  4. Turn on encryption and choose a strong password. Write it down and keep it somewhere safe.
  5. Check the list of folders to include and exclude. Leave out large folders you do not need, such as game installs.
  6. Click 'Back Up Now' and wait for the first backup to finish. The first one takes the longest.
  7. Open the Schedule tab and turn on regular backups (for example daily).
Everyday tips
  • Plug the backup drive in regularly so scheduled backups can run.
  • To get a file back, open the Archives tab, pick a date and browse the backup. It opens like a normal folder and you can copy files out.
  • Test a restore every now and then, so you know your backup works.
  • Keep one backup away from the laptop, such as a home server or a drive kept somewhere else.
  • Use the Schedule settings to automatically remove old backups and save space.
Privacy & security
  • Turn on encryption so nobody can read the backup if the drive is lost or stolen.
  • If you forget the encryption password, the backup cannot be opened. Nobody can recover it for you.
  • Remote backups travel over SSH, which is encrypted.
  • Network protection may ask the first time Pika connects to a remote server. Allow it only for your own server.
If something goes wrong
  • Scheduled backup did not run: the drive must be plugged in and the computer switched on. Pika shows a reminder when a backup is overdue.
  • Cannot reach the remote server: check the address, that the server is on, and that SSH login works.
  • The first backup is very slow: this is normal. Later backups only copy what has changed.
  • Pika backs up personal files, not the system itself. System snapshots (Snapper) cover the system side.

Learn more: https://apps.gnome.org/PikaBackup/  ·  All apps

System snapshots (Snapper + Btrfs Assistant)

fullSystem tools

Automatically saves restore points of the system so you can roll back after a bad update.

This laptop uses the Btrfs file system, which can take instant 'snapshots' of the system. Snapper takes these snapshots automatically on a timeline. Btrfs Assistant is the window you use to view, create and restore them. Together they are similar to Windows 'System Restore'.

Why it's here

If an update or a settings change breaks something, you can put the system back to how it was earlier. This makes trying things on Linux much less scary.

What to do next

Btrfs Assistant (or terminal: sudo snapper list)

What it can do
  • Automatic timeline snapshots of the system (the root file system)
  • Create a manual snapshot before risky changes
  • Restore the system to an earlier snapshot
  • Browse snapshots and see what changed
  • Old snapshots are cleaned up automatically
  • Snapshots take very little space at first, because only changes are stored
Getting started
  1. Open Btrfs Assistant from the app launcher and enter your password.
  2. Go to the Snapper tab to see the list of snapshots with their dates.
  3. Before a big change, create a new snapshot and give it a clear description (for example 'before driver install').
  4. If something breaks, open Btrfs Assistant, go to Snapper, and pick a snapshot from before the problem.
  5. Choose restore and confirm.
  6. Restart the computer to finish the restore.
Everyday tips
  • From a terminal, 'sudo snapper list' shows your snapshots.
  • Restore to the most recent snapshot that was working, not the oldest one.
  • Snapshots cover the system, not your home folder. Your documents and settings in /home are not rolled back.
  • Make a manual snapshot before trying something new from an internet guide.
Privacy & security
  • Snapshots are not backups. They live on the same drive, so if the drive dies they are lost too. Keep using Pika Backup for your files.
  • Restoring needs your admin password.
  • Deleted system files can still exist inside older snapshots until those snapshots are removed.
If something goes wrong
  • Disk filling up: lots of snapshots plus big updates use space. Delete old snapshots in Btrfs Assistant, or reduce how many are kept in its Snapper settings.
  • Your files in /home did not come back: that is expected. Home is not part of the system snapshots; restore those from Pika Backup.
  • Restore did not seem to work: make sure you restarted the computer afterwards.
  • Fedora does not show snapshots in the boot menu by default. If the system will not start at all, use the rescue USB stick.

Learn more: https://gitlab.com/btrfs-assistant/btrfs-assistant  ·  All apps

Warehouse

fullSystem tools

A tool for managing Flatpak apps, cleaning up their leftover data and switching app versions.

Many apps on this laptop are Flatpaks, which are self-contained, sandboxed apps. Warehouse gives you one place to see all of them and tidy them up. It is a bit like 'Apps & features' in Windows Settings, but with extra tools just for Flatpaks.

Why it's here

It helps you free up space by removing data left behind by apps you uninstalled. It can also roll an app back to an older version if an update breaks it.

What to do next

Warehouse

What it can do
  • List all installed Flatpak apps and runtimes
  • Uninstall apps
  • Find and delete leftover data from removed apps
  • Install an older version of an app (downgrade)
  • Stop an app from updating (pin or mask it)
  • Manage Flatpak remotes (sources such as Flathub)
  • Take snapshots of an app's user data
Getting started
  1. Open Warehouse from the app launcher.
  2. Browse the list of installed Flatpak apps and runtimes.
  3. Click an app to see details such as its size and ID.
  4. Look for the leftover data section to find data from apps you have removed.
  5. Review the list, then delete only data you are sure you no longer need.
Everyday tips
  • Clean up leftover data now and then to recover disk space.
  • If an app update breaks something, use Warehouse to install the previous version, then stop it updating until a fix arrives.
  • Remember to allow updates again later, so you still get security fixes.
  • Runtimes are shared parts that apps need. Do not remove them by hand; let Flatpak clean unused ones.
Privacy & security
  • Deleting an app's data removes its settings, logins and saved files inside that app. Make sure you do not need them.
  • Pinning an old version means it will not get security updates. Only do it for a short time.
  • Warehouse manages Flatpaks only; for changing an app's permissions, use Flatseal.
If something goes wrong
  • An app is missing from the list: it is probably a normal Fedora (RPM) package, not a Flatpak. Manage it in Discover instead.
  • Downgrading needs an internet connection to fetch the older version. Network protection may ask for permission.
  • Deleted data by mistake: restore it from your Pika Backup if you have one.

Learn more: https://github.com/flattool/warehouse  ·  All apps

Gear Lever

fullSystem tools

Adds AppImage apps to your app launcher and helps keep them updated.

Some Linux apps are shared as a single 'AppImage' file that runs without installing, a bit like a 'portable' .exe on Windows. On their own they do not appear in the app launcher. Gear Lever moves them to one tidy folder, adds them to the launcher with an icon, and can check for updates.

Why it's here

Some apps are only offered as AppImages. Gear Lever makes them behave like normal installed apps.

What to do next

Gear Lever

What it can do
  • Add AppImages to the app launcher with their icon
  • Keep all AppImages in one folder
  • Check for and install updates, when the AppImage supports it
  • Remove AppImages cleanly
  • Drag-and-drop to add a new AppImage
Getting started
  1. Download an AppImage from the app's official website.
  2. Open Gear Lever.
  3. Drag the .AppImage file into the Gear Lever window, or open it with Gear Lever.
  4. Check the details and click to unlock and move it to the app menu.
  5. Find and start the app from the normal app launcher.
Everyday tips
  • Prefer Discover (Fedora or Flathub versions) when an app is available there. Use AppImages only when it is not.
  • Use Gear Lever's update check now and then, because AppImages do not update through Discover.
  • Remove AppImages through Gear Lever so the launcher entry is removed too.
Privacy & security
  • AppImages are not sandboxed like Flatpaks. They can access everything your user account can.
  • Only download AppImages from the official website of the app.
  • Network protection will ask when a new AppImage first tries to connect to the internet. Think about whether it needs to.
If something goes wrong
  • AppImage will not start: some older AppImages need an extra library called FUSE 2. Search for the app's error, or check the app's website for help.
  • No update option: not every AppImage includes update information. Download the new version manually and add it again.
  • The app does not appear in the launcher right away: log out and back in, or search for it by name.

Learn more: https://github.com/mijorus/gearlever  ·  All apps

Filelight

fullSystem tools

Shows what is filling up your disk as easy-to-read coloured rings.

Filelight scans a folder or drive and draws it as rings, where bigger slices mean bigger folders. This makes it quick to spot what is using the most space. It is similar to WinDirStat or TreeSize on Windows.

Why it's here

When the disk gets full, Filelight shows you where the space has gone in seconds.

What to do next

Filelight

What it can do
  • Scan your home folder, a drive or any folder
  • Show disk use as clickable rings
  • Click into a folder to zoom in
  • Hover to see folder sizes
  • Open a folder in the file manager from Filelight
Getting started
  1. Open Filelight from the app launcher.
  2. Choose to scan your home folder, or pick another folder.
  3. Wait for the scan to finish.
  4. Hover over the rings to see names and sizes.
  5. Click a large slice to zoom into it, and keep going until you find what is big.
Everyday tips
  • Common space users are Downloads, videos, game installs and Flatpak data.
  • Delete files in Dolphin (the file manager), not by guessing. Check what a file is first.
  • Use the back button to zoom out again.
  • Rescan after cleaning up to see the new picture.
Privacy & security
  • Filelight only reads file sizes. It does not change or send anything.
  • Do not delete system folders you do not recognise. Stick to your own home folder.
If something goes wrong
  • Some folders cannot be scanned: Filelight is a sandboxed Flatpak, so it may not see everything. Use Flatseal to grant access if needed.
  • Sizes look odd on the system drive: the Btrfs file system and its snapshots can make totals confusing. Focus on your home folder.
  • Space was not freed after deleting: empty the Trash in Dolphin.

Learn more: https://apps.kde.org/filelight/  ·  All apps

Czkawka

fullSystem tools

Finds duplicate files, similar photos and videos, empty folders and big files so you can clean up.

Czkawka (pronounced 'chav-ka', Polish for 'hiccup') is a cleaning tool. It searches your folders for duplicate files, similar-looking pictures and videos, empty folders, very large files and more. It is similar to duplicate finders on Windows such as dupeGuru.

Why it's here

Photo and download folders fill up with copies over time. Czkawka finds them quickly so you can free up space.

What to do next

Czkawka

What it can do
  • Find exact duplicate files
  • Find similar images (resized or slightly edited copies)
  • Find similar videos
  • Find empty folders and empty files
  • List the biggest files
  • Find broken files and temporary files
  • Select files in bulk for deletion or moving
Getting started
  1. Open Czkawka from the app launcher.
  2. Add the folders you want to search, such as Pictures or Downloads.
  3. Choose a tool from the list, for example Duplicate Files.
  4. Click Search and wait for the results.
  5. Look through the results carefully. Open files to check them if you are unsure.
  6. Select the copies you want to remove and keep one of each.
  7. Only then use the delete option.
Everyday tips
  • Start with a small folder to learn how it works.
  • Similar-image results are guesses. Always check them before deleting.
  • Use the selection helpers to keep the newest or oldest copy, but still review the result.
  • Back up first (for example with Pika Backup) before a big clean-up.
Privacy & security
  • Always review before deleting. Deleted files may not go to the Trash, so they could be gone for good. Look in the settings for how deletion works.
  • Do not scan system folders. Stick to your own files in your home folder.
  • Czkawka works offline.
If something goes wrong
  • Folder not found or empty results: the Flatpak sandbox may block it. Grant access with Flatseal.
  • Search is slow: big folders take time, especially for similar images and videos. Let it run.
  • Deleted something you needed: check the Trash first, then restore from your backup.

Learn more: https://github.com/qarmin/czkawka  ·  All apps

Distrobox + BoxBuddy

fullSystem tools

Runs apps made for other Linux versions (like Ubuntu or Arch) inside containers that blend into your desktop.

Distrobox lets you create a 'container', which is like a lightweight mini copy of another Linux system, such as Ubuntu or Arch. Apps inside it can still see your home folder and open windows on your desktop. BoxBuddy is a simple window for managing these containers without typing commands. Containers are run by a tool called Podman.

Why it's here

Sometimes an app or guide is only made for Ubuntu or another Linux. Distrobox lets you use it without changing your main Fedora system.

What to do next

BoxBuddy (or in a terminal: distrobox)

What it can do
  • Create containers for Ubuntu, Debian, Arch and many others
  • Install software inside a container with that system's own tools
  • Add apps from a container to your app launcher (distrobox-export)
  • Containers share your home folder, so files are easy to reach
  • Delete a container to undo everything you installed in it
  • BoxBuddy gives a point-and-click way to create, open and remove containers
Getting started
  1. Open BoxBuddy from the app launcher.
  2. Create a new box and choose a system image, for example Ubuntu.
  3. Wait while it downloads. The first time can take a few minutes.
  4. Open a terminal in the box from BoxBuddy.
  5. Install what you need using that system's commands (for Ubuntu: sudo apt install <app>).
  6. To add an app to your launcher, run 'distrobox-export --app <app>' inside the box.
  7. Terminal version: 'distrobox create --name ubuntu --image ubuntu:24.04', then 'distrobox enter ubuntu'.
Everyday tips
  • Try Discover first. Only use Distrobox when an app is not available for Fedora.
  • Give boxes clear names, such as 'ubuntu' or 'arch'.
  • 'distrobox list' shows all your boxes.
  • If a box gets messy, delete it and make a new one. Your main system is not affected.
  • Update software inside each box separately, using that box's own update command.
Privacy & security
  • Distrobox is not a security sandbox. Apps in a box can see and change your home folder.
  • Only install software from trusted sources, just as on the main system.
  • Container images are downloaded from the internet. Network protection may ask the first time.
If something goes wrong
  • Box takes a long time to start the first time: it is downloading and setting up. Later starts are quicker.
  • Exported app is missing from the launcher: log out and back in, or check that you ran distrobox-export inside the right box.
  • Software installed in a box is not available outside it unless you export it.
  • Disk space: each box uses space. Remove boxes you no longer use (in BoxBuddy, or 'distrobox rm <name>').

Learn more: https://distrobox.it/  ·  All apps

Bottles

fullSystem tools

Runs many Windows programs on Linux using Wine, each in its own separate 'bottle'.

Bottles uses Wine, a compatibility layer that lets many Windows programs run on Linux. Each 'bottle' is a separate pretend Windows setup, so one program cannot mess up another. It is the easiest way to try a Windows-only app on this laptop.

Why it's here

Some Windows programs have no Linux version. Bottles gives you a good chance of running them anyway.

What to do next

Bottles

What it can do
  • Run Windows .exe and .msi programs
  • Separate bottles for different programs
  • Ready-made environments for gaming or general apps
  • Install common Windows extras (such as fonts or runtimes) as dependencies
  • Choose different Wine versions (runners)
  • Add a launcher shortcut for a Windows program
  • Snapshots of a bottle so you can undo changes
Getting started
  1. Open Bottles. The first time, it downloads the parts it needs.
  2. Create a new bottle, give it a name, and choose an environment (Application for normal programs, Gaming for games).
  3. Open the bottle and choose 'Run Executable'.
  4. Pick the Windows installer (.exe) you downloaded and follow the installer as you would on Windows.
  5. After installing, add the program to the bottle's program list if it is not shown, then launch it from there.
  6. If it does not work, check online whether others got it running and which dependencies they used.
Everyday tips
  • Use one bottle per program. If something goes wrong, only that bottle is affected.
  • Search the program's name plus 'Wine' or check the Wine AppDB to see how well it works.
  • For games, use Steam or Heroic first. They are usually easier.
  • Take a snapshot of a bottle before installing extra dependencies.
Privacy & security
  • Windows programs in Bottles can still contain malware. Only run installers from trusted sources.
  • Bottles is sandboxed as a Flatpak. By default it may not see all your folders; use Flatseal or Bottles' own settings to allow more.
  • Network protection will ask before a Windows program connects to the internet. This is a good chance to deny programs that do not need it.
If something goes wrong
  • Not every Windows program works. Programs with strong anti-cheat or anti-piracy, and some Office or Adobe versions, often fail.
  • Program cannot see your files: the sandbox is blocking it. Give Bottles access to that folder with Flatseal.
  • Program crashes on start: try the other environment type, a different runner, or installing a dependency the program needs.
  • Fonts look wrong: install the core fonts dependency in that bottle.

Learn more: https://usebottles.com/  ·  All apps

Automatic updates

fullliteSystem tools

Background timers that keep the system, Flatpak apps and firmware checks up to date without you doing anything.

This computer is set up to update itself, similar to Windows Update running in the background. On the main laptop, updates download and prepare themselves every day and install while the computer restarts ("offline updates"), with a snapshot taken first. On older PCs the updates install straight away each day. A daily timer updates Flatpak apps, and another checks for firmware updates for your hardware. They use "timers", which are Linux's version of Windows scheduled tasks.

Why it's here

Updates fix security holes. Doing them automatically means you stay protected even if you forget.

What to do next

Terminal: systemctl list-timers

What it can do
  • Prepares all system updates every day on the laptop (installed at the next restart, snapshot first)
  • Installs updates daily on old PCs (restart at 04:00 only if you choose that)
  • Updates Flatpak apps daily (secure-linux-flatpak-update)
  • Checks regularly for new firmware (fwupd-refresh)
  • Never restarts the computer by itself on the laptop
  • Secure Linux Status shows "Install updates now" and "Restart the computer" when needed
  • Warns if updates have been waiting more than 7 days for a restart
Getting started
  1. You do not need to do anything. Updates run in the background.
  2. To see the update timers, open a terminal and type: systemctl list-timers
  3. Look for secure-linux-offline-updates, secure-linux-flatpak-update and fwupd-refresh in the list, with their next and last run times.
  4. Watch for notifications from Secure Linux Status and Discover.
  5. Restart the computer about once a week, so prepared updates install and fully take effect.
  6. To see everything at once, open Secure Linux Status & Fixes.
Everyday tips
  • Restarting once or twice a week is a good habit, so updated parts are actually in use.
  • Firmware updates are only checked automatically. Install them from the Status window ("Update firmware") with the laptop plugged in.
  • To see what the system updater did recently on an old PC, run: journalctl -u dnf5-automatic
  • If you ever want to update right away, open Discover and click Update All, or "Install updates now" in the Status window.
Privacy & security
  • Automatic security updates close known security holes quickly.
  • Updates come from Fedora's and Flathub's official sources and are checked with digital signatures.
  • Because the laptop never restarts by itself, you will not lose unsaved work, but you need to restart yourself for updates to install.
  • Before a big change, a system snapshot (Snapper) lets you roll back if an update causes trouble.
If something goes wrong
  • Something stopped working after an update: restart first. If it is still broken, open Repair This Computer and choose "Go back to an earlier snapshot" (or Btrfs Assistant).
  • Updates seem to not run: the computer must be on and connected to the internet. Check 'systemctl list-timers' for the last run time.
  • A Flatpak app changed after an update: if the new version is broken, Warehouse can install an older version for a while.
  • Firmware updates may ask you to restart and can take a few minutes. Keep the laptop plugged in and do not switch it off.

Learn more: https://dnf5.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dnf5_plugins/automatic.8.html  ·  All apps

setup.sh (re-run your setup)

fullliteSystem tools

The script that installed and configured everything on this computer. You can run it again, safely, to repair things.

This computer was set up automatically by a script stored at /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh, together with the other Secure Linux files in that folder. It installs the apps in this guide and applies the settings. It is safe to run again: it fills in anything missing and repairs things without overwriting a file you changed. On the first start, it ran automatically as a service called firstboot-setup.

Why it's here

If an app goes missing, something failed during setup, or a setting has drifted, re-running the script in repair mode is the easiest fix. Secure Linux Status & Fixes has a "Repair setup" button that does exactly this.

What to do next

Secure Linux Status & Fixes, "Repair setup" (or: sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair)

What it can do
  • Installs and repairs the apps and settings in this guide
  • Safe to run more than once ("repair" mode adds only what is missing)
  • Profiles (full, lite or atomic) are remembered; you do not need to type one
  • Writes a full log to /var/log/secure-linux/setup.log
  • Lists anything that failed in /var/log/secure-linux/failures.log
  • Ran automatically on first boot as the firstboot-setup service
  • Leaves a SETUP-REPORT.txt summary on your Desktop
Getting started
  1. First read SETUP-REPORT.txt on your Desktop. It summarises what was installed and anything that failed.
  2. Make sure you are connected to the internet and the laptop is plugged into power.
  3. Easiest: open Secure Linux Status & Fixes and press "Repair setup". Or open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T).
  4. Run: sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair
  5. Type your password when asked (nothing shows as you type) and press Enter.
  6. Network protection may ask about programs connecting to the internet while it runs; the usual ones (dnf, flatpak, curl) are pre-approved.
  7. Wait until it finishes. It can take a long time, so do not close the window.
  8. Check for problems: sudo cat /var/log/secure-linux/failures.log. If it is empty or missing, nothing failed.
Everyday tips
  • Read the full log with: sudo less /var/log/secure-linux/setup.log. Use arrow keys to scroll and q to quit. Press G to jump to the end.
  • While the first-boot setup is still running, watch it live with: journalctl -fu firstboot-setup. Press Ctrl+C to stop watching (setup keeps running).
  • Check whether first-boot setup has finished: systemctl status firstboot-setup. Press q to leave.
  • If one app failed because of a network problem, simply running repair again usually fixes it.
  • Run it after a big Fedora upgrade (the upgrade helper does this by itself) to make sure everything is still in place.
  • Your saved choices (secure-linux-choice list) take effect at the next repair.
Privacy & security
  • The script runs with administrator rights (sudo), so only run this copy from /usr/local/lib/secure-linux, never a version sent to you by someone else.
  • It downloads software from Fedora, Flathub and a few official project sites, checking fingerprints where the makers publish them.
  • The log files may contain your username and computer details. Check them before sharing online.
If something goes wrong
  • 'command not found' or 'Permission denied': type the full path exactly, starting with sudo: sudo /usr/local/lib/secure-linux/setup.sh --repair
  • Script stops or many items fail: check your internet connection, then run it again. If it still fails, check that Network Monitor did not block dnf or flatpak (secure-linux-netguard pause 15 tests this).
  • Running it while the first-boot setup is still going: wait for firstboot-setup to finish first (check with systemctl status firstboot-setup), because two package installs cannot run at the same time.
  • Software updates are running in Discover at the same time: let them finish, then re-run the repair.

Learn more: https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/quick-docs/  ·  All apps

Secure Linux Status & Fixes

fullliteSystem tools

One window with a green, orange or red dot for every check on your computer, and a Fix it button.

It lists checks such as disk encryption, firewall, updates, backups, antivirus, VPN, battery health and SSD wear, in plain English, worst first. Pick an orange or red line and press Fix it. A terminal version is called Terminal view.

Why it's here

It is the one place to look when you wonder "is my computer OK?", and it is where the one-click fixes live.

What to do next

Secure Linux Status & Fixes (app launcher), or secure-linux-status in a terminal

What it can do
  • Plain-English list of every check
  • One-click fixes (install updates, restart, repair setup, update firmware, make a recovery key and more)
  • Shows alerts from every part of the system
  • Opens this guide
  • Terminal view for text-only use
Getting started
  1. Open Secure Linux Status & Fixes from the app launcher.
  2. Read the list: the worst lines are at the top.
  3. Click an orange or red line, then press Fix it.
  4. Press "Check again" (or run secure-linux-status --refresh) after fixing.
Everyday tips
  • A notification opens it when something needs you (at most once a day per problem).
  • Repair setup re-applies the whole setup safely if anything is missing.
  • On Apple Silicon Macs, apps with no ARM version appear in a calm "Not available on this computer" line.
Privacy & security
  • It only reads the state of your computer. Fixes ask for your password and show what they do.
If something goes wrong
  • A fix says it is not available: run Repair setup, which adds any missing tool.
  • The window does not open: try secure-linux-status in a terminal.

Learn more: the matching chapter in this guide  ·  All apps

Hardware Health Check

fullliteSystem tools

Looks at every part of the computer and says in plain English whether it is healthy.

It checks the drive, memory, processor, temperatures, battery, screen, graphics, sound, camera, keyboard, touchpad, USB, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the security chip and more. Parts you do not have are shown as "not present". It only looks; it never changes your drives. The full version adds a stress test and tests where you listen or look.

Why it's here

Hardware often warns before it fails. Finding a failing drive or swollen battery early lets you back up and replace it on your terms.

What to do next

Hardware Health Check or Hardware Test (full, 5 minutes) (app launcher); secure-linux-health in a terminal

What it can do
  • Standard check in about a minute
  • Full check with stress test and listen-and-look tests (about 5 minutes)
  • Each warning says what to do
  • A quick check runs by itself every week
  • Works from the USB stick too, with no installation
Getting started
  1. Open Hardware Health Check from the app launcher and type your password (it needs it for drive and memory details).
  2. Read each line: OK, WARN, FAIL, NOT-PRESENT or SKIPPED.
  3. Follow the advice on any WARN or FAIL line.
  4. For the thorough version, open Hardware Test (full, 5 minutes).
Everyday tips
  • secure-linux-health --part battery checks just one part.
  • A complete memory test needs a restart: use Memtest86+ from the USB stick.
  • A FAIL on a drive means back up now.
Privacy & security
  • Nothing is sent anywhere. Reports stay in /var/lib/secure-linux/health/.
If something goes wrong
  • SKIPPED means a tool is missing or it needs your password: run sudo secure-linux-parts --install, or use the menu entry.
  • It cannot repair hardware, only report on it.

Learn more: the matching chapter in this guide  ·  All apps

Repair This Computer

fullliteSystem tools

A guided repair menu for a computer that will not start, a damaged disk, a black screen, no internet or a forgotten password.

A numbered menu that explains each step in plain English, shows what it is about to do and waits for your yes. It also runs from SystemRescue on the USB stick, so it works when the computer will not start. It can first look for the cause by itself ("Find out what is wrong").

Why it's here

When something breaks you want one calm place that knows the fixes and protects your files first.

What to do next

Repair This Computer (app launcher); secure-linux-repair in a terminal; from the USB stick: bash secure-linux-rescue.sh

What it can do
  • Find out what is wrong (looks only)
  • Rescue my files before any repair
  • Repair the boot loader, check disks, go back to a snapshot, start an older kernel
  • Safe graphics, repair software, fix Wi-Fi
  • Windows help, Linux and local-Windows password reset
  • Virus scan, clone a drive, factory reset, wipe before selling
  • A dry-run mode that changes nothing
Getting started
  1. Open Repair This Computer.
  2. Choose "Find out what is wrong" if you are unsure.
  3. Pick the menu item it recommends and read what it will do.
  4. Say yes only when you understand; dangerous steps need a typed sentence.
  5. If the computer will not start at all, boot the USB stick, choose SystemRescue and run the rescue script.
Everyday tips
  • Use secure-linux-repair --dry-run first to see what a repair would do.
  • Every command it runs is printed.
  • A failing drive always gets a loud warning to rescue your files first.
Privacy & security
  • A safety copy of the boot files is made first. BitLocker drives are never opened without their key. A local Windows password can be cleared only after you confirm the computer is yours.
If something goes wrong
  • The repair did not help: run Find out what is wrong again, then secure-linux-diag and ask for help.
  • It cannot recover a lost disk-encryption password.

Learn more: the matching chapter in this guide  ·  All apps

Bring My Stuff from Windows

fullSystem tools

A helper that moves your passwords, bookmarks, photos, OneDrive, notes and more across from Windows.

A list of short pages, one per topic: passwords, bookmarks, Google Photos, OneDrive and notes, Office files, study tools, games, printers, screen, streaming, video calls, accessibility, extras, devices and more. The same pages run once in the welcome wizard.

Why it's here

Moving house is easier with a checklist that does the heavy lifting and asks before each step.

What to do next

Bring My Stuff from Windows (app launcher); secure-linux-migrate in a terminal

What it can do
  • Google passwords to Bitwarden
  • Bookmarks to LibreWolf
  • Google Takeout to Immich
  • OneDrive copy that never deletes anything
  • Notes vault via Syncthing
  • Printer, screen, Netflix, video-call and accessibility set-up

  1. Open Bring My Stuff from Windows.

Gaming

Steam

fullGaming

Valve's game store and launcher, which can also run many Windows games on Linux using Proton.

Steam is the same game store and launcher you may know from Windows. On Linux it includes Proton, a built-in tool that lets many Windows-only games run. Your existing Steam library and saves (with Steam Cloud) carry over when you log in.

Why it's here

It is the easiest way to play games on Linux. Your Steam games, including Rocket League if you own it there, can be played on this laptop.

What to do next

Steam

What it can do
  • Buy, download and play games
  • Run many Windows games through Proton
  • Steam Cloud saves sync between computers
  • Controller support, including Steam Input
  • Per-game launch options
  • Choose a specific Proton version for each game
  • Friends, chat and screenshots
Getting started
  1. Open Steam. It may download updates the first time.
  2. Sign in with your Steam account (type your password yourself).
  3. Open Steam > Settings > Compatibility and turn on Steam Play for all other titles.
  4. Restart Steam if it asks.
  5. Go to your Library, pick a game and click Install.
  6. Before buying or installing, look the game up on protondb.com to see how well it runs.
  7. Click Play.
Everyday tips
  • ProtonDB reports show tips from other players, such as launch options that help.
  • To change the Proton version for one game: right-click it > Properties > Compatibility.
  • Rocket League runs through Proton according to ProtonDB reports. Check ProtonDB for the latest status.
  • Add 'gamemoderun %command%' in a game's Properties > Launch Options to use GameMode.
  • Plug the laptop in while gaming for better performance.
  • The first launch of a game can be slow while shaders are prepared. Later launches are faster.
Privacy & security
  • Only type your Steam password into the Steam window itself. Turn on Steam Guard for your account.
  • Steam is a Flatpak and is sandboxed. Giving it access to extra drives needs Flatseal.
  • Network protection already approves Steam, but a game's own launcher may ask the first time it goes online. Steam needs internet access to work.
  • Some games use anti-cheat that does not support Linux. Check ProtonDB before buying.
If something goes wrong
  • Game will not start: try a different Proton version (including GE-Proton from ProtonUp-Qt) and check ProtonDB tips.
  • Cannot add a game library on another drive: give Steam access to that drive using Flatseal.
  • Controller not working: check Steam > Settings > Controller, and try reconnecting it.
  • Online multiplayer game refuses to run: its anti-cheat may block Linux. There is no fix on your side.

Learn more: https://store.steampowered.com/  ·  All apps

Why it's here

You own Rocket League on Epic, and Heroic is the main way to play Epic games on Linux. It also covers GOG and Amazon games.

What to do next

Heroic Games Launcher

What it can do
  • Log into Epic Games, GOG and Amazon Games

  3. Sign in on the store's own login page that Heroic opens. Type your password yourself.

ProtonUp-Qt

GameMode

fullGaming

Temporarily tunes the computer for best performance while a game is running.

GameMode is a small background tool from Feral Interactive. When a game asks for it, it switches the computer into a faster performance mode, then back again when the game closes. It is similar to 'Game Mode' in Windows settings, but you turn it on per game.

Why it's here

It can make games run a little smoother on the laptop, with no lasting changes to the system.

What to do next

In Steam: game Properties > Launch Options, type gamemoderun %command% (check status in a terminal with: gamemoded -s)

What it can do
  • Raises processor performance while a game is running
  • Gives the game higher priority
  • Returns everything to normal when the game closes
  • Turn it on per game with a launch option
  • Works with Steam, Heroic and other launchers
Getting started
  1. In Steam, right-click a game and choose Properties.
  2. In the General section, find Launch Options.
  3. Type: gamemoderun %command%
  4. Close the window and start the game.
  5. In Heroic, look for a GameMode option in the game's settings and turn it on.
  6. To check it is working, run 'gamemoded -s' in a terminal while the game is running.
Everyday tips
  • Keep other launch options if a game already has some. Put them together with a space, keeping %command% in place.
  • Plug the laptop in while gaming. GameMode cannot fix a laptop in battery-saving mode.
  • If a game runs worse with GameMode, just remove the launch option.
Privacy & security
  • GameMode only changes performance settings while the game is running and does not use the internet.
  • It is installed from Fedora's official repositories.
If something goes wrong
  • Game will not start after adding the option: check you typed 'gamemoderun %command%' exactly, including the percent signs.
  • No noticeable difference: this is normal for some games. The benefit depends on the game and the laptop.
  • Laptop gets hotter and louder: that is expected while it runs faster.

AI & coding

Ollama and Private AI

fullAI & coding

Compare and run the maintained local-model catalogue through Private AI, with Ollama as one available engine.

Ollama is a local model engine. Secure Linux's Private AI window and secure-linux-ai helper add model comparison, workload routing, reviewed downloads, chat and explicit benchmarks. Qwen2.5-Coder models are Ollama-only in this catalogue.

Why it's here

It provides private, offline AI after a model is downloaded, without making you guess which model fits from a generic parameter-count slogan.

What to do next

Open Private AI, or run secure-linux-ai gui

What it can do
  • Compare the fixed maintained model catalogue
  • Route interactive, balanced, quality and low-storage workloads
  • Download, install, remove and chat with selected models
  • Measure CPU and Vulkan decode on this device
  • Work offline after the required model files are present
Getting started
  1. Run secure-linux-ai models to inspect the catalogue.
  2. Run secure-linux-ai route --workload balanced and review the fit result.
  3. Use secure-linux-ai download MODEL --engine ollama --confirm or the Private AI window to approve a download.
  4. Chat with secure-linux-ai chat MODEL --prompt TEXT, optionally adding --session ID.
Everyday tips
  • The router excludes fewer-refusals models, ranks feasible fit gates first and uses only same-device measured decode results as interactive tie-breakers.
  • Fit gates are wrapper heuristics, not tokens-per-second predictions. Measure on this computer before choosing a backend for speed.
  • Benchmarks require --backend cpu|vulkan and --confirm. Their short fixed prompt does not assess answer quality or long coding-agent prefill.
  • Cold-process means a new model process, not a cold operating-system page cache.
  • Use remove for unused models and check free disk space before another download.
Privacy & security
  • Once all required files are local, supported chat runs on this computer rather than sending prompts to a cloud account.
  • AI can be confidently wrong. Review facts and code, especially before running any generated command.
  • The frontend guidance does not enable shell or agent tools.
  • Fewer-refusals models are excluded from normal routing and need an explicit alternative workflow.
If something goes wrong
  • Colibri's pinned registry does not support qwen2. Do not alias Qwen2.5-Coder to Qwen3.
  • Qwen3.6 is general-purpose and may help with code; it is not labelled a coding specialist.
  • A model that fails a fit gate is not made feasible by a generic claim about RAM or GPU presence.
  • The legacy Qwen2.5 ChatML template still needs comparison with ollama show ... --modelfile; tools and FIM are omitted.

Learn more: the matching chapter in this guide  ·  All apps

Alpaca

fullAI & coding

A graphical chat frontend that can connect to local Ollama models.

Alpaca provides a chat window for an Ollama instance. It is a frontend, separate from the maintained Private AI model router and benchmark workflow.

Why it's here

It offers a familiar chat interface while Private AI remains the place to compare fit, download the maintained catalogue and measure this device.

What to do next

Open Alpaca, or open Private AI first to choose and install a model

What it can do
  • Chat with models exposed by a configured Ollama instance
  • Keep separate conversations
  • Copy answers and code
  • Work offline when the selected local model and frontend support it
Getting started
  1. Use secure-linux-ai route --workload interactive to review a suitable maintained model.
  2. Install that model through Private AI or secure-linux-ai install MODEL --engine ollama --confirm.
  3. Connect Alpaca to the same Ollama instance, normally http://localhost:11434 for the system service.
  4. Select the installed model in Alpaca before chatting.
Everyday tips
  • Use Private AI rather than a generic 3B–8B recommendation to compare the maintained catalogue.
  • Start a new chat for a new topic; long conversations use more context.
  • If a model is missing, check that Alpaca and Private AI are using the same Ollama instance.
  • Do not interpret a fast benchmark decode number as proof of answer quality.
Privacy & security
  • A local Ollama instance keeps supported chats on this computer; adding a remote service changes that privacy boundary.
  • Review important facts and generated code. Alpaca does not make an answer trustworthy.
  • The Secure Linux frontend guidance does not enable shell or agent tools.
If something goes wrong
  • No models listed: check the configured Ollama address and whether the model was installed in that instance.
  • Cannot connect: check secure-linux-ai status and the Ollama service before downloading again.
  • Qwen2.5-Coder remains Ollama-only; Colibri must not substitute Qwen3 under that name.
