VSCodium

fullAI & coding

VSCodium is a powerful code editor: Visual Studio Code without Microsoft's tracking.

VSCodium is built from the same source code as Microsoft's Visual Studio Code, so it looks and works almost the same. The difference is that Microsoft's telemetry (usage tracking) and branding are removed. Extensions come from Open VSX, an open extension store, instead of Microsoft's marketplace. It is installed as a Flatpak, which runs it inside a safety sandbox.

Why it's here

It is a modern, free editor for Python, JavaScript, Java, web pages and almost any other language, without sending usage data to Microsoft.

What to do next

VSCodium

What it can do
  • Edit code with colours, auto-complete and error hints
  • Open whole project folders with a file tree on the left
  • Built-in Git support for tracking changes
  • Built-in terminal panel
  • Install extensions for languages and tools from Open VSX
  • Search and replace across many files
  • Split the editor to view files side by side
  • Edit Markdown with a live preview
Getting started
  1. Open the app launcher and type VSCodium.
  2. Click File > Open Folder and choose a project folder (for example make a folder called Projects in your Home folder).
  3. Create a new file with File > New File, then save it with a name ending in the right extension, such as hello.py.
  4. Click the Extensions icon on the left (four squares) and search for a language, for example Python. Click Install.
  5. If Network protection asks whether VSCodium may connect to the internet, allow it if you want to install extensions (they come from open-vsx.org).
  6. Open the built-in terminal with Ctrl+` (the key above Tab) or View > Terminal.
Everyday tips
  • Ctrl+Shift+P opens the Command Palette, where you can search for any action by name.
  • Ctrl+P quickly opens a file by typing part of its name.
  • Ctrl+S saves. Turn on File > Auto Save if you often forget.
  • Ctrl+/ comments or uncomments the selected lines.
  • Some Microsoft-only extensions are not on Open VSX. Look for an open alternative with a similar name.
  • Change the colour theme in File > Preferences > Theme > Color Theme.
Privacy & security
  • Microsoft telemetry is removed. You can double-check in Settings by searching for telemetry.
  • Extensions can run code on your computer. Only install well-known extensions with many downloads.
  • The Flatpak sandbox limits what VSCodium and its extensions can reach, but it is not a perfect barrier.
  • Be careful when opening folders from strangers. If VSCodium asks whether you trust a folder's authors, choose No unless you are sure.
If something goes wrong
  • The built-in terminal or an extension cannot find python, node, java or gcc: because of the Flatpak sandbox, VSCodium cannot always see programs installed on the main system. The simplest fix is to run those commands in Konsole instead.
  • Advanced fix for the terminal: in a VSCodium terminal you can reach the main system by starting a command with flatpak-spawn --host, for example flatpak-spawn --host bash. Some people set this as the default terminal profile in settings.
  • Extension not found: it may only exist on Microsoft's marketplace. Search Open VSX for an alternative.
  • Cannot open a file outside your Home folder: the sandbox may block it. Copy the file into your Home folder, or adjust permissions with a tool like Flatseal if it is installed.

Learn more: https://vscodium.com  ·  All apps

Python + pipx

fullAI & coding

Python is a beginner-friendly programming language, and pipx safely installs Python command-line apps.

Python is one of the most popular programming languages and comes with Fedora. pip installs Python libraries, and pipx installs Python programs (command-line apps) each in their own private space so they do not clash. Unlike on Windows, you do not need to download Python from a website.

Why it's here

Python is great for learning to code, automating boring tasks and working with AI. pipx lets you install Python tools without breaking the system.

What to do next

python3

What it can do
  • Run Python scripts and an interactive Python prompt
  • Create virtual environments (venvs) for each project
  • Install libraries into a venv with pip
  • Install Python command-line apps with pipx
  • Upgrade or remove pipx apps cleanly
  • Use Python for automation, data and AI scripts
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and type python3 --version to check Python is installed.
  2. Type python3 and press Enter to get an interactive prompt (>>>). Try print("hello"). Type exit() to leave.
  3. Make a project folder: mkdir myproject then cd myproject (mkdir makes a folder, cd moves into it).
  4. Create a virtual environment (a private library folder for this project): python3 -m venv .venv
  5. Turn it on: source .venv/bin/activate. Your prompt now shows (.venv).
  6. Install libraries only while the venv is on, for example pip install requests. Type deactivate to turn it off.
  7. For Python apps you want to use everywhere, use pipx instead, for example pipx install <app-name>. Run pipx ensurepath once and then open a new terminal so the apps can be found.
Everyday tips
  • Run a script with python3 myscript.py.
  • Use one venv per project. If a venv gets messy, delete the .venv folder and create it again.
  • pip freeze > requirements.txt saves the list of libraries in a venv. pip install -r requirements.txt installs them again later.
  • pipx list shows your pipx apps. pipx upgrade-all updates them. pipx uninstall <app-name> removes one.
  • Some libraries are also available as Fedora packages (names start with python3-). For system-wide use, sudo dnf install python3-<name> is the safe way.
  • Write code in VSCodium, then run it in Konsole.
Privacy & security
  • Never use sudo pip install. It can overwrite files Fedora relies on and break system tools.
  • Anyone can upload to PyPI (the Python package store). Check the exact spelling of a package name before installing, because fake look-alike packages exist.
  • pip and pipx download from pypi.org. Network protection may ask you to allow this the first time.
  • Only run Python scripts from sources you trust. A script can do anything your user account can do.
If something goes wrong
  • 'externally-managed-environment' error when using pip: Fedora protects its own Python. Fix: activate a venv first, or use pipx for apps.
  • 'command not found' after pipx install: run pipx ensurepath, then close and reopen Konsole.
  • Command python not found: on Fedora use python3 (and pip inside a venv).
  • Forgot to activate the venv, so a library is 'missing': run source .venv/bin/activate in the project folder and try again.

Learn more: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/  ·  All apps

Node.js + npm

fullAI & coding

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the web browser, and npm installs JavaScript libraries and tools.

JavaScript is the language of web pages. Node.js lets you run it on your computer to build websites, web servers and command-line tools. npm is its package manager: it downloads libraries into your project. Both were installed from Fedora's own packages.

Why it's here

Many web development and coding tools need Node.js and npm, so having them ready saves setup time.

What to do next

node

What it can do
  • Run JavaScript files with node
  • Create new projects with npm init
  • Install libraries into a project with npm install
  • Run project scripts with npm run
  • Run tools once without installing them using npx
  • Build websites and small web servers
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and check the versions: node --version and npm --version.
  2. Make a project folder and move into it: mkdir myapp then cd myapp.
  3. Start a project: npm init -y. This creates a package.json file that describes the project.
  4. Create a file called index.js in VSCodium containing: console.log("Hello");
  5. Run it: node index.js
  6. Add a library, for example: npm install express. It goes into a node_modules folder inside the project.
Everyday tips
  • Type node on its own to get an interactive prompt for quick tests. Press Ctrl+D to leave.
  • When you download someone's project, run npm install in its folder to fetch everything it needs.
  • npm run lists a project's scripts. npm run <name> runs one, for example npm run dev.
  • npx <tool> runs a tool once without installing it permanently.
  • Do not copy node_modules folders between computers. Delete it and run npm install again instead.
  • Fedora updates Node.js with normal system updates (sudo dnf upgrade).
Privacy & security
  • npm downloads from registry.npmjs.org. Network protection may ask you to allow this.
  • Anyone can publish to npm. Check package names carefully and prefer popular, well-maintained packages.
  • Installing a package can run its install scripts on your computer, so only install packages you trust.
  • Avoid sudo npm install -g. It changes system folders and is rarely needed.
If something goes wrong
  • Permission error with npm install -g: do not add sudo. Either install the tool locally in the project, use npx, or set a personal folder with npm config set prefix ~/.local (then ~/.local/bin is used).
  • A project says it needs a different Node version: Fedora ships one main version. For other versions, tools like nvm exist, but try the Fedora version first.
  • Errors after copying a project: delete node_modules and package-lock.json only if told to, then run npm install again.
  • node_modules is huge: that is normal. Delete it from old projects to free space; npm install brings it back.

Learn more: https://nodejs.org/en/learn  ·  All apps

Java (OpenJDK)

fullAI & coding

OpenJDK is the free, open-source Java toolkit for running and writing Java programs.

Java is a popular programming language used in schools, Android development, business software and games like Minecraft. OpenJDK includes java (to run programs) and javac (to compile, meaning turn your code into a runnable form). This laptop has Fedora's java-latest-openjdk-devel package, which is the newest Java version with the full developer tools.

Why it's here

It lets you learn Java and run Java programs and tools that need it, without installing anything from Oracle's website.

What to do next

java -version

What it can do
  • Run Java programs and .jar files
  • Compile Java code with javac
  • Run a single-file Java program directly with java
  • Use developer tools such as jshell for quick experiments
  • Works with build tools and editors such as VSCodium
  • Updated through normal Fedora system updates
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and check Java: java -version and javac -version.
  2. Create a file Hello.java in VSCodium with a class named Hello that prints a message.
  3. Compile it: javac Hello.java. This creates Hello.class.
  4. Run it: java Hello (no .class on the end).
  5. For a quick test of small code snippets, type jshell. Type /exit to leave.
  6. To run a downloaded .jar program: java -jar program.jar
Everyday tips
  • The file name must match the public class name, for example class Hello goes in Hello.java.
  • For a single file you can skip javac and just run java Hello.java.
  • Install a Java extension in VSCodium for auto-complete and error hints.
  • If more than one Java version is installed, sudo alternatives --config java lets you choose the default.
  • Java updates arrive with normal system updates (sudo dnf upgrade).
Privacy & security
  • OpenJDK is open source and has no tracking.
  • Only run .jar files from sources you trust. They can do anything your user account can do.
  • Keep Java updated with system updates to get security fixes.
If something goes wrong
  • A program needs an older long-term-support version (such as Java 21): Fedora also packages specific versions. Search with dnf search openjdk and install the one needed.
  • 'Could not find or load main class': run java from the folder that has the .class file, and do not type the .class extension.
  • VSCodium's Java extension cannot find Java: the Flatpak sandbox may hide the system Java. Compile and run in Konsole instead.
  • 'javac: command not found': the -devel package is missing. Re-run the setup script or install java-latest-openjdk-devel with dnf.

Learn more: https://openjdk.org  ·  All apps

GitHub CLI

fullAI & coding

GitHub CLI (gh) lets you use GitHub from the terminal: sign in, copy projects, and manage issues and pull requests.

GitHub is a website where people store and share code. The gh command connects your terminal to your GitHub account so you can download (clone) projects, create new ones and work with issues and pull requests without the web browser. It works alongside git, the tool that tracks changes in code.

Why it's here

It makes signing in to GitHub and copying projects simple, especially the login part, which is otherwise fiddly for beginners.

What to do next

gh

What it can do
  • Sign in to GitHub safely through your web browser
  • Clone (download) repositories
  • Create new repositories
  • List and create issues
  • List, view and create pull requests
  • Open a repository's web page with one command
  • Set up git to use your GitHub login
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T).
  2. Type gh auth login and press Enter.
  3. Answer the questions with the arrow keys and Enter: choose GitHub.com, HTTPS, and say yes to using your GitHub credentials for git.
  4. Choose to log in with a web browser. gh shows a one-time code; copy it, press Enter, and paste the code into the GitHub page that opens.
  5. If Network protection asks whether gh may connect to the internet, allow it (it talks to github.com).
  6. Check it worked: gh auth status.
  7. Download a project: gh repo clone owner/repo-name (for example gh repo clone cli/cli). It creates a folder with the project inside.
Everyday tips
  • gh repo create makes a new repository and asks you simple questions.
  • gh repo view --web opens the current project's GitHub page in your browser.
  • gh issue list and gh pr list show open issues and pull requests in the current project folder.
  • gh pr create opens a pull request from your current branch.
  • Add --help to any gh command to see what it can do, for example gh pr --help.
Privacy & security
  • Logging in through the browser means you never type your GitHub password into the terminal.
  • Turn on two-factor authentication for your GitHub account on the GitHub website.
  • gh stores a login token on this laptop. Use gh auth logout if you hand the laptop to someone else.
  • Never paste access tokens or passwords into code you push to GitHub.
If something goes wrong
  • Browser does not open during login: copy the address gh shows and open it in your browser manually, then enter the code.
  • git push asks for a password: run gh auth setup-git so git uses your gh login.
  • 'not a git repository': many gh commands must be run inside a project folder. Use cd to move into it first.
  • Login fails: check that Network Monitor did not block gh from github.com.

Learn more: https://cli.github.com/manual/  ·  All apps

Development tools

fullAI & coding

A bundle of basic programming tools such as the gcc compiler, make and git.

Fedora's development-tools group installs the standard tools programmers expect, including gcc (a C compiler), make (runs build recipes) and git (tracks changes in code). On Windows you would usually get these by installing something like Visual Studio's build tools. Many other programs need these tools when you build or install them from source code.

Why it's here

They are needed to compile C programs, build some Python and Node.js packages, and use git for version control.

What to do next

git --version

What it can do
  • Compile C programs with gcc
  • Build projects that use a Makefile with make
  • Track changes in your code with git
  • Let pip and npm build packages that need compiling
  • Download and update projects from GitHub with git
  • Install with one command: sudo dnf group install development-tools
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and check the tools: gcc --version, make --version and git --version.
  2. Tell git who you are (needed once): git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com".
  3. Try C: create hello.c in VSCodium that prints a message, then compile it with gcc hello.c -o hello.
  4. Run your program: ./hello (the ./ means 'in this folder').
  5. Start tracking a project with git: cd into its folder and run git init.
  6. Save a snapshot of your work: git add . then git commit -m "describe the change".
Everyday tips
  • git status shows what has changed since your last commit. Use it often.
  • git log --oneline shows a short history of your commits.
  • In a folder with a Makefile, just type make to build.
  • If the tools seem missing, re-install with: sudo dnf group install development-tools
  • Use gh (GitHub CLI) together with git to work with GitHub.
Privacy & security
  • The email you set in git config appears in every commit you publish. GitHub offers a private 'noreply' email you can use instead.
  • Do not build and run code from unknown sources. Compiled programs run with your user's permissions.
  • Never commit passwords or keys into a git project.
If something goes wrong
  • 'Please tell me who you are' when committing: run the two git config commands from the getting started steps.
  • 'Permission denied' when running ./hello: make it runnable with chmod +x hello.
  • Building something fails with a missing header file (an error mentioning a .h file): you usually need the matching -devel package from dnf. Search with dnf search followed by the library name.
  • Typing hello instead of ./hello gives 'command not found': Linux does not run programs from the current folder unless you add ./ in front.

Learn more: https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/quick-docs/  ·  All apps

GNU Octave

fullAI & coding

A free program that runs most MATLAB scripts (.m files) unchanged.

Octave is an open-source numerical computing environment. It is installed from Fedora when you choose it on the "Study and coding tools" page.

Why it's here

A free stand-in for MATLAB for most coursework.

What to do next

octave in a terminal

What it can do
  • Runs most MATLAB .m scripts
  • Command window and plotting
  • Free and open source
Getting started
  1. Run "Study and coding tools" and choose GNU Octave (or Both).
  2. Type octave in a terminal, or open your .m file.
Everyday tips
  • Official MATLAB can be installed too; if it will not start on Fedora, run it inside an Ubuntu container with Distrobox (BoxBuddy).
  • Release your old Windows MATLAB licence at mathworks.com, My Account, Licenses.
Privacy & security
  • Everything runs on this computer.
If something goes wrong
  • A MATLAB toolbox is missing: Octave does not have every toolbox. Use the official MATLAB for those.

Learn more: https://octave.org/  ·  All apps

Android Studio

fullAI & coding

Google's Android development environment, with adb, fastboot and fast emulators ready.

Installed from the "Study and coding tools" page: Android Studio (about 3 GB on first start), adb and fastboot, a rule so your user can talk to any Android phone over USB, and membership of the kvm group for fast emulators.

Why it's here

For app-development coursework or tinkering with your phone.

What to do next

Android Studio (app launcher)

What it can do
  • Android Studio and the Android SDK
  • adb and fastboot
  • Fast emulator support (kvm)
Getting started
  1. Choose it on the "Study and coding tools" page.
  2. On the phone: Settings, Developer options, USB debugging.
  3. Plug the phone in and tap Allow.
  4. Log out and in once so the emulator speed-up applies.
Everyday tips
  • The first start downloads the Android SDK, which takes a while and needs the internet.
Privacy & security
  • USB debugging gives a plugged-in computer a lot of power over the phone. Only allow computers you trust, and switch it off afterwards.
If something goes wrong
  • The phone is not seen: use a data cable (some are charge-only) and tap Allow on the phone.

Learn more: https://developer.android.com/studio  ·  All apps

Python: uv and conda

fullAI & coding

uv is the modern, fast way to make Python projects; conda recreates your old Anaconda environments.

uv is installed on the full setup (uv init myproject, uv add numpy, uv run python script.py). If you used Anaconda, choose "Yes, install conda" on the study page: environments you exported on Windows are recreated, with Windows-only packages removed automatically.

Why it's here

Your Python work carries over without redoing the set-up by hand.

What to do next

uv or conda in a terminal

What it can do
  • uv projects and packages
  • conda environments recreated from .yml files
  • Windows-only packages dropped automatically
Getting started
  1. On Windows export with conda env export --from-history > name.yml (or use the backup).
  2. Run "Study and coding tools" and choose conda.
  3. Use an environment with conda activate NAME.
Everyday tips
  • secure-linux-migrate conda-envs FOLDER recreates environments from a folder.
Privacy & security
  • Packages come from public package servers; check what you install.
If something goes wrong
  • One environment fails: the window says how to export it again on Windows.

Learn more: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/  ·  All apps

Terminal tools

Terminal & Konsole basics

fullliteTerminal tools

Konsole is the terminal app, where you type commands to control the computer directly.

A terminal is a text window where you type commands, like Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows. Konsole is KDE's terminal app. You do not need it for daily use, but many guides and fixes use short terminal commands, and it is often the quickest way to install or repair things.

Why it's here

Knowing a handful of basics makes Linux far less scary and lets you follow help guides safely.

What to do next

Konsole (or press Ctrl+Alt+T)

What it can do
  • Open quickly with Ctrl+Alt+T
  • Run commands as administrator with sudo
  • Install system software with dnf
  • Install desktop apps with flatpak
  • Read built-in help with man and --help
  • Auto-complete names with Tab
  • Repeat earlier commands with the Up arrow
  • Open several tabs in one window
Getting started
  1. Press Ctrl+Alt+T to open Konsole. You can also search for Konsole in the app launcher.
  2. Try a safe command: type ls and press Enter to list the files in your Home folder. Type pwd to see which folder you are in.
  3. Move into a folder with cd, for example cd Documents. Type cd on its own to go back to your Home folder.
  4. Commands that change the system start with sudo (administrator rights). It asks for your password; nothing appears as you type, which is normal. Press Enter when done.
  5. Update everything: sudo dnf upgrade updates system software, and flatpak update updates Flatpak apps.
  6. Copy from the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+C and paste into it with Ctrl+Shift+V. Plain Ctrl+C does something else (see tips).
  7. Get help for any command: add --help (for example ls --help) or read the manual with man ls. Press q to leave the manual.
Everyday tips
  • Press Tab to auto-complete file, folder and command names. Press Tab twice to see all choices.
  • Press the Up arrow to bring back earlier commands, then Enter to run one again.
  • Ctrl+C stops the command that is running. It does not copy in the terminal.
  • dnf installs system software from Fedora (sudo dnf install <name>, dnf search <word>). flatpak installs sandboxed desktop apps, mostly from Flathub (flatpak install flathub <app-id>).
  • Ctrl+Shift+T opens a new tab. Type exit or close the window when you are done.
  • Commands and file names are case-sensitive: Documents and documents are different.
  • Type clear to tidy up a cluttered screen.
Privacy & security
  • Only use sudo when a command really needs it, and only for commands you understand or trust.
  • Be very careful copying commands from random websites, especially ones with sudo, rm (delete) or a pipe into sh or bash.
  • Files deleted with rm do not go to the Trash. They are gone.
  • Your sudo password is your normal login password. Never type it into anything other than sudo or a system prompt you expect.
If something goes wrong
  • Typing your password shows nothing: that is normal and safe. Just type it and press Enter.
  • Ctrl+V pastes nothing or a strange symbol: use Ctrl+Shift+V in Konsole, or right-click and choose Paste.
  • 'command not found': check the spelling and capitals, or the program may not be installed. Try dnf search with the name.
  • The terminal seems stuck: a command may still be running or waiting. Press Ctrl+C to stop it. If you see a ':' at the bottom (in man or less), press q.
  • 'Permission denied': the action may need sudo, or the file is not yours. Do not add sudo to everything blindly; check what you are doing first.

Learn more: https://docs.kde.org/stable5/en/konsole/konsole/  ·  All apps

btop

fullliteTerminal tools

btop is a colourful, live system monitor in the terminal, like a fancy Task Manager.

btop shows your CPU, memory, disks, network and running programs as live graphs inside the terminal. It is similar to Windows Task Manager but runs in Konsole. You can sort programs, search for them and stop ones that misbehave.

Why it's here

It is an easy, good-looking way to see what is slowing your computer down.

What to do next

btop

What it can do
  • Live graphs of CPU use per core
  • Memory and swap usage
  • Disk usage and activity
  • Network upload and download speed
  • List of running programs with sorting
  • Search and filter programs by name
  • Stop (kill) a stuck program
  • Works with mouse clicks as well as keys
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T), type btop and press Enter.
  2. Look at the boxes: CPU at the top, memory and disks, network, and the process (program) list.
  3. Use the Up and Down arrows (or the mouse) to select a program in the list.
  4. Press f to filter the list by name, type part of a name, then press Enter.
  5. Press Esc or m to open the menu, including Options for themes and settings.
  6. Press q to quit.
Everyday tips
  • Make the Konsole window bigger or full screen to see more.
  • Click the column names in the process list or use the sort options to sort by CPU or memory use.
  • Select a program and press k to kill (stop) it. Use this only for programs that are frozen.
  • Use btop when running local AI models to watch memory and CPU usage.
  • Many themes are available in the Options menu.
Privacy & security
  • btop only reads information from your own computer. It does not go online.
  • Do not kill programs you do not recognise; some are part of the system and stopping them can log you out or freeze the desktop.
If something goes wrong
  • The layout looks squashed or broken: make the terminal window larger.
  • Strange symbols instead of graphs: the terminal font may be missing characters. Konsole's default font normally works.
  • Cannot kill a program owned by the system: it needs administrator rights. Usually you should leave system programs alone.

Learn more: https://github.com/aristocratos/btop  ·  All apps

fastfetch

fullliteTerminal tools

fastfetch shows a neat summary of your computer and system next to a Fedora logo.

fastfetch prints information about your computer in the terminal: Fedora version, desktop, CPU, graphics, memory, disk and more. It is like the System Information page in Windows Settings, but in one quick, colourful screen. People often use it in screenshots to show off their setup.

Why it's here

It is the fastest way to answer 'what hardware and system do I have?', which is useful when asking for help online.

What to do next

fastfetch

What it can do
  • Show Fedora version and kernel
  • Show the desktop (KDE Plasma) and its version
  • Show CPU, graphics and memory
  • Show disk usage and uptime
  • Display a logo next to the information
  • Can be customised with a config file
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T).
  2. Type fastfetch and press Enter.
  3. Read the list on the right of the logo.
  4. When asking for help on a forum, copy the text with Ctrl+Shift+C and paste it into your post.
Everyday tips
  • fastfetch --help lists all options.
  • To customise it, fastfetch --gen-config creates a config file in your Home folder (under .config/fastfetch) that you can edit.
  • Use it to quickly check how much memory and disk space you have.
  • Before sharing a screenshot, check it does not show anything you consider private, such as your username or computer name.
Privacy & security
  • fastfetch only reads local information and does not go online by default.
  • The output can include your username and computer name. Remove them before posting publicly if you prefer.
If something goes wrong
  • Logo looks broken or misaligned: make the terminal window wider.
  • Graphics shows a generic name: integrated Radeon graphics may be listed by a technical name. That is normal.

Learn more: https://github.com/fastfetch-cli/fastfetch  ·  All apps

fzf

fullliteTerminal tools

fzf is a fuzzy finder: type a few letters and it instantly narrows down a list of files or anything else.

fzf is an interactive search tool for the terminal. You give it a list (by default, files under the current folder) and type a few letters, and it filters the list as you type, even if the letters are not next to each other. It is like the search box in the Windows Start menu, but for anything in the terminal.

Why it's here

It makes finding files and old commands much faster, and other tools such as zoxide can use it.

What to do next

fzf

What it can do
  • Search files under the current folder as you type
  • Fuzzy matching: letters do not need to be next to each other
  • Pick an item with arrow keys and Enter
  • Filter the output of other commands
  • Optional shortcut to search your command history (Ctrl+R)
  • Optional shortcuts to insert file paths and jump to folders
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and move to a folder with files, for example cd Documents.
  2. Type fzf and press Enter. A list of files appears.
  3. Start typing part of a file name. The list shrinks as you type.
  4. Use the Up and Down arrows to choose, then press Enter. fzf prints the chosen file's path.
  5. Press Esc or Ctrl+C to cancel.
  6. To open the chosen file in an editor in one go, try: nano "$(fzf)"
Everyday tips
  • Filter any list by sending it into fzf with a pipe (the | symbol), for example: ls | fzf
  • Add a single quote before a word for an exact match, for example 'report.
  • fzf can add handy shortcuts to the terminal, such as Ctrl+R to search past commands. If Ctrl+R does not show an fzf list, they are not enabled yet.
  • With recent fzf versions you can enable the shortcuts by adding this line to the end of the .bashrc file in your Home folder: eval "$(fzf --bash)". Then open a new terminal.
  • zoxide's zi command uses fzf to let you pick a folder from a list.
Privacy & security
  • fzf only works with information on your own computer and does not go online.
  • Your command history may contain sensitive text you typed. Be careful when screen-sharing a history search.
If something goes wrong
  • Ctrl+R shows the normal history search, not fzf: the key bindings are not enabled. Add the eval line from the tips to .bashrc and open a new terminal.
  • 'unknown option: --bash': your fzf version is older. Look in the fzf package's shell folder (for example /usr/share/fzf/shell) for a key-bindings.bash file to source instead, or skip the shortcuts.
  • fzf is slow in your Home folder: it is listing many thousands of files. Move into a smaller folder first.

Learn more: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf  ·  All apps

ripgrep

fullliteTerminal tools

ripgrep (command rg) searches inside files for words or text, very quickly.

ripgrep looks through all the files in a folder and its subfolders and shows every line that contains your search text. It is like the Find in Files feature of a code editor, or Windows search for file contents, but much faster. The command is rg.

Why it's here

It is the quickest way to answer 'which file did I write that in?' for notes, code and config files.

What to do next

rg

What it can do
  • Search text inside all files in a folder tree
  • Show file names and line numbers for each match
  • Ignore case with -i
  • List only file names that match with -l
  • Search only certain file types
  • Skips hidden files and files ignored by git by default
  • Very fast, even on large folders
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T) and move to the folder you want to search, for example cd Documents.
  2. Search for a word: rg holiday
  3. Results show the file name, the line number and the matching line.
  4. Ignore upper and lower case: rg -i holiday
  5. Show only the names of matching files: rg -l holiday
  6. Use quotes for phrases with spaces: rg "meeting notes"
Everyday tips
  • Search a specific folder without moving there: rg holiday ~/Documents (the ~ means your Home folder).
  • Search only certain file types, for example only Python files: rg -t py import
  • Hidden files are skipped by default. Add --hidden to include them.
  • Add -uu to also search files that would normally be ignored (such as those listed in .gitignore).
  • rg searches text files. It does not search inside Word documents or PDFs.
Privacy & security
  • ripgrep only reads files on your computer and does not go online.
  • Search results can show private text from your files. Be careful when screen-sharing.
If something goes wrong
  • 'rg: command not found' or typing ripgrep fails: the command is rg, not ripgrep.
  • Expected matches are missing: the files may be hidden or ignored. Try rg --hidden or rg -uu.
  • Too many results: search in a smaller folder, add more words, or use -l to see just file names.

Learn more: https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep  ·  All apps

bat

fullliteTerminal tools

bat shows the contents of a file in the terminal with colours and line numbers.

bat is a nicer version of the classic cat command, which prints a file's contents in the terminal. bat adds syntax highlighting (colours for code and config files), line numbers and scrolling for long files. It is like a quick read-only preview of a text file.

Why it's here

It makes reading code, config files and logs in the terminal much easier on the eyes.

What to do next

bat

What it can do
  • Show a file with colours for many languages
  • Line numbers and a header with the file name
  • Scroll through long files automatically
  • Show changes in files tracked by git
  • Plain mode for simple output
  • Many colour themes
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T).
  2. Show a file: bat followed by the file name, for example bat ~/.bashrc
  3. For long files, scroll with the arrow keys or Page Up/Page Down.
  4. Press q to quit the scrolling view.
  5. Try it on a code file to see the colours.
Everyday tips
  • bat -p (plain) hides line numbers and the header, handy for copying text.
  • bat --paging=never prints the whole file without the scrolling view.
  • bat -l followed by a language name forces the colours for that language, for example bat -l json for a file without an extension.
  • bat --list-themes shows the available colour themes.
  • bat is only for reading. Use an editor such as nano or VSCodium to change files.
Privacy & security
  • bat only reads files on your computer and does not go online.
  • Viewing system log or config files may need sudo. Only use sudo when necessary.
If something goes wrong
  • Instructions online say batcat: that is the name on Debian and Ubuntu. On Fedora the command is bat.
  • Stuck in the scrolling view: press q to get back to the prompt.
  • No colours for a file: bat may not recognise the type. Use -l with the language name.

Learn more: https://github.com/sharkdp/bat  ·  All apps

zoxide

fullliteTerminal tools

zoxide is a smarter cd: type z and part of a folder name to jump straight there.

Normally you move between folders with cd and the full path. zoxide remembers the folders you visit most, so you can jump to one by typing z and a few letters of its name. It is like a 'recent folders' list for the terminal.

Why it's here

It saves lots of typing for people who move around folders in the terminal often.

What to do next

z <folder>

What it can do
  • Jump to a folder with z and part of its name
  • Learns your most-used folders automatically
  • Pick from matching folders interactively with zi (uses fzf)
  • Still works like cd with full paths
  • Show where a name would jump to with zoxide query
  • Go up a folder or home just like cd
Getting started
  1. zoxide needs one line in your terminal settings file. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T).
  2. Check if it is already set up: grep zoxide ~/.bashrc. If you see a line containing zoxide init bash, skip the next step.
  3. Add the line to the end of .bashrc: echo 'eval "$(zoxide init bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc (the >> adds text to the end of the file without erasing it).
  4. Close Konsole and open it again so the change takes effect.
  5. Visit folders normally at first, for example z ~/Documents/Projects. zoxide remembers them.
  6. Later, just type z proj to jump back to Projects from anywhere.
Everyday tips
  • z with two words narrows it down, for example z doc proj.
  • zi opens an interactive list of matching folders (needs fzf, which is installed).
  • z .. goes up one folder, just like cd ..
  • z on its own goes to your Home folder.
  • zoxide query proj shows which folder z proj would go to, without moving.
Privacy & security
  • zoxide stores a list of folders you visit on your own computer. It does not go online.
  • Only add the documented init line to .bashrc. Do not paste unknown lines into it.
If something goes wrong
  • 'z: command not found': the init line is missing from ~/.bashrc, or you have not opened a new terminal since adding it.
  • z jumps to the wrong folder: use more of the name, or use zi to choose from a list.
  • z cannot find a folder you never visited: zoxide only knows folders you have been to. Use the full path once and it will remember.
  • You added the line twice: open .bashrc in a text editor and delete the extra copy.

Learn more: https://github.com/ajeetdsouza/zoxide  ·  All apps

htop

fullliteTerminal tools

htop is a simple, classic terminal task manager showing running programs and resource use.

htop lists running programs with their CPU and memory use, with bars at the top showing how busy each CPU core is. It is like the Processes tab of Windows Task Manager. It is lighter and simpler than btop and is available on almost every Linux system.

Why it's here

It is a reliable, lightweight way to find and stop programs that slow the computer down, and it works well on older PCs.

What to do next

htop

What it can do
  • Live CPU bars for each core
  • Memory and swap usage bars
  • List of running programs
  • Sort by CPU, memory and more
  • Search and filter programs
  • Tree view showing which program started which
  • Stop (kill) a stuck program
  • Mouse support
Getting started
  1. Open Konsole (Ctrl+Alt+T), type htop and press Enter.
  2. Look at the bars at the top for CPU and memory use.
  3. The menu along the bottom shows what the F keys do.
  4. Press F6 to choose how to sort, for example by CPU% or MEM%.
  5. Press F3 to search for a program by name.
  6. Press F10 or q to quit.
Everyday tips
  • F4 filters the list to show only matching programs.
  • F5 switches to tree view to see which programs belong together.
  • Select a program and press F9 to kill (stop) it. Choose the default signal and press Enter.
  • F2 opens setup, where you can change what is shown.
  • Clicking column headers with the mouse also changes sorting.
Privacy & security
  • htop only reads information from your own computer and does not go online.
  • Avoid killing system programs you do not recognise.
If something goes wrong
  • F keys do nothing: on some laptops you must hold the Fn key. You can also click the menu labels at the bottom with the mouse.
  • Cannot kill some programs: they belong to the system and need sudo. Usually leave them alone.
  • Memory looks almost full: Linux uses spare memory as a cache. Look at the green part of the memory bar for memory really used by programs.

Learn more: https://htop.dev  ·  All apps

Rescue tools (USB stick)

SystemRescue

fullliteRescue tools (USB stick)

SystemRescue is a complete repair system that starts from the USB stick when your computer will not boot.

SystemRescue is a small Linux system that runs from the USB stick without touching your installed system. It includes tools to repair disks, resize partitions, recover deleted files and fix a broken boot. It is similar to a Windows recovery or repair USB, but with many more tools.

Why it's here

If Fedora will not start, or a disk has problems, you can boot SystemRescue to rescue your files or repair the system.

What to do next

Boot from the USB stick and choose SystemRescue in its boot menu

What it can do
  • Starts from USB without changing your installed system
  • GParted for viewing and resizing partitions
  • TestDisk to recover lost partitions
  • PhotoRec to recover deleted photos and files
  • fsck to check and repair file systems
  • Read and copy files from Windows (NTFS) disks
  • chroot into your installed system to repair it (advanced)
  • Optional graphical desktop with a web browser
Getting started
  1. Plug in the USB stick and turn the computer on (or restart it).
  2. Press the boot menu key straight away. It is often F12, F9 or Esc depending on the maker; the start-up screen usually shows it.
  3. Choose the USB stick, then pick SystemRescue from the USB stick's menu.
  4. In SystemRescue's own menu, pick the default option, or the one that starts the graphical environment if offered.
  5. If you land at a text prompt, type startx and press Enter to get a simple desktop.
  6. Open the tool you need from the desktop menu or terminal, for example gparted to look at disks.
  7. When finished, shut down properly (type poweroff), then remove the USB stick.
  8. For guided repairs, mount the stick and run bash /mnt/usb/linux-setup/rescue/secure-linux-rescue.sh (see the chapter "My computer is broken: how do I fix it?").
Everyday tips
  • First rescue your files: plug in an external drive and copy important files to it before trying repairs.
  • In GParted, look at sizes and labels to work out which disk is which before changing anything.
  • PhotoRec can recover deleted files, but always save recovered files to a different drive, never the same one.
  • Fedora usually uses the Btrfs file system. If the disk is encrypted, you must unlock it first (cryptsetup open) before you can mount it.
  • Nothing you do in SystemRescue is saved after shutdown unless you save it to a disk.
  • If you are unsure, take photos of the screen and ask for help before making changes.
Privacy & security
  • SystemRescue has full access to all disks, so keep the USB stick somewhere safe.
  • Encrypted disks stay locked unless you enter the password, which protects your data if the stick is lost.
  • Wrong commands here can erase data. Read carefully before confirming anything that writes to a disk.
If something goes wrong
  • The computer ignores the USB stick: use the boot menu key, check the stick is fully inserted, or try another USB port.
  • USB stick will not start with a security error: Secure Boot may block some rescue tools. You may need to temporarily turn off Secure Boot in the BIOS/UEFI settings, then turn it back on afterwards.
  • Cannot see your files on the Fedora disk: the disk may be encrypted or use Btrfs subvolumes. Unlock it first, then look inside the root and home subvolumes.
  • Changes to partitions in GParted are only made when you click Apply. Check everything before you do.

Learn more: https://www.system-rescue.org  ·  All apps

Clonezilla

fullliteRescue tools (USB stick)

Clonezilla makes a complete backup image of a disk, or copies one disk to another.

Clonezilla starts from the USB stick and copies a whole disk or partition. It can save an image (a backup file of the whole disk) to another drive, or copy one disk directly onto another. It is like Macrium Reflect or Acronis True Image on Windows, with a text-based menu.

Why it's here

A full disk image lets you put the whole laptop back exactly as it was after a disaster or before a risky change.

What to do next

Boot from the USB stick and choose Clonezilla in its boot menu

What it can do
  • Save a whole disk as an image to another drive (device-image)
  • Restore a disk from a saved image
  • Clone one disk directly to another (device-device)
  • Back up or restore single partitions
  • Only copies used space on supported file systems, saving time
  • Check that an image can be restored
Getting started
  1. Plug in the USB stick and an external drive with enough free space for the backup.
  2. Start the computer from the USB stick (use the boot menu key, often F12, F9 or Esc) and choose Clonezilla.
  3. Choose your language and keyboard, then Start Clonezilla.
  4. Choose device-image to save a backup file to another drive, or device-device to copy straight onto another disk.
  5. For device-image, pick local_dev and choose the external drive where the image will be saved.
  6. Choose Beginner mode, then savedisk to back up a whole disk (or restoredisk to restore one).
  7. Carefully choose the source disk, check the summary, and confirm. Wait until it says it has finished.
Everyday tips
  • Write down the size and model of each disk before you start, so you can recognise them in the menus.
  • Unplug any drives you do not need, so there is less chance of picking the wrong one.
  • Give your images clear names that include the date.
  • When offered, let Clonezilla check the saved image so you know it can be restored.
  • Make a fresh image after big changes, and keep at least one older image too.
  • Repair This Computer also has "Back up or clone a whole drive" if you prefer a guided straight copy with safety checks.
Privacy & security
  • A disk image contains everything on the disk. Store the backup drive safely.
  • If the laptop disk is encrypted, the image is a copy of the encrypted data and still needs your password to use.
  • Restoring an image or cloning overwrites the target disk completely. Everything on it is erased.
If something goes wrong
  • Picking the wrong target disk erases it. Read the names, sizes and models twice before confirming. When restoring or cloning, the target is the disk that gets overwritten.
  • Target disk too small: for disk-to-disk cloning, the target usually needs to be at least as big as the source.
  • Backup drive not listed: plug it in before choosing local_dev, then follow the prompt to rescan.
  • The USB stick will not boot: try another USB port, or check Secure Boot settings in the BIOS/UEFI.

Learn more: https://clonezilla.org  ·  All apps

Memtest86+

fullliteRescue tools (USB stick)

Memtest86+ tests your computer's memory (RAM) for faults.

Memtest86+ starts from the USB stick and checks every part of your RAM by writing and reading test patterns. It is like Windows Memory Diagnostic, but more thorough. Faulty RAM can cause random crashes, freezes and corrupted files.

Why it's here

When a computer crashes or freezes for no clear reason, testing the memory is one of the first checks to rule out a hardware fault.

What to do next

Boot from the USB stick and choose Memtest86+ in its boot menu

What it can do
  • Tests all installed RAM
  • Runs without any operating system
  • Shows a live count of passes and errors
  • Detects faults that cause random crashes
  • Runs repeatedly until you stop it
  • Shows details of the CPU and memory it found
Getting started
  1. Plug in the USB stick and restart the computer.
  2. Press the boot menu key (often F12, F9 or Esc), choose the USB stick, then choose Memtest86+.
  3. The test starts by itself. You do not need to press anything.
  4. Let it run several full passes. Watch the Pass counter and the Errors counter.
  5. With 16 GB of RAM, one pass can take a long time, so running it overnight is a good idea.
  6. When finished, press Esc to exit and restart the computer, then remove the USB stick.
Everyday tips
  • Plug the laptop into power before a long test.
  • Run at least two to four full passes for a trustworthy result.
  • Zero errors after several passes means the RAM is very likely fine.
  • Take a photo of the screen if errors appear, to show to a repair shop or for warranty claims.
  • The Hardware Health Check does only a quick memory pass; Memtest86+ is the thorough test.
Privacy & security
  • Memtest86+ only tests memory. It does not read or change your files or disks.
  • Nothing goes online.
If something goes wrong
  • Any error at all means the RAM is faulty or unstable. If the RAM can be replaced, replace it; if it is soldered (common in thin laptops), contact the maker or a repair shop.
  • It will not start with a security error: Secure Boot may need to be turned off temporarily in the BIOS/UEFI settings. Turn it back on afterwards.
  • The test seems to run forever: that is normal. It repeats until you stop it. Check the pass count and press Esc when done.

Learn more: https://www.memtest.org  ·  All apps

Smart home

Home Assistant (window)

fullSmart home

Opens your Home Assistant smart-home dashboard in its own window, plus lessons and a security check.

Home Assistant is free software on a home server that joins your smart-home gadgets in one place. This menu entry opens its web page in a window. Related entries: Security check (grade A to F), Learn Home Assistant, and Is it working? (status).

Why it's here

It makes the smart home reachable from your laptop without any company's cloud.

What to do next

Home Assistant (app launcher); secure-linux-ha open in a terminal

What it can do
  • Opens your dashboard
  • Security check graded A to F
  • Eight beginner lessons
  • Practice copy on this laptop
  • Ready-made automations
Getting started
  1. Open Home Assistant from the app launcher.
  2. First time: create the owner account with a long password from Bitwarden.
  3. Run the security check and aim for a B or better.
Everyday tips
  • Set the address once: secure-linux-choice set ha_url http://10.0.30.50:8123.
  • secure-linux-ha doctor explains any problem.
Privacy & security
  • Never forward a router port for Home Assistant. See "Keep your smart home safe".
If something goes wrong
  • "Can't connect": is the server on, and are you on your home Wi-Fi or Meshnet? Run secure-linux-ha doctor.

hass-cli and Butler

fullSmart home

Optional extras for Home Assistant: a command-line tool and a native dashboard window.

hass-cli talks to Home Assistant from the terminal. Butler (from Flathub) is an optional native window for a dashboard; it does not provide location, notifications or sensors, which is what the phone app is for.

Why it's here

For people who like the terminal or want the dashboard in a separate window.

What to do next

hass-cli (terminal), Butler (app launcher)

What it can do
  • hass-cli state list and service calls
  • Butler dashboard window
  • esphome tool when switched on (choice ha_esphome)
Getting started
  1. Set HASS_SERVER and HASS_TOKEN in the environment (do not type the token on a command line you keep in history).
  2. Run hass-cli state list.
Everyday tips
  • There is no official Home Assistant desktop app for Linux; the web window is the trustworthy option.
Privacy & security
  • A token is a password that skips two-step login. Create one only when needed and delete it afterwards.
If something goes wrong
  • Butler asks for the address on first run (not verified here).

Review and confirm the computer's protection settings in one native window.

Control Centre manages firewall, OpenSnitch, DNS, VPN, updates, ClamAV, USBGuard, Fail2ban, screen lock and auditd, with Secure Boot/encryption information and links to Flatseal and Home & Server Helper.

Why it's here

It makes the Recommended, Stricter and Custom protection choices visible and verifiable.

What to do next

Secure Linux Control Centre, or secure-linux-control-center

What it can do
  • Apply a reviewed protection preset
  • Change individual controls
  • Verify results and roll back reversible earlier changes where possible
Getting started
  1. Choose Recommended, Stricter or Custom.
  2. Read the exact change list and choose Confirm.
  3. Read the verification result before closing.
Everyday tips
  • Custom preserves current settings until you tick or untick something.
  • DNS off is a 15-minute pause, not a permanent switch.
Privacy & security
  • USBGuard is never preselected.
  • Auditd can be enabled but not disabled here.
  • Secure Boot and disk encryption are informational.
If something goes wrong
  • A partial or failed rollback is reported; do not ignore it or assume every setting returned to its old value.

What to do next

My Computer Activity, or secure-linux-activity

What it can do

Privacy & security

Secure Linux USB Creator and USB Fixer

fullliteSecure Linux tools

Create verified installer copies and recover a failing USB image-first.

USB Creator supports masters, exact raw clones and portable Ventoy/file-tree copies. USB Fixer diagnoses, images, recovers and repairs a disposable copy.

Why it's here

It distinguishes verified output from interrupted writes and protects the original during repair.

What to do next

Linux USB Installer Creator - Turn any blank USB into a Linux installer, or Secure Linux USB Fixer

What it can do
  • Calculate required USB capacity
  • Clone a raw master or make a portable copy
  • Verify output
  • Capture and recover a USB image
Getting started
  1. Identify the exact removable disk and serial/WWN.
  2. Choose clone or portable copy and review the calculated size.
  3. Wait for verification before relying on the result.
Everyday tips
  • On a larger exact-clone target, only the master-sized beginning is overwritten and verified; the tail may retain old data.
Privacy & security
  • Erase confirmation is ERASE SERIAL-OR-WWN and has no timeout.
  • Fixed disks, partitions and the system disk are refused by formatting.
If something goes wrong
  • Interrupted output is incomplete and not verified.
  • Formatting is destructive and is not secure erase.
